In winter, **waxwings** sometimes come from the north and feed almost only on berries. The edible dormouse also likes to eat fruit, nuts and beechnuts.

Many fruits are red, black or orange so that animals can see them easily. The plant attracts the animals with sweet **fruit flesh** and gets help in spreading its seeds in return. This is an example of co-operation for mutual benefit, which is called **symbiosis**. If frugivores disappear, some trees can hardly reproduce any more.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that feeds mainly on fruit.
A plant-eater.
How seeds get from the parent plant to a new place.
Living together in which both sides gain an advantage.

gewusst: Some flying foxes have a wingspan of over a metre and still eat only fruit and nectar.
Some tree seeds germinate better after passing through an animal's gut.

teile.einleitung: The red squirrel is a nimble rodent with a bushy tail that lives in woods, parks and gardens. It climbs and leaps skilfully from branch to branch. In autumn it hides nuts and seeds and, without knowing it, helps to plant new trees.
wichtigste: The red squirrel is a rodent from the squirrel family (Sciuridae).
Its coat is often red-brown, but can also be dark brown to almost black.
It is active in the daytime, especially in the morning and evening.
In autumn it hides nuts and seeds as a winter store.
Its front gnawing teeth keep growing throughout its life.
Forgotten hiding places let new trees grow, which is why it is important for the forest.
When in danger it flees up a tree in a flash.

abschnitte.text: A red squirrel is about 20 to 25 centimetres long without the tail and weighs around 200 to 400 grams. The bushy **tail** is almost as long as the body and serves when leaping as a rudder and for balance. The coat is often red-brown, and the belly is pale. In winter long tufts of hair grow on its ears, which are called **ear tufts**.

Red squirrels live in coniferous woods, mixed woods, parks and large gardens in almost the whole of Europe and parts of Asia. They build ball-shaped nests of twigs, moss and leaves high up in the trees. Such a nest is called a **drey** (“Kobel”). A squirrel often has several dreys, between which it switches.

Red squirrels eat nuts, acorns, beechnuts, seeds from fir cones, berries, mushrooms and sometimes insects or birds' eggs. They look for their food in the trees and also on the forest floor. In autumn they bury many stores in the ground, which they later often find again with their fine nose. What they forget can germinate, so they spread **seeds** and let new trees grow. When the stores are used up in winter, they nibble at buds and bark.

Red squirrels do not hibernate properly, but simply rest longer in the drey when it is cold. On the ground they move forward with small **hops**, and in the trees they leap skilfully from branch to branch. Their sharp claws allow them even to climb down a trunk head first. When a squirrel is excited, it twitches its tail back and forth and scolds with loud calls.

A female has young once or twice a year, usually 3 to 5 at a time. The young are born naked and blind in the drey. After about eight to ten weeks they are independent. Enemies such as the **pine marten**, the goshawk or cats catch many young squirrels, which is why in nature they usually live only a few years.

In Switzerland the red squirrel is widespread, from the lowlands up to the mountain forests. In many cities such as Zurich or Bern you can watch it well in parks. A worry is the **grey squirrel**, introduced from North America, which in Great Britain and northern Italy is displacing the native red squirrel. Experts are therefore watching closely whether it spreads as far as Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mammal with gnawing teeth that grow constantly, for example a mouse or a beaver.
The ball-shaped nest of the squirrel in the trees.
Long tufts of hair on the ears that grow in winter.
Food that an animal collects in autumn so as to have enough to eat in winter.

gewusst: A squirrel can make several thousand hiding places in a year.
Squirrels can climb down a tree trunk head first because they can turn their hind feet backwards.
Black squirrels are also quite normal squirrels, only with darker fur.

teile.einleitung: Lacewings are delicate, mostly green insects with large, transparent wings and golden shining eyes. Their larvae are voracious hunters that eat so many aphids that they are called aphid lions. That is why lacewings are very welcome beneficial insects in the garden.
wichtigste: Lacewings are delicate insects with wings veined like a net.
Many species are green and have golden shining eyes.
Their larvae hunt aphids with pincer-like jaws.
Because of their hunger, the larvae are also called aphid lions.
Lacewings lay their eggs on thin stalks.
In organic gardens they are encouraged as beneficial insects, for example with insect hotels.
Some lacewings spend the winter in houses and turn brownish as they do so.

abschnitte.text: **Lacewings** belong to the insect order of the **net-winged insects**. They are about one to two centimetres long and have a slim, usually pale green body. Their four wings are transparent, finely veined and, at rest, folded like a roof over the body. The golden shining eyes are striking, which is why they are also called goldeyes. In Switzerland the **common green lacewing** is especially frequent.

The larvae look quite different from the adults. They are elongated, mobile and have large, **pincer-like jaws** at the front. With these they seize aphids, pierce them and suck them dry. A single larva can eat hundreds of aphids during its development. Because of this voraciousness, they are called **aphid lions**.

The female lays her eggs singly on thin, hair-fine **stalks**, often on leaves near aphid colonies. The stalks protect the eggs from being eaten by ants or by their own siblings. After hatching, the larva eats for about two to three weeks and moults several times. Then it spins a small, round cocoon and pupates. From this the adult lacewing finally emerges.

Adult common green lacewings eat mainly flower pollen, nectar and **honeydew**, the sweet liquid that aphids give off. Other species of lacewing also eat aphids as adults. Lacewings are active mainly at dusk and at night. Some species can detect the ultrasound calls of bats with their wings. Then they drop in a flash so as not to be eaten.

Because the larvae eat so many aphids, lacewings are regarded as important **beneficial insects**. Gardeners and farmers even buy lacewing larvae to use them against pests in greenhouses. This is called **biological pest control**. In an organic garden you help lacewings with flower meadows, insect hotels and special lacewing boxes. In autumn the adults often look for shelter in houses, attics or garden sheds, where they should be left in peace to spend the winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of insects with finely veined, net-like wings.
The young form of an insect, which often looks quite different from the adult.
A sweet liquid that aphids give off.
An animal that eats pests and so helps people.

gewusst: Some lacewing larvae camouflage themselves by piling the empty skins of their prey on their backs.
The green common lacewing turns yellowish to brownish in winter and green again in spring.
With an organ in their wings, lacewings can hear the calls of hunting bats.

teile.einleitung: Colour vision is the ability to perceive light of different wavelengths as different colours. People and animals see colours in quite different ways. Some animals see fewer colours than we do, while others even see colours that are invisible to us.
wichtigste: Colours are made in the brain from light of different wavelengths.
The sense cells in the retina called cones are responsible for colour vision.
Humans have three kinds of cone, for red, green and blue.
Dogs see fewer colours than humans, mainly shades of blue and yellow.
Many birds and insects can see ultraviolet light.
About eight per cent of men have red-green colour vision deficiency.

abschnitte.text: Light consists of waves of different **wavelengths**. White sunlight contains all the colours, which you can see in a rainbow. An object looks red because it mainly reflects red light and swallows up the other colours. It is the brain that turns these light signals into the impression of a colour.

In the **retina** at the back of the eye there are two kinds of sense cell. The **rods** are very sensitive to light but do not see colours, which is why everything looks grey at night. The **cones** need more light and are responsible for colour vision. Humans have three kinds of cone, which respond mainly to red, green and blue light. From the mixture of their signals, millions of shades arise.

Dogs and cats have only two kinds of cone and see mainly shades of blue and yellow. They find it hard to tell red and green apart. Many birds have four kinds of cone and can also see **ultraviolet light**. Bees also see UV light, but cannot see red. The mantis shrimp has an especially large number of kinds of light-sensing cell, but still does not necessarily see more colours.

With colours, animals recognise ripe fruit, poisonous animals or a suitable mate. Many flowers have UV patterns that only insects see and that show them the way to the nectar. For people, colours help in everyday life, for example with traffic lights and warning signs. A bull in a bullfight, by the way, does not react to the red colour of the cloth, but to its **movement**.

If one kind of cone is missing or works differently, this is called **colour vision deficiency**. The most common is red-green deficiency, which affects about eight per cent of men but only very few women. The English scientist John Dalton described his own colour blindness in 1794. In the 19th century, Thomas Young and Hermann von Helmholtz explained colour vision with three primary colours.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sense cells in the retina with which we see colours.
Sense cells that tell light from dark in dim light.
The thin layer at the back of the eye that turns light into nerve signals.
Light that is invisible to people but not to many animals.

gewusst: At night, humans see almost no colours, because then only the rods are working.
Some birds see patterns on the feathers of others of their kind that are invisible to us.
After John Dalton, colour blindness is sometimes also called daltonism.

teile.einleitung: The Fox and the Raven is an ancient fable in which a clever fox tricks a raven out of its piece of cheese with flattery. In a few sentences it shows that you should be careful when someone flatters you too much.
wichtigste: The Fox and the Raven is a famous fable.
In it a clever fox tricks a raven out of its piece of cheese.
The fable goes back to the Greek writer Aesop.
The Frenchman Jean de La Fontaine wrote a well known version in the 17th century.
The lesson is that you should not trust flatterers.
In fables animals act like humans and stand for certain characteristics.
In real life too, foxes and ravens are regarded as very clever.

abschnitte.text: A raven sits on a branch holding a piece of **cheese** in its beak. A hungry fox comes by and praises the raven's beautiful plumage. Then he says that such a splendid bird surely has a wonderful voice too. Flattered, the raven opens its beak to caw, and the cheese falls down. The fox snaps it up and runs away.

At the end of a fable there is often a **moral**, that is a lesson. Here it is: anyone who listens too much to **flatterers** is easily tricked. The fox does not praise the raven honestly, but only because he wants something from it. That is true today too, for example with advertising or with strangers on the internet who pay you many compliments.

The fable is attributed to the Greek writer **Aesop**, who probably lived in the 6th century BC. Around 2,000 years later the Frenchman **Jean de La Fontaine** wrote a version in verse in 1668 that every child in France knows. The German writer Gotthold Ephraim Lessing retold the fable: in his version the meat that the fox snatches is poisoned. So in Lessing the cunning flatterer is punished as well.

A **fable** is a short story in which animals speak and act like humans. Each animal stands for a characteristic: the fox is cunning, the lion strong, the donkey stubborn. In this way human faults can be shown without pointing the finger at a particular person. Fables are gladly read at school because they are short and have a clear lesson.

The **red fox** and the common **raven** both live in Switzerland. The red fox is very adaptable and occurs from the Central Plateau to the mountains and even in towns. Ravens are the largest of the crow family and are among the cleverest birds of all. They can solve problems and remember where they have hidden food. In real life, then, a raven would probably not be so easy to outwit.

begriffe.erklaerung: A short story in which animals act like humans and which has a lesson.
The lesson that you are meant to draw from a story.
Someone who praises too much in order to get something.
The largest bird of the crow family, completely black and very clever.

gewusst: In the French version by La Fontaine it is a corbeau, which can mean raven or crow.
In very many fables and fairy tales the fox is the clever trickster.
Ravens can imitate noises and even human words.

teile.einleitung: Drones are the male bees in a honey bee colony. They do not collect honey and have no sting, but they have an important task: they mate with young queens. In autumn they are often driven out of the hive.
wichtigste: Drones are the male honey bees.
Their main task is mating with a young queen.
Drones arise from unfertilised eggs.
They are bigger and stouter than workers and have huge eyes.
Drones have no sting and so cannot sting.
In summer a colony has a few hundred to a few thousand drones.
In late summer or autumn the drones are driven out of the hive.

abschnitte.text: Drones are clearly **stouter** than the workers and about 15 to 17 millimetres long. Striking are their large **compound eyes**, which meet at the top of the head. With these they can spot the queen well in flight. They have no sting, no pollen baskets and cannot make wax.

The queen lays **unfertilised eggs** in larger comb cells, and from these drones develop. From fertilised eggs, by contrast, female bees arise. A drone therefore has a mother but no father. Development from egg to finished drone takes about 24 days, longer than in workers and queen.

On warm afternoons drones fly to so called **drone congregation areas**, where thousands of males from different colonies meet. A young queen also comes there on her **nuptial flight**. The fastest drones mate with her in the air. After mating the drone dies. The queen stores the sperm and uses it to lay eggs for years.

In the hive, drones often let the workers feed them or help themselves to honey from the combs. They do not help with collecting, building or cleaning. Some researchers suppose that with their body warmth they warm the brood a little. Drones are often also allowed to fly into other bees' hives.

When hardly any flowers are in bloom in late summer, the drones are no longer needed. The workers no longer feed them and drag them out of the hive. This process is called the **drone massacre**. Outside, the drones starve or freeze, and in this way the colony saves food for the winter.

In Switzerland beekeepers keep about 170,000 bee colonies (as of around 2023). Many cut part of the drone brood out of the combs. The reason is the **varroa mite**, a dangerous parasite that especially likes to multiply in drone cells. In this way the beekeepers can reduce the number of mites.

begriffe.erklaerung: A male honey bee.
The only bee in the colony that lays eggs.
A female bee that collects, builds, cleans and looks after the brood.
A small parasite that weakens bees and transmits diseases.

gewusst: Unmanned aircraft are called drones because remote controlled target aircraft were given this name early on, after the humming male bees.
A drone has no father, but it does have a grandfather.
Drone congregation areas are often used in the same place for many years.

teile.einleitung: The German Giant is one of the largest rabbit breeds in the world. A fully grown animal can become as heavy as a small dog and is nevertheless usually very calm and good natured.
wichtigste: The German Giant is a well known, especially large rabbit breed.
Adult animals usually weigh over 6 kilograms, and many even clearly more.
The breed descends from the Belgian Giant and was bred further in Germany.
It comes in many colours, for example grey, black, blue and white.
German Giants are regarded as calm and good natured.
Because of their size they need especially much space.
Like all rabbits, they are group animals and should never live alone.

abschnitte.text: The German Giant has a long, powerful body, a large head and long, upright **ears**. Fully grown animals usually weigh between 6 and 10 kilograms, a few even more. By comparison, many other domestic rabbits weigh only 2 to 4 kilograms. The coat is short and dense and comes in colours such as **wild grey**, black, blue, white or steel grey.

The German Giant descends from the **Belgian Giant**, which was bred in Flanders in Belgium. Breeders in Germany crossed these animals and always chose the largest ones. In this way a breed of its own arose with fixed characteristics, which are described in a standard. All domestic rabbits originally descend from the **wild rabbit**, which comes from Spain and southern France.

German Giants are regarded as **calm, relaxed and trusting**. They often like to be stroked, but, like all rabbits, do not like to be picked up. Because of their weight, the back and hind legs have to be well supported when carrying them. Children should therefore stroke the heavy animals on the ground instead.

A rabbit this big needs a **large enclosure** with plenty of room to run, in which it can hop and stand fully upright. Normal rabbit cages from the pet shop are far too small. Rabbits are **group animals** and should be kept at least in pairs. They eat mainly hay, grass, herbs and vegetables, and their teeth keep growing throughout their lives and are worn down by chewing.

In Switzerland there are many small animal breeders who show rabbits at **exhibitions**. There experts judge how well an animal matches the breed standard, for example in body shape, coat and weight. The German Giant is always an eye catcher at such shows because of its size. Large breeds usually do not live as long as small ones, and often they reach about six to eight years.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of domestic animals with the same, deliberately bred characteristics.
An exact description of how an animal of a breed should look.
The animal group to which rabbits and hares belong, and they are not rodents.
The wild ancestor of all domestic rabbits.

gewusst: Rabbits are not rodents, but belong to the lagomorphs.
A large German Giant can weigh more than a miniature dachshund.
The teeth of rabbits keep growing their whole life long.

teile.einleitung: Dian Fossey was an American researcher who for almost two decades observed and protected mountain gorillas in Rwanda. Through her work the world learned that gorillas are peaceful, social animals and not dangerous monsters.
wichtigste: Dian Fossey was a researcher who worked especially hard for the protection of mountain gorillas.
She was born in 1932 in San Francisco in the USA.
In 1967 she founded the Karisoke research station in Rwanda.
For years she lived with the gorillas in the mountain forests of the Virunga volcanoes.
Her book Gorillas in the Mist appeared in 1983 and was later made into a film.
She fought bravely against poachers.
In 1985 she was murdered in her cabin, and the crime was never fully solved.

abschnitte.text: **Dian Fossey** was born on 16 January 1932 in San Francisco. She first worked as an occupational therapist with children. Her great dream was Africa, and in 1963 she travelled there and saw mountain gorillas for the first time. The famous researcher **Louis Leakey** encouraged her to observe the gorillas over a long period. He also supported Jane Goodall with the chimpanzees and Biruté Galdikas with the orangutans.

In 1967 Fossey founded the **Karisoke** research station in Rwanda at a height of about 3,000 metres. The name is made up of the names of the volcanoes Karisimbi and Visoke. She imitated the behaviour of the gorillas, chewed plants and made their sounds so that the animals would accept her. Little by little she was allowed to come very close to the groups. She gave the gorillas names and described exactly how they live together in their families.

At that time mountain gorillas were hunted by **poachers**, and many were caught in snares that had been set for antelopes. In 1977 poachers killed her favourite gorilla **Digit**. Fossey then founded a fund for the protection of gorillas and had traps in the forest destroyed. With her hard attitude she made many enemies.

In 1983 her book **Gorillas in the Mist** appeared, in which she tells of her research. In December 1985 Dian Fossey was murdered in her cabin at Karisoke, and who committed the crime has still not been clearly established to this day. She was buried beside Digit and other gorillas in the station's cemetery. In 1988 the film Gorillas in the Mist with Sigourney Weaver came to the cinemas.

Thanks to Fossey and many successors, the protection of mountain gorillas is much better today. The number of **mountain gorillas** has risen again, and around the year 2020 a little over 1,000 animals were counted. They live in Rwanda, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. **Gentle tourism**, in which visitors watch gorillas in small groups, brings money for conservation and for the people on the spot. The organisation Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund continues her work to this day.

begriffe.erklaerung: A subspecies of gorilla that lives in cool mountain forests in Central Africa.
Someone who hunts or catches wild animals illegally.
A place where researchers live and work in order to study something closely.
A group of mammals to which monkeys, apes and humans belong.

gewusst: Dian Fossey, Jane Goodall and Biruté Galdikas were together sometimes called Leakey's Angels.
Mountain gorillas are the only great ape subspecies whose numbers have risen again in recent decades.
An adult male gorilla with silver fur on his back is called a silverback.

teile.einleitung: The Chinese calendar is an ancient calendar that follows the moon and the sun. Best known are its twelve animal signs: every year belongs to an animal, for example the tiger or the dragon. The year 2026 is the Year of the Horse.
wichtigste: The Chinese calendar follows the moon and the sun, and is a lunisolar calendar.
There are twelve animal signs, which repeat every twelve years.
Each animal sign stands for a whole year, and the tiger, for example, is one such sign.
Chinese New Year falls each year on a date between the end of January and the middle of February.
In addition there are five elements, and together they make a 60 year cycle.
The year 2026 is the Year of the Horse, and 2027 is followed by the goat.

abschnitte.text: The Chinese calendar is a **lunisolar calendar**, so it follows the moon and the sun. A month begins with the new moon, and so that the year agrees with the seasons, a leap month is sometimes added. In everyday life in China today the same calendar is used as in Switzerland. For festivals, lucky days and traditions, however, the Chinese calendar is still important.

The twelve **animal signs** always follow in the same order: rat, ox, tiger, rabbit, dragon, snake, horse, goat, monkey, rooster, dog and pig. Each animal stands for a whole year, and then the circle begins again from the start. Anyone who was born after the New Year festival of 2022, for example, has the animal sign of the tiger. Certain characteristics are ascribed to many animals, and the tiger is regarded as brave, for instance, and the horse as free and full of energy.

abschnitte.titel: The legend of the great race
abschnitte.text: A well-known **legend** tells how the Jade Emperor invited the animals to a race across a river. The clever rat rode on the back of the ox and, shortly before the finish, jumped ashore first. In this way the story explains the order of the twelve animals. The cat is said to have been missing because the rat had not woken it, which is why there is no year of the cat.

In addition to the animals there are five **elements**: wood, fire, earth, metal and water. Animal and element together make a combination that repeats only after 60 years. The year 2026, for example, is a Fire Horse year. That is why some people in China celebrate their 60th birthday in a particularly big way.

The **New Year festival**, also called the Spring Festival, is the most important festival in China and many other countries of Asia. It falls on the second new moon after the winter solstice, that is between 21 January and 20 February, and in 2026 it was on 17 February. Families come together, eat dumplings, decorate everything in red and give red envelopes with money. Fireworks and dragon dances are meant to drive away bad luck, and in Swiss cities too the festival is celebrated by the Chinese community.

begriffe.erklaerung: A calendar that follows the moon and the sun.
One of twelve animals that stands for a year in the Chinese calendar.
An extra month so that the calendar agrees with the seasons.
An old tale that wants to explain something, but did not really happen.

gewusst: In Vietnam there is a year of the cat instead of the year of the rabbit.
Chinese New Year begins on a different date every year, because it follows the moon.
A combination of animal and element, such as the Fire Horse, occurs only every 60 years.

teile.einleitung: A badger sett is the underground home of the badger, a whole labyrinth of tunnels and chambers. Some setts are so old that many generations of badgers have lived in them.
wichtigste: The underground home of the badger is called a sett.
A large badger sett can have several entrances, sometimes over ten.
The tunnels can be many metres to over a hundred metres long in total.
In the warm, narrow nursery chamber deep in the sett the young grow up.
If the sett becomes too small, the badger digs extra tunnels and chambers.
Many setts are used over decades by new badgers again and again.
Foxes and other animals also sometimes live as lodgers in the badger sett.

abschnitte.text: The badger sett is an **underground** system of tubes and chambers. It usually lies on a slope in a wood or at the edge of a wood, where the ground is loose and dry. The tunnels can reach several metres deep under the earth. Here the badger sleeps during the day, spends the cold winter days and raises its young.

A small sett has only a few holes, while a large one can have **several entrances, sometimes over ten**. In front of the entrances lie big heaps of dug out earth, by which a badger sett is easily recognised. The tubes are about wide enough for a badger to pass through comfortably. Several exits are practical so that the animals can flee quickly in case of danger.

Inside there are several larger caves, which are called **“Kessel”** (literally cauldrons) or chambers. The badgers line them with dry grass, leaves and moss, which they drag backwards into the sett. Deep in the sett lies the narrow, warm **nursery chamber**, in which the young are born and grow up. The bedding is changed regularly and taken outside to air.

abschnitte.titel: A sett grows with its occupants
abschnitte.text: If the sett becomes too small in the course of time, **the badger digs new tunnels** and chambers. In this way a badger sett can keep growing over decades and sometimes even longer. Whole families, the so called badger clan, share a large sett. Young badgers often take over the sett of their parents.

In large badger setts **foxes**, rabbits or even wildcats sometimes live too, in parts of their own. The badger usually tolerates them, although the foxes are less tidy. Outside the sett the badger digs small pits as toilets, the **latrines**. Anyone who finds a badger sett should keep their distance and not disturb the animals, especially in spring, when young are in the sett.

begriffe.erklaerung: A larger living chamber in a badger or fox sett.
A warm, padded chamber in which the young are born.
A small pit that badgers use as a toilet.
Another animal that shares part of the sett.

gewusst: In England badger setts have been found that have probably been inhabited for centuries.
In a single night a badger sometimes drags dozens of bundles of grass into its sett.
From the fresh heap of earth in front of the entrance you can tell whether a sett is still inhabited.

teile.einleitung: In donkey-assisted therapy, donkeys help people to become calmer, braver or happier. Specialists accompany the encounters between person and animal. Donkeys are particularly suitable for this because they are patient, slow and attentive.
wichtigste: Donkey-assisted therapy is a form of animal-assisted therapy.
Visits with donkeys can help people to calm down.
Trained specialists lead the therapy.
Donkeys move calmly and react sensitively to the mood of people.
The therapy is used with children, adults and older people.
The welfare of the animals is just as important as that of the people.

abschnitte.text: In **donkey-assisted therapy**, specialists such as therapists, educators or carers work together with donkeys. The donkeys are not doctors but helpers who make an encounter pleasant. You stroke them, brush them, lead them on walks or simply watch them. It belongs to the larger group of **animal-assisted therapy**, in which dogs, horses or llamas also take part.

Donkeys are calm, curious and do not react in a hectic way. They walk slowly and in danger tend to stand still rather than run away. Many people find their soft fur and their large ears especially friendly. Donkeys sense exactly whether someone is nervous or relaxed and show it with their **body language**.

The therapy is used, for example, with children with fears, learning difficulties or a disability. People with autism or after severe experiences can also benefit. In old people’s homes residents are pleased about **donkey visits**, which awaken memories and bring joy. Some people who otherwise speak little begin to talk with the donkey.

Often a session begins with greeting and grooming the animals. Then the participants lead a donkey along a path or through a small **obstacle course**. In doing so they learn to be clear and patient, because a donkey only follows if it feels safe. At the end there is often a reward for the donkey and a conversation about what was experienced.

Therapy donkeys need plenty of rest breaks, a herd and enough room to roam. They must never be forced to do anything. In Switzerland the **Animal Welfare Act** lays down how donkeys must be kept, for example never alone. Good providers make sure that the donkeys are healthy and enjoy the work.

begriffe.erklaerung: A treatment that is meant to help a person become healthier or more content.
With the support of animals.
Feelings that you show without words, for example with ears, posture or gaze.
A path with small tasks and obstacles.

gewusst: Even the calm stroking of an animal can lower a person’s heart rate.
Donkeys cannot be rushed, which is why many people learn patience with them.

teile.einleitung: Antennae are the two movable feelers on the head of an insect. With them, insects smell, touch and taste their surroundings. They are something like a nose and fingers in one.
wichtigste: Every insect has exactly one pair of antennae on its head.
Another word for antennae is feelers.
With their antennae, insects pick up stimuli from their surroundings, above all smells and touches.
The praying mantis, too, senses smells and touches with its antennae.
In the pond skater, the antennae likewise pick up stimuli from the surroundings.
Antennae can be thread-like, feathery, clubbed or elbowed.
Spiders have no antennae, but crustaceans even have two pairs.

abschnitte.text: **Antennae** are long, movable appendages on the head of insects, centipedes and crustaceans. They consist of many small parts that are called segments. Insects always have exactly one pair of antennae. That is why spiders, which have no antennae, do not belong to the insects.

On the antennae sit thousands of tiny hairs and pores that work as **sense organs**. With them, insects smell scents, taste, touch and sense warmth or moisture. The praying mantis uses its antennae to sense smells and touches. The pond skater uses them to pick up stimuli from its surroundings.

Antennae look quite different depending on the insect. Butterflies that fly by day have thin antennae with a thickening at the end, which is called **clubbed**. Ants have elbowed antennae, and cockchafers have fan-like plates at the tip. The males of some moths carry large, **feathery** antennae that look like small fern leaves.

The males of the silk moth and other moths can smell the scent of a female from a great distance. Such attractants are called **pheromones**. A few scent particles are enough for the male to find his way to the female. Male mosquitoes even hear the buzzing of the females with their bushy antennae.

abschnitte.titel: Antennae in the daily life of insects
abschnitte.text: Ants touch each other with their antennae and in this way recognise whether another animal comes from their own nest. Bees recognise the scent of flowers with their antennae and so find nectar. Because antennae are so important, insects clean them regularly. Ants even have a small notch on their front legs with which they clean their antennae like a **comb**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for a feeler.
A part of the body with which a living thing perceives something, for example an eye, an ear or an antenna.
A scent with which animals of the same species send each other messages.
A single link or section, for example of an antenna.

gewusst: The antennae of some longhorn beetles are much longer than their whole body.
Crustaceans such as lobsters have two pairs of antennae, so four instead of two.

teile.einleitung: Chamois is a particularly soft, absorbent leather that was originally made from the skin of chamois goats. The French word “chamois” in fact means chamois goat, and in German it is also called “Gämsleder” or “Sämischleder”. Today it is usually made from sheep or goat leather and is used, for example, as a window leather.
wichtigste: Chamois is a soft leather that was originally made from chamois skin.
In German it is called “Gämsleder” or “Sämischleder”.
The word “chamois” is French and means chamois goat.
It is tanned with fish oil instead of plant substances or chromium.
Today it usually comes from sheep.
It is used for cleaning windows, cars and glasses.
A light brown-yellow colour is also called “chamois”.

abschnitte.titel: The chamois as the name giver
abschnitte.text: The **chamois** is a nimble climber of the Alps and is also common in Switzerland. In the past chamois were hunted not only for meat but also for their skin. From this skin a very fine, soft leather was made. After the French word for chamois, “chamois”, the leather got its name.

Chamois comes about through a special kind of **tanning**, called oil tanning. The prepared animal skin is rubbed again and again with fish oil, pounded and stored in the air. The oil changes the fibres of the skin so that it becomes durable but stays soft and stretchy. In the process the leather gets its typical yellowish colour.

Chamois are protected today or are hunted only in small numbers, so their skin is not enough for mass-produced goods. That is why most chamois leather today is made from **sheepskin**, often from the inner layer of the skin. Even so, the product is still called chamois or “Sämischleder”. There are also artificial cloths made of plastic that look similar.

Chamois can soak up a great deal of **water** and leaves no streaks and no fluff when wiping. That is why it is used as a window leather, for drying cars and for cleaning glasses, silver or musical instruments. It can be washed, and when it is dry it becomes soft again with gentle rubbing. In the past gloves and fine clothes were also made from it.

Because the leather has a light, yellowish beige colour, this shade is also called **chamois**. It is found on paper, envelopes and fabrics. Photographic paper and books are sometimes also sold with “chamois” as the colour description. In this way a colour recalls an animal from the mountains.

begriffe.erklaerung: A process in which raw animal skin is turned into durable leather.
Oil that is obtained from fish or sea animals.
A nimble, goat-like wild animal that lives in the Alps.
Strong kneading and pounding of leather or cloth so that it becomes soft.

gewusst: A good window leather can take up many times its own weight in water.
Many window leathers that say “chamois” on them do not come from the chamois goat at all, but from sheep.

teile.einleitung: Chameleons are special lizards with movable eyes, a super fast flicking tongue and grasping feet. All species belong to the family Chamaeleonidae, and today a good 200 species are known. About half of them live exclusively on the island of Madagascar.
wichtigste: All chameleons belong to the family Chamaeleonidae.
Their closest relatives are the agamas.
Today a good 200 species have been described.
About half of all species live only on Madagascar.
The word “chameleon” literally means “ground lion” in Greek.
Their teeth sit on top of the jawbone, which is called acrodont.
In Europe the common chameleon lives, for example in southern Spain and southern Portugal.

abschnitte.text: Chameleons form the family **Chamaeleonidae** within the lizards. Their closest relatives are the agamas, which include the bearded dragon. A special feature is their dentition: the teeth sit on top of the jawbone, which experts call **acrodont**. The name comes from Greek and means “ground lion” or “earth lion”.

Today a good 200 species of chameleon are known, and researchers keep discovering new ones. Most live in Africa, and about half of all species occur only on **Madagascar**. Other species live on the Arabian Peninsula, in India and in Sri Lanka. In Europe the **common chameleon** is native, for example in southern Spain, southern Portugal and on some Mediterranean islands, and it was probably brought to Malta by humans in the 19th century.

Chameleons come in very different sizes. According to measurements of males, the longest is **Oustalet's chameleon** from Madagascar, which can grow to over 60 centimetres long. The largest chameleon of the African mainland is Meller's chameleon from East Africa. Quite tiny, by contrast, is **Brookesia nana**, which was described in 2021 and is among the smallest reptiles in the world, and the male fits on a fingertip.

Chameleons can turn their eyes independently of each other and so see almost all around. They shoot out their tongue in a flash, and it can be about as long as their whole body. The toes are fused into pincer-like **grasping feet**, and many species have a prehensile tail with which they hold on to branches. They are also well known for being able to change their colour.

Most chameleons lay eggs, which they bury in the ground, but some species give birth to live young. In the common chameleon it takes about 10 to 12 months until the young hatch from the eggs. The little chameleons are on their own at once and hunt insects themselves. Many species are endangered by the clearing of the **forests** on Madagascar.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reptile with four legs and scaly skin, for example a wall lizard or a gecko.
Teeth that sit on top of the jawbone instead of in sockets.
A foot whose toes can grip round a branch like a pincer.
A species that occurs only in one particular area, for example only on Madagascar.

gewusst: Brookesia nana is so small that an adult male has room on a fingertip.
In some chameleons it takes almost a year until the young hatch from the egg.
In many chameleon species the males are decorated with striking horns, crests or nose projections.

teile.einleitung: The Eurasian lynx is the largest wild cat in Switzerland and the largest of the lynx species worldwide. With its ear tufts, its ruff of fur on the cheeks and its short tail it is unmistakable. Because it lives so secretively, few people ever get to see it.
wichtigste: The lynx belongs to the cat family.
The Eurasian lynx is the largest species of lynx in the world.
Adult lynxes usually have a spotted coat.
It stalks its prey and surprises it with a short leap.
Only the mother looks after the young.
In Switzerland, depending on the estimate, around 150 to 300 lynxes live.
From 1971 the lynx was resettled in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The Eurasian lynx has long legs, large paws and a short tail with a black tip. On the ears it wears black **tufts**, and on the cheeks grows a light ruff. Adult lynxes are mostly spotted, and every animal has its own **spot pattern**. A male weighs about 20 to 25 kilograms and is thus about as big as a medium-sized dog.

The lynx lives in large forests from western Europe to Siberia. In Switzerland it occurs mainly in the north-western Alps and in the **Jura**. It needs a lot of space, and a territory can be over 100 square kilometres in size. During the day it rests well hidden in rocks or thicket.

In Switzerland the lynx hunts mainly **roe deer** and **chamois**, sometimes also foxes, hares or marmots. It stalks silently and surprises the prey with a short leap, because long chases do not suit it. What it does not eat at once, it hides under leaves or snow and returns later. A lynx needs about one roe deer per week.

The mating season, the **rut**, takes place in late winter from about February to March. In May or June the female usually gives birth to two to three young in a sheltered hiding place. Only the mother looks after the young and teaches them to hunt. The young lynxes stay with her for about 10 months, then they look for a territory of their own.

At the beginning of the 20th century the lynx was exterminated in Switzerland. From 1971 lynxes from the **Carpathians** were released again, first in central Switzerland. Today researchers monitor the animals with **camera traps** and recognise individual lynxes again by their spot pattern. The lynx is protected in Switzerland, but traffic and illegal shooting continue to threaten it.

The lynx sees and hears excellently and climbs trees skilfully. The German word **“luchsen”**, that is to watch secretly and closely, probably comes from the sharp gaze of the lynx. The expression “eyes like a lynx” also means that someone sees very well. Its eyes also work at dusk, when it likes to hunt best.

begriffe.erklaerung: The mating season in lynxes, foxes and other predators.
The area in which an animal lives and hunts.
A camera in the forest that automatically takes a picture when an animal moves.
Black tufts of hair on the ear tips of the lynx.

gewusst: The broad, hairy paws act like snowshoes in the snow.
Because every spot pattern is unique, it acts like a fingerprint of the lynx.

teile.einleitung: The feline immunodeficiency virus, FIV for short, is a virus that weakens the defence system of cats. It is related to the human HIV and is therefore sometimes called “cat AIDS”. For people and other pets, however, it is completely harmless.
wichtigste: FIV is the cat immune deficiency virus.
It is similar to the human HIV but cannot be passed on to people.
It is mainly passed on through deep bite wounds in fights.
Especially often affected are unneutered tomcats that go outdoors.
There is no cure, but many cats still live well for years.
A blood test at the vet shows whether a cat has FIV.

abschnitte.text: FIV stands for **feline immunodeficiency virus**, where “feline” means cat-like. It belongs to the **lentiviruses**, a group of viruses that work slowly. It was discovered in 1986 in California in cats with a weakened defence system. The virus attacks certain white blood cells that are important for fighting disease.

The virus is found mainly in the saliva of infected cats. It is usually passed on through deep **bite wounds** in territorial fights. That is why unneutered tomcats that spend a lot of time outside and often fight are especially often affected. When eating together or grooming one another, the virus is only rarely passed on.

After infection, many cats show hardly any signs for years. Over time the **immune system** becomes weaker, and the cat catches other infections more easily. Common examples are inflammation in the mouth, colds or skin problems. Many FIV-positive cats still reach a normal age if they are well looked after.

A **blood test** at the vet shows whether a cat has antibodies against FIV in its blood. The infection cannot be cured. However, the accompanying illnesses can be treated, for example with medicines against bacteria. A healthy diet, little stress and regular check-ups at the vet are especially important.

**Neutering** lowers the risk, because neutered tomcats fight less often. FIV-positive cats live best as indoor cats or with secured balconies, so that they do not infect other cats. They can often live together with peaceful cats that do not bite. There is no **risk of infection** at all for children, adults and dogs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny germ that causes disease and can multiply only inside living cells.
The body's own defence against disease-causing germs.
Defensive substances in the blood that the body makes against a particular germ.
An operation at the vet after which an animal can no longer have young.

gewusst: FIV does not occur only in house cats; similar viruses exist in lions and pumas too.
Many animal shelters successfully rehome FIV-positive cats with new owners.
Although FIV and HIV are related, neither of the two viruses can infect the other's species.

teile.einleitung: Catnip is a plant from the labiate family that drives many cats almost crazy. Its scent compound nepetalactone makes cats roll, rub and leap around happily. The plant grows wild in Europe and Asia and is often planted in gardens.
wichtigste: Catnip is called Nepeta cataria scientifically.
It belongs to the labiates (mint family), like mint, sage and thyme.
Its scent compound nepetalactone triggers a short, euphoric behaviour in many cats.
Only about two thirds of cats react to it, and this is inborn.
Large cats such as lions and leopards can also react to catnip.
Nepetalactone keeps mosquitoes and some insects away.
With its flowers the plant attracts many bees and bumblebees.

abschnitte.text: Catnip is a **perennial** plant and grows about 40 centimetres to one metre tall. Its stem is square, typical of the **labiates**. The heart shaped, toothed leaves are grey-green and softly hairy. From July to September it bears small white flowers with purple dots.

The plant originally comes from southern Europe and Asia. Today it also grows in North America and other parts of the world. In Switzerland you find it growing wild rather rarely, for example at path edges, on walls and on rubble sites. More often you see in gardens the blue flowering garden catmint, a related cultivated form.

When a cat smells the plant, **nepetalactone** gets into its nose. Many cats then begin to sniff, lick, rub against it and roll on the ground. Some purr or leap about playfully. After about five to fifteen minutes the intoxication is over, and the cat does not react for a while. Young kittens usually do not react yet, and the effect is harmless for cats.

Researchers found out in 2021 that nepetalactone repels **mosquitoes**. When cats rub against the plant, they spread the scent in their fur. Perhaps in this way they protect themselves from annoying insect bites. That is why nepetalactone is also being researched as a natural mosquito repellent.

In the past catnip was used as a **medicinal plant**, for example as a tea for colds and stomach ache. In the Middle Ages it was often planted in monastery gardens. Today it is sold mainly as a filling for cat toys. Gardeners value it because its flowers attract many **bees** and bumblebees.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant family with flowers that look like two lips, for example mint and sage.
The scent compound of catnip that excites cats.
Very cheerful and excited.
A plant that is supposed to help with illnesses.

gewusst: Whether a cat reacts to catnip is inherited, which is why some cats are left completely cold by the plant.
Another plant from Asia, silver vine, has a similar or even stronger effect on many cats.
Cats sometimes bite catnip so hard that hardly anything of the plant is left in gardens.

teile.einleitung: The kingfisher is a small bird with a bright blue back and an orange belly. It lives on clear streams, rivers and lakes and catches small fish with a lightning fast dive. Because, on account of its colours, it is also called a flying gem, many people are delighted when they get to see one.
wichtigste: The kingfisher belongs to the bird family of kingfishers with the scientific name Alcedinidae.
It eats mainly small fish.
It hunts by plunging head first into the water from a perch.
Its nest is a hole it has dug itself in a steep bank.
It flies fast, straight and low over the water.
In Switzerland it is on the Red List and is regarded as endangered.
Straightened river banks without natural steep walls threaten it especially.

abschnitte.text: The kingfisher is only about 16 to 18 centimetres long and weighs around 35 to 40 grams. Back and head gleam turquoise to blue, and chest and belly are orange. The long, pointed **bill** is ideal for seizing fish. The blue colour comes not from pigment, but from the refraction of light in the feathers, like a rainbow.

Kingfishers live on slow flowing streams, rivers and lakes with clear water. They need branches over the water as a **perch** and steep bank walls of earth or sand for their nesting hole. The kingfisher lives in large parts of Europe, Asia and North Africa. Each bird defends its stretch of river as a **territory** and aggressively drives away other kingfishers.

The kingfisher sits still on a branch and watches the water. When it sees a small fish, it plunges in head first and dives briefly under. With the fish in its bill it flies back and strikes it against the branch, before swallowing it head first. Besides fish it also eats water insects, tadpoles and small crustaceans.

At courtship the male sometimes gives the female a caught fish as a **bridal gift**. Together the two dig a tube into a steep wall with bill and feet, which is often half a metre to one metre long. At the end lies a nest chamber in which the female usually lays 6 to 7 white eggs. Both parents feed the young with small fish, and often there are two or three broods a year.

In Switzerland the kingfisher is rare and is on the **Red List**. Many rivers were straightened in the past and reinforced with stones, so natural steep banks for breeding are lacking. Very cold winters are also dangerous, when waters freeze over and it can no longer catch fish. Through the **restoration** of rivers such as on the Thur or the Aare, new habitats are arising again.

Wild kingfishers usually live only a few years, because cold and enemies kill many animals. Even so, they have taught humans something. Japanese engineers gave a **high speed train** a nose in the shape of the kingfisher's bill. In this way the train became quieter and needed less electricity, because the bird's bill dips into the water almost without a splash.

begriffe.erklaerung: A spot such as a branch from which a bird watches for prey.
An area that an animal defends against others of its species.
A list of the animal and plant species that are rare or threatened.
When a river or a landscape is made more natural again.

gewusst: The blue colour of the kingfisher comes from light, not from pigment in the feathers.
A kingfisher always swallows a fish head first, so that the scales do not get stuck in its throat.
The nose of the Japanese Shinkansen train of the 500 series was modelled on the kingfisher's bill.

teile.einleitung: A fish ladder is a structure that lets fish get past an obstacle in a river, such as a weir or a power station. Instead of a high wall, they find many small steps there or a natural side stream. In this way lake trout, salmon or eels can migrate upstream again.
wichtigste: Fish ladders help fish to get past weirs, dams and steps.
Many fish migrate upstream to their spawning grounds.
Weirs and dams block lake trout from reaching their spawning streams.
A fish ladder often consists of many small pools one behind the other.
There are also natural bypass streams and even fish lifts.
Fish ladders help salmon, trout, eels and many other species.
In Switzerland, obstacles in rivers have to be gradually made passable again.

abschnitte.text: A **fish ladder**, also called a **fish pass**, is a channel of water beside an obstacle in a river. It divides the difference in height into many small steps. Each step is only so high that a fish can manage it with a leap or powerful swimming. Between the steps lie calmer pools in which the fish can rest. In this way they get upwards step by step.

Many fish have to migrate in order to spawn or find food. The **lake trout**, for example, goes from the lake up into the streams, where it lays its eggs. **Weirs**, dams and power stations block its way. In Switzerland there are tens of thousands of such artificial obstacles in the waters. Without a fish ladder, the fish cannot reach their spawning grounds, and the population collapses.

In a **pool pass**, the water flows through a series of pools separated by small walls. In a vertical slot pass, the fish swim through vertical slots from pool to pool. A **bypass channel** is a natural stream with stones and gravel that leads round the obstacle. At very high dams there are sometimes fish lifts or locks. It is always important that the entrance is easy to find, because fish follow the current.

Salmon and trout leap and swim powerfully against the current. Weaker swimmers such as bullheads or young fish need gentle steps and rough bottoms. Young eels even crawl across damp surfaces and use special eel passes with bristles. Good fish ladders are built so that as many as possible of the river's species can get through. Some installations have windows or counting pools in which experts count the fish.

On the High Rhine, for example at the Rheinfelden power station, large fish passes have been built. They are also meant to help bring the **salmon** back to Switzerland, where it disappeared around the middle of the 20th century. Since 2011, the Swiss **Water Protection Act** has required power stations to make fish migration possible again. The operators therefore have to modify their installations bit by bit. Migration downstream is also important, because fish must not get into the turbines.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for fish ladder.
A structure across a river that dams up the water.
A place where fish lay their eggs.
A natural stream that leads round an obstacle.

gewusst: The first simple fish ladders were built several hundred years ago.
In some fish ladders, cameras count every fish that swims through.
Salmon can leap more than three metres high at waterfalls.

teile.einleitung: “The Golden Goose” is a well known fairy tale that the Brothers Grimm collected and wrote down. A simple young man is given a goose with feathers of pure gold as thanks for his kindness. Whoever touches it sticks fast, and so a funny procession arises that makes a sad princess laugh.
wichtigste: “The Golden Goose” is in the Children's and Household Tales of the Brothers Grimm.
The main character is the youngest of three brothers, whom everyone just calls “Dummling” (simpleton).
Because he shares his food with a little grey man, he gets the golden goose.
All who touch the goose or those stuck to it get stuck too.
A princess who never laughs has to laugh at the sight of the procession.
After further difficult tasks, the Dummling marries the princess and becomes king.
The message is: whoever is kind and helpful is rewarded.

abschnitte.titel: Where the fairy tale comes from
abschnitte.text: In the 19th century the brothers **Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm** collected folk tales from Germany. From 1812 they published them in the **Children's and Household Tales**. “The Golden Goose” has the number 64 there. Similar stories were also told in other countries of Europe.

abschnitte.titel: The Dummling and the little man
abschnitte.text: A man has three sons, and everyone thinks the youngest is simple minded. The two older brothers go into the forest to chop wood and do not want to share their food with a **little grey man**. Both afterwards hurt themselves with the axe. The Dummling, by contrast, shares his plain bread, and suddenly it turns into fine cake. As thanks the little man shows him an old tree in whose roots sits a goose with golden feathers.

The Dummling spends the night with the goose in an inn. The innkeeper's three daughters want to steal a golden feather and **stick** to the goose. The next day the Dummling travels on, and more and more people get stuck, among them a parson, a sexton and two farmers. So a long, comical procession arises that stumbles across the country.

In the city lives a king whose daughter never laughs. He has promised to marry her to whoever makes her **laugh**. When the princess sees the strange procession, she has to laugh out loud. The king, however, sets three more tasks: to drink a cellar full of wine, to eat a mountain of bread and to build a ship that travels on land and on water. With the help of the little man the Dummling manages everything and later becomes **king**.

The fairy tale shows that **kindness** is rewarded and meanness punished. The clever brothers fail, and the underestimated youngest brother succeeds. Such characters appear in many fairy tales. Greed is also punished, for the innkeeper's daughters wanted to steal a feather.

Geese belong to the **waterfowl**. Our domestic goose descends from the wild **greylag goose**, which can be observed in Switzerland on lakes and rivers. Geese are watchful and cackle loudly when strangers come. Golden feathers, of course, exist only in the fairy tale.

begriffe.erklaerung: An invented story in which magic, talking animals or miracles often appear.
Two German language scholars who collected many folk tales in the 19th century.
A mocking name for someone whom others think simple minded.
The wild goose from which the domestic goose descends.

gewusst: The collection of the Brothers Grimm is part of the UNESCO Memory of the World register.
In many countries there are fairy tales about princesses who cannot laugh, and every time laughter is the solution.
A ship that travels on land and on water also appears in other old fairy tales.

teile.einleitung: Goose bumps are the small bumps that suddenly appear on our skin when we are cold or experience something exciting. The fine hairs stand on end as they do. The German name, Gänsehaut, literally “goose skin”, probably comes from the skin of a plucked goose.
wichtigste: Goose bumps appear when tiny muscles at the hair roots contract.
The hairs stand up and small bumps form around them.
You get goose bumps in the cold, but also with fear, joy or beautiful music.
The body controls them automatically, and you cannot trigger them at will.
The name probably comes from the skin of a plucked goose with small bumps.
In animals with thick fur, raising the hairs helps against the cold.
In humans, goose bumps are a leftover from earlier times.

abschnitte.text: **Goose bumps** are a reaction of our skin in which the hairs stand up and small dots become visible. They often show on the arms and legs, sometimes also on the neck. In medicine they are also called **cutis anserina**, which is Latin for goose skin. After a few seconds or minutes they disappear again by themselves.

At every hair root sits a tiny muscle called the **arrector pili**. In the cold or with strong feelings, the nervous system sends a signal, and these muscles contract. This makes the hair stand up, and the skin around the hair root bulges into a small bump. It is controlled by the **autonomic nervous system**, which works without our will, and by the stress hormone **adrenaline**.

In animals with thick fur, raising the hairs has a clear use. More air stays trapped between the raised hairs, which insulates like a warm blanket. In danger, an animal with bristling fur looks bigger and more dangerous, like a hissing cat with a fluffed-up tail. In humans, with their fine body hair, this hardly achieves anything any more. It is a leftover from **evolution**.

Many people get goose bumps when they hear music that moves them. They can also appear during an exciting film, a scary story or a great win in sport. Researchers suspect that reward areas in the **brain** are active when this happens. People then sometimes speak of a “goose bump moment”.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the name come from?
abschnitte.text: The name probably comes from the skin of a plucked goose. If you remove the feathers from a goose, you see small bumps in the places where the **feathers** sat. These resemble the little bumps on our skin. In English they are called “goose bumps” too, while in French people say “chair de poule”, that is, chicken skin.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny muscle at the hair root that makes the hair stand up.
An automatic reaction of the body that you do not control at will.
A hormone that the body releases in excitement or danger.
The slow change of living things over very many generations.

gewusst: A very few people can reportedly trigger goose bumps at will, but this is very rare.
Hedgehogs, too, raise their spines in danger using similar muscles.

teile.einleitung: The domestication of the dog is the long road by which the wild wolf became our domestic dog. It began at least 15,000 years ago, when humans still lived as hunters and gatherers. That makes the dog the first animal that humans tamed.
wichtigste: The dog descends from the wolf.
Domestication is dated back to at least 15,000 years ago.
The dog was the first domestic animal of humans, long before sheep, goat or cattle.
With difficult tasks, dogs rather seek eye contact with humans, whereas wolves try on their own.
Dogs can digest plant starch relatively well, unlike pure meat eaters such as cats.
Through breeding, hundreds of breeds arose, from the Chihuahua to the Great Dane.
In Switzerland too, remains of very early dogs have been found.

abschnitte.text: All dogs, from the tiny Chihuahua to the large St Bernard, descend from the **wolf**. **Domestication** means that a wild animal becomes a domestic animal over many generations. In the process body and behaviour change. Dogs are today so closely related to the wolf that both are counted as the same species.

Researchers date the beginning to at least 15,000 years ago, and some estimates go back clearly further. At that time the last **Ice Age** still prevailed, and people lived as hunters and gatherers. Exactly where it began is still disputed, probably in Europe or Asia. A famous find is a grave in Bonn-Oberkassel in Germany in which two people were buried together with a dog about 14,000 years ago.

Probably less shy wolves approached the camps of humans, because food scraps lay there. The tamer animals had advantages and had more offspring. People noticed that the animals helped with hunting and warned of dangers. So, step by step, the wolves became **tamer** and more dependent on humans.

In experiments, dogs and wolves raised by humans were given a task that they could not solve. The wolves kept trying on their own, whereas the dogs looked at the human and sought **eye contact** and help. Dogs also understand human pointing gestures especially well. So they have learned to work together with us.

Dogs have more copies of a gene that is important for the digestion of **starch**. That is why they can digest grain and other plant food better than wolves or cats. This fits with the fact that, with agriculture, humans ate more and more grain and the dogs got the leftovers. In addition many dogs have smaller teeth, shorter muzzles and sometimes floppy ears.

In the **Kesslerloch** cave near Thayngen in the canton of Schaffhausen, bones were found that are counted among the oldest dog finds in the world. They are about 14,000 to 15,000 years old. Later, dogs also lived with the pile dwellers on the Swiss lakes. Today there are famous Swiss **breeds** such as the Bernese Mountain Dog, the Appenzeller and the St Bernard.

begriffe.erklaerung: The conversion of a wild animal into a domestic animal over many generations.
A wild living predator from which all dogs descend.
A nutrient in grain and potatoes that gives the body energy.
A group of dogs with a similar appearance and nature that was deliberately bred.

gewusst: The dog was tamed thousands of years before all other domestic animals, even before there was arable farming.
Worldwide there are today several hundred recognised dog breeds.
Dogs can tell from a person's face whether they are cheerful or angry.

teile.einleitung: Meerkats are small predators from southern Africa that live in large families in underground burrows. They are famous for standing upright on their hind legs and looking out for dangers. Because they are so active and sociable, they are among the favourites of visitors in many zoos.
wichtigste: Meerkats belong to the mongoose family.
In the wild they live in Africa, above all in the Kalahari.
They live in groups that are called a family clan.
Usually only one dominant female and one dominant male reproduce.
Other group members help to raise the young, which is called a helper system.
With their long claws they dig burrows with several entrances.
They are largely insensitive to the venom of scorpions.

abschnitte.text: Without its tail a meerkat is about 25 to 35 centimetres long and weighs only around three quarters of a kilogram. The fur is light brown to grey with dark crossbars on the back. Around the eyes it has dark patches that act like **sunglasses** against the glaring light. On the front paws sit long **claws**, which serve above all for digging.

Meerkats live in dry regions of southern Africa, for example in the **Kalahari**, in Namibia, Botswana and South Africa. They live in underground burrows that they dig themselves or take over from other animals. A burrow has several entrances so that they can flee quickly in danger. In the morning they like to warm up in the sun, with the belly towards the sun.

Meerkats eat above all insects, beetle larvae, spiders and **scorpions**. They are largely insensitive to the venom of scorpions, and often they bite off the venomous sting first. Small lizards, snakes, birds’ eggs and plants are also on the menu. Young meerkats learn from the older ones how to catch dangerous prey correctly.

While the others dig for food, a **sentinel** stands upright on a mound or bush and looks out. If it sees an enemy, it warns the group with different calls, depending on whether the danger comes from the air or from the ground. Their enemies include birds of prey and the **jackal**. If danger threatens from a snake, they often surround it together and try to drive it away.

Meerkats live in a **family clan** of often 10 to 30 animals. Usually only one dominant female and one dominant male reproduce. The female usually has two to four young per litter. The other group members babysit, bring food and protect the young, and this **helper system** is typical of meerkats.

Meerkats are very popular in zoos because they stand upright and are very active and social. In Switzerland you can watch them, for example, at Zurich Zoo and Basel Zoo. In the wild they are not threatened. They also became known through the character Timon from the film “The Lion King”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of small predators from Africa and Asia, to which the meerkat also belongs.
A group of meerkats that lives together.
When other group members help to raise the young.
An animal that looks out for enemies for the group.

gewusst: Meerkats have different warning calls for enemies from the air and from the ground.
The dark rings round the meerkats’ eyes help against being dazzled by the sun.
Meerkats can close their ears when digging so that no sand gets in.

teile.einleitung: The badger is a powerful, shy animal with a black and white striped face and belongs to the weasel family. It is out and about mainly at night and lives in large underground setts that it digs itself with its strong claws.
wichtigste: The badger belongs to the weasel family.
It grows about as big as a medium-sized dog and weighs about 10 to 20 kilograms.
With its powerful front paws and strong claws it digs large setts.
It is active mainly at night and sees rather badly, but has a very good sense of smell.
A badger family that lives together in a sett is called a clan.
A mother badger usually has two to three young.
In winter it lives off its fat reserves.
In Switzerland the badger is protected, and road traffic is a great danger.

abschnitte.text: The European badger is stocky, with short legs and grey, bristly fur. Most striking is its white head with two **black stripes** over the eyes and ears. Without the tail it is 65 to 90 centimetres long and weighs about 10 to 20 kilograms, and it is heaviest in autumn. Its **front paws** carry long, strong claws with which it can dig superbly. It belongs to the weasel family and is a relative of the pine marten and the polecat.

Badgers live in woods, hedges and at woodland edges near meadows and fields. They occur in almost the whole of Europe, and in Switzerland on the Central Plateau, in the Jura and in the Alpine valleys. During the day they sleep in their **sett**, which is often used over generations. Sometimes they even live on the edge of villages and towns.

The badger is an **omnivore**. Its favourite food is earthworms, which it collects from meadows on damp nights. In addition it eats beetles, insect larvae, snails, mice, fruit, berries, mushrooms and maize. It also digs out wasp nests and eats the larvae. Because it sees badly, it finds its food mainly with its nose.

Badgers are usually active **at night** and rarely meet humans, because they flee shyly. Several animals live together as a **badger clan** in one sett. In winter they do not hibernate properly but have a winter rest, living on their fat. The two to three young are born in late winter and leave the sett for the first time in spring. Badgers are very clean and dig small pits outside the sett as toilets.

Adult badgers have hardly any natural enemies in Switzerland. The greatest danger today is **road traffic**, and every year many badgers are run over. In the past badgers were heavily persecuted in the fight against rabies, because their setts were gassed together with those of foxes. Today the badger in Switzerland is protected by the hunting law, and it has long closed seasons. Wildlife bridges and passages under roads help so that fewer badgers are run over.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal family with a long body and short legs, for example badger, marten and otter.
A badger family that lives together in a sett.
A light resting state in winter in which the animal wakes up now and then.
An animal that eats plant and animal food.

gewusst: A badger can eat hundreds of earthworms in a single night.
The young are born only months after mating, because the fertilised egg does not develop further for a time.
In fairy tales and fables the badger is often called Master Grimbart.

teile.einleitung: The painted lady is a pretty butterfly with an orange, black and white pattern that occurs almost all over the world. It is a world champion at migrating: every year painted ladies fly from Africa to Europe and back again. In doing so they even cross the Sahara, the Mediterranean and the Alps.
wichtigste: The painted lady belongs to the nymphalid family (“Edelfalter”).
It is one of the butterflies that fly especially far on their migration.
Its journey from Africa to northern Europe and back is up to about 15,000 kilometres long.
The migration is managed not by a single butterfly, but by several generations one after another.
The caterpillars eat mainly thistles and nettles.
The painted lady occurs almost worldwide.
In Switzerland it cannot survive the winter and migrates in anew every spring.

abschnitte.text: The painted lady has a **wingspan** of about five to six centimetres. The upper side is orange with black spots, and the wing tips are black with white dots. The underside is paler, patterned grey-brown, and has small eyespots. Like the peacock butterfly and the red admiral, it belongs to the **nymphalids**.

abschnitte.titel: A butterfly for the whole world
abschnitte.text: The painted lady lives in Europe, Africa, Asia and North America. That is why it counts as one of the most widespread butterflies on Earth. It likes open, flower-rich landscapes such as meadows, fields, gardens and path edges. In the mountains it flies up to great heights.

In spring painted ladies fly from North Africa to Europe. On the way they lay eggs, and the next **generation** flies on further north, in part as far as Scandinavia. In autumn their descendants travel back south at great height, as far as tropical Africa south of the Sahara. Researchers have calculated that this round trip is up to about 15,000 kilometres long. That is the longest known **migration** of a butterfly.

The female lays her eggs singly on food plants. The **caterpillars** eat mainly **thistles**, hence the German name “Distelfalter”, but also nettles and mallows. They build themselves a small tent of leaves and silk threads as a hiding place. The adult butterflies suck nectar from flowers, for example from thistles, knapweeds and buddleia.

In Switzerland you can see painted ladies from spring to autumn. In some years huge numbers come, for example in 2009 and 2019, when millions of butterflies flew over the Alps. They do not survive the cold winter here, however. That is why all painted ladies in Switzerland descend from **immigrants** from the south.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large butterfly family (“Edelfalter”) with species such as the red admiral, the peacock butterfly and the painted lady.
All the animals that are born at about the same time, for example parents or children.
A butterfly that regularly travels over long distances into other areas.
The distance from one wing tip to the other with the wings spread out.

gewusst: On their journey painted ladies often fly at more than 500 metres' height and use favourable winds.
For a long time researchers did not know that the butterflies fly back in autumn, because they fly so high that they are hardly seen.
A painted lady weighs less than half a gram and still manages thousands of kilometres.

teile.einleitung: The Ugly Duckling is a famous fairy tale by the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen from the year 1843. It tells of a chick that is mocked by everyone and in the end grows into a wonderfully beautiful swan.
wichtigste: The Ugly Duckling is a fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen.
It appeared in 1843 in Denmark.
A large grey chick hatches in a duck's nest and is laughed at by everyone.
After a hard winter it realises that it is a swan.
The fairy tale shows that you should not judge anyone by their looks.
Many see in it Andersen's own life story.
Young mute swans really are grey-brown and turn white only later.

abschnitte.text: A duck is hatching her eggs on a farm, but from one large egg comes a **grey, clumsy chick**. The other ducks, hens and even its brothers and sisters mock it. The duckling runs away and goes through a long, cold winter full of hardship. In spring it sees magnificent swans and swims over to them. In the reflection in the water it recognises that it has itself become a **swan**.

**Hans Christian Andersen** was born in 1805 in Odense in Denmark and died in 1875 in Copenhagen. He grew up in poverty and as a young man was often smiled at because of his looks and his manner. Later he became one of the most famous fairy tale writers in the world. He also wrote The Little Mermaid, The Emperor's New Clothes and The Princess and the Pea.

The fairy tale shows that you must not shut others out because of their **looks**. It gives courage, because the duckling keeps going despite mockery and loneliness. Many people see in it Andersen's own path from a mocked boy to a celebrated writer. The expression ugly duckling is used today for someone who later develops surprisingly well.

In nature a swan does not lay its eggs in a duck's nest. But young **mute swans** really do look quite different from their parents: their plumage is grey-brown. Only over the course of about two years do they become snow white. Mute swans also live on many Swiss lakes and rivers, for example on Lake Zurich and Lake Geneva.

The fairy tale has been translated into very many languages and often adapted as a film, a play and a picture book. The **Hans Christian Andersen Award**, the most important international prize for children's and young people's books, is named after Andersen. His birthday on 2 April is International Children's Book Day. In Odense a museum recalls his life.

begriffe.erklaerung: An invented story, often with magic and talking animals.
A large white swan with an orange bill and a black knob.
All the feathers of a bird together.
A fairy tale that a particular writer made up himself.

gewusst: Unlike the fairy tales of the Brothers Grimm, Andersen mostly invented his fairy tales himself.
2 April, Andersen's birthday, is children's book day worldwide.
A young swan is called a cygnet in English.

teile.einleitung: A compound eye is an eye made up of many tiny individual eyes. Insects such as butterflies, flies, bees and ants see their surroundings with it. Each single eye supplies one small picture point, and together they form a picture like a mosaic.
wichtigste: A compound eye is made up of many tiny single eyes, called ommatidia.
It is also called a complex eye.
Insects and many crustaceans have compound eyes.
A butterfly's eyes can have thousands of facets.
Compound eyes are especially good at detecting movement.
Bees can see ultraviolet light, which is invisible to us.
A grasshopper has two large compound eyes.

abschnitte.text: A **compound eye** is made up of many tiny, six-sided single eyes called **ommatidia**. Each single eye has its own small lens and looks in a slightly different direction. The brain puts the many picture points together into one overall picture. Experts also call it a **complex eye**.

The number of facets varies greatly from animal to animal. Ants often have only a few hundred facets, and some workers even fewer. A butterfly's eyes can have thousands of facets, and in large dragonflies there are around 30,000 per eye. The more facets, the sharper the picture usually is.

Compound eyes do not see as sharply as our eyes, but they are especially good at detecting movement. A fly therefore notices straight away when a hand comes near.
