Butterflies can detect movement and colours especially well with their compound eyes. Bees can even see **ultraviolet light**, and so they find patterns on flowers that are invisible to us.

A grasshopper has two large compound eyes at the sides of its head. Ants also see their surroundings with compound eyes, but they rely heavily on their sense of smell. Many insects also have small **simple eyes** on the forehead, which mainly tell light from dark. Crustaceans such as crabs and shrimps also have compound eyes.

Compound eyes have existed on Earth for a very long time. The **trilobites**, extinct sea animals, already had such eyes over 500 million years ago. Their fossilised eyes can still be recognised in fossils today. Researchers are now building tiny cameras modelled on the compound eye.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single small eye within a compound eye.
A transparent part of the eye that focuses light.
Light that people cannot see but bees can.
Small, simple eyes on the forehead of many insects.

gewusst: Because flies perceive many more images per second than we do, an approaching fly swatter looks to them as if it were in slow motion.
A dragonfly's large compound eyes cover almost its whole head.

teile.einleitung: The adipose fin is a small, soft fin on the back of some fish, between the dorsal fin and the tail fin. It is typical of salmon-like fish such as trout, salmon and whitefish. For a long time it was thought to be useless, but today more is known about its job.
wichtigste: The adipose fin sits between the dorsal fin and the tail fin.
It has no fin rays and is soft and fleshy.
It is typical of salmon-like fish such as salmon, trout, lake trout and whitefish.
Many catfish and characins also have an adipose fin.
Researchers suspect that it helps to sense currents in the water.
In Switzerland, many salmon-like fish are easy to recognise by their adipose fin.

abschnitte.text: The adipose fin is a small, rounded fin at the back of the back. Unlike the other fins, it has no supporting **fin rays**. It is made of skin, connective tissue and sometimes a little fat, which is where its name comes from. Fish cannot raise or move it themselves.

The adipose fin is best known in the **salmon-like fish**. These include salmon, brown trout, lake trout, Arctic char, grayling and whitefish. Many catfish, the colourful **characins** from the aquarium and some deep-sea fish also have one. Altogether it occurs in several thousand species of fish.

For a long time people believed the adipose fin was a useless leftover from the past. Research has shown, however, that many **nerves** run through it. It is thought to work like a sensor and to help fish to sense eddies in the water. In this way they can swim better in flowing streams.

In some countries, fish farmers cut off the adipose fin of young salmon before they are released. In this way you can later tell whether a caught fish comes from a **farm** or grew up wild. This marking is quick to do and easy to see. Today, because of the fin's possible importance, it is also discussed critically.

In Swiss lakes and rivers, many fish with an adipose fin live. The **whitefish** are the most important food fish for professional fishers in many lakes. Lake trout, brown trout and grayling also belong to them. Anyone who spots a small fin between the back and the tail while fishing very probably has a salmon-like fish on the hook.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thin, supporting rods that spread out most fins.
A family of fish that includes salmon, trout, char and whitefish.
Silvery salmon-like fish that are often caught in Swiss lakes.
Small, often colourful fish that many people keep in aquariums.

gewusst: The adipose fin can help to identify fish species at a glance.
In salmon, it has been found that animals without an adipose fin beat their tails harder in a current.
Depending on the region, whitefish in Switzerland are also called Albeli, Balchen or Blaufelchen.

teile.einleitung: Coregonids, in Switzerland mostly called “Felchen” (whitefish), are slim, silvery gleaming fish from the salmon family. They live in cool, oxygen-rich lakes and are the most important food fish of Swiss professional fishing.
wichtigste: Coregonids are called “Felchen” in Switzerland and often “Maränen” in northern Germany.
They belong to the salmon family.
Whitefish live mainly in cool, oxygen-rich lakes.
They are slim and silvery gleaming and have a small mouth with almost no teeth.
Many species are told apart by the number of their gill rakers.
Most whitefish spawn in winter.
In Switzerland they are caught mainly as a food fish.
Whitefish and their relatives occur in the north of Europe, Asia and North America.

abschnitte.text: Whitefish have a **slim, silvery** body with a greenish to bluish back. Their mouth is small and almost toothless. Like all members of the salmon family, they carry a small **adipose fin** between the dorsal fin and the tail. Most species grow to 25 to 50 centimetres long.

Whitefish need **cool, oxygen-rich** water. In Switzerland they live in almost all the larger lakes, for example Lake Constance, Lake Zurich, Lake Lucerne, Lake Thun and Lake Geneva. Worldwide, coregonids occur in the north of Europe, Asia and North America. In North America they are called whitefish.

Many whitefish eat tiny **plankton**, that is small water fleas and small crustaceans. To do this they filter the water with their gill rakers (“Kiemenreusen”), which are fine spines on the gill arches. The more numerous and the denser these **gill rakers** are, the smaller the food they can catch. That is why experts count the spines in order to tell whitefish species apart. Other species with fewer spines look for their food more on the lake bed.

Most whitefish in Swiss lakes **spawn in winter**. They lay their eggs in open water or above the lake bed, at different depths depending on the species. The young fish hatch in spring. In many lakes **fish hatcheries** help by raising eggs from caught whitefish and then releasing the young fish.

In Switzerland over 30 species of whitefish are known, and many of them exist in only a single lake. They are called, for example, Balchen, Albeli, Gangfisch or Blaufelchen. Some species died out in the 20th century because too many nutrients got into the lakes and oxygen was lacking at the bottom. Today the lakes are cleaner again, but in some lakes there is now less food and the catches fell sharply. In Lake Constance the catching of whitefish was therefore banned for several years.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fine spines on the gills with which fish sieve small food out of the water.
Tiny living things that drift in the water.
A small fin without rays on the back, typical of the salmon family.
Occurs in only a single place in the world.
The northern German name for whitefish and their close relatives.

gewusst: In some Swiss lakes several species of whitefish live side by side, and they only developed apart after the last Ice Age.
Whitefish fillets are a popular speciality in restaurants by the lake.
Experts often need a magnifying glass to count the gill rakers of a whitefish.

teile.einleitung: Earth centipedes (“Erdläufer”) are long, very slender centipedes that live hidden in the soil. They have many short pairs of legs and move through the earth almost like small earthworms. There they hunt other soil animals as small predators.
wichtigste: Earth centipedes are a group of the centipedes.
They have an elongated, very slender body with many pairs of legs.
Depending on the species they have about 27 to over 190 pairs of legs.
The number of their pairs of legs is always odd.
Earth centipedes are blind and find their prey with their antennae.
They hunt small soil animals with venom claws.
The native earth centipedes are harmless to humans.

abschnitte.text: Earth centipedes form an order within the **centipedes**, which is called Geophilomorpha scientifically. Centipedes belong to the myriapods in the wider sense, but they are predators. Worldwide there are over a thousand species of earth centipedes. In Switzerland several dozen species live, and they are mostly yellowish to brownish in colour.

The body of an earth centipede is long, thin and flexible like a thread. Each **body segment** carries a pair of short legs. Depending on the species there are about 27 to over 190 pairs of legs, and it is always an odd number. Earth centipedes have no eyes but feel their way through the dark earth with their **antennae**.

Earth centipedes live in the earth, under stones, in leaf litter and in rotting wood. Instead of running fast, they push their body through narrow tunnels like an **earthworm**. In doing so they can stretch their body and contract it again. Most species are only a few centimetres long, but tropical species can reach 20 centimetres.

Earth centipedes are small **predators**. They eat worms, insect larvae, springtails and other small soil animals. Their front legs are converted into venom claws, with which they seize and paralyse the prey. For humans this venom is harmless in our native species.

The female earth centipede lays her eggs in a small cavity in the soil. Then she curls protectively round the eggs and stays with them, and this care is called **brood care**. She licks the eggs clean so that they do not go mouldy. The mother also guards the newly hatched young for a while.

Earth centipedes are among the many small creatures that make up a healthy soil. Because they hunt other soil animals, they keep their numbers in balance. They are themselves food for birds, shrews and ground beetles. In the **compost heap** or under stones in the garden you can often discover them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A predatory arthropod with many pairs of legs and venom claws.
A section of the body, many of which lie one behind the other.
Converted front legs with which centipedes inject venom into prey.
When parent animals protect and look after their eggs or young.

gewusst: No centipede has exactly a hundred legs, because the number of pairs of legs is always odd.
Some earth centipedes can glow when disturbed.
Earth centipedes can push themselves through the earth both forwards and backwards.

teile.einleitung: Destruents or decomposers are living things that break down dead plants and animals and turn them back into nutrients for the soil. Without them the Earth would disappear under mountains of leaves, wood and carcasses.
wichtigste: Destruents are also called decomposers.
They eat and break down dead organic remains such as leaves, wood, droppings and dead animals.
They include bacteria, fungi and many small soil animals.
Dung beetles are decomposers and carry nutrients back into the soil.
From the remains, fertile humus is formed.
Destruents close the cycle of nature between plants and animals.
In a compost heap you can watch them at work.

abschnitte.text: The word **destruent** comes from the Latin destruere, which means to destroy or to break down. Destruents feed on **dead organic matter**, that is on everything that was once alive. This includes fallen leaves, dead tree trunks, droppings and animal carcasses. They break down these substances into smaller and smaller pieces until in the end simple nutrients are left.

Experts divide the living things in an ecosystem into three groups. **Producers** such as plants make food with the help of sunlight. **Consumers** such as animals eat plants or other animals. Destruents break down the dead remains of all the others and give the nutrients back to the soil. There the plants take them up again, and the cycle begins anew.

Many decomposers are small animals: **earthworms**, woodlice, millipedes, springtails and snails chop up leaves and pull them into the soil. Dung beetles bury droppings and so bring them into the earth. Burying beetles, a kind of beetle, bury dead mice. The real fine work is done by **bacteria** and **fungi**, which chemically break the remains down into simple substances.

In the forest the autumn leaves almost completely disappear by the next summer, because decomposers break them down. A fallen tree is broken down over many years by beetle larvae and fungi, and this **dead wood** is a habitat for many species. In the **compost** in the garden, worms and microbes turn kitchen waste into dark, crumbly earth. Fallen fruit that rots on the ground is also put to use by destruents.

Without destruents there would be no **humus**, that is no fertile earth for farmers and gardens. The nutrients would stay trapped in dead plants and animals, and new plants could not grow. The researcher Charles Darwin already studied how earthworms turn over the soil. In a handful of healthy earth live more living things than there are people on Earth.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that breaks down dead remains, also called a decomposer.
Dark, fertile earth made of broken down plant and animal remains.
A living thing that makes its own food, for example a plant.
A living thing that eats other living things.
A habitat with all the living things in it, for example a forest or a lake.

gewusst: In a handful of earth live more living things than there are people on Earth.
Earthworms pull leaves into their tubes at night in order to eat them there slowly.
Without decomposers, after a few decades there would be a layer of old leaves metres high in the forest.

teile.einleitung: In everyday life “fit” means sporty and healthy, but in biology the word has a different meaning. There, fitness describes how successfully a living thing has offspring that themselves survive and reproduce. This idea is a key to understanding evolution.
wichtigste: Biological fitness is the ability to produce offspring successfully and to secure their survival.
In biology, fitness does not mean strong or sporty.
Animals with high fitness pass on their features to more offspring.
This is the core of natural selection according to Charles Darwin.
Fitness always depends on the environment in which an animal lives.
Helping relatives can also raise fitness.
The expression “survival of the fittest” comes from Herbert Spencer.

abschnitte.text: In **evolutionary biology**, **fitness** describes how many offspring that can survive a living thing has compared with others of its species. An animal with many young that themselves grow up and reproduce has a high fitness. An animal that leaves no offspring has a fitness of zero, no matter how strong it is. Fitness therefore measures reproductive success. It is always a comparison between individuals of the same species.

The English naturalist **Charles Darwin** described **natural selection** in 1859. Living things that are better adapted to their environment have, on average, more offspring. Their features are therefore passed on more often to the next generation. Over many generations, whole species change in this way. The philosopher Herbert Spencer coined the expression “survival of the fittest” for this, which means more “survival of the best adapted” than “of the strongest”.

A feature is not equally useful everywhere. A thick coat is an advantage for a mountain hare in the Alps, but in the desert it would be a hindrance. A white winter coat camouflages in snow, but on brown ground it gives the animal away. If the environment changes, for example through **climate change**, the advantages can also shift. That is why there is no “fittest” animal in general.

The peacock has a magnificent tail that actually hinders it and attracts enemies. But because females prefer males with beautiful tails, these have more offspring. This is called **sexual selection**. A rabbit that has many litters a year can achieve a high fitness even if many young are eaten. An elephant has only a few young but looks after them for a long time and intensively.

Workers among honeybees have no offspring of their own. Even so, they contribute to passing on their genes, because they support their sisters and the queen. The biologist William D. Hamilton explained this in 1964 with **inclusive fitness**. It counts not only one's own young but also the success of close relatives. This explains why some animals help others.

begriffe.erklaerung: Slow change of living things over many generations.
Better adapted living things have more offspring and pass on their features.
Reproductive success including help given to relatives.
Selection through the choice of a mate, for example when females prefer attractive males.

gewusst: A healthy, strong stag with no offspring has, biologically speaking, a lower fitness than a weakly one with many young.
Darwin used the expression “survival of the fittest” only in later editions of his famous book.
In bees, a worker can pass on her genes through her sisters without laying eggs herself.

teile.einleitung: The Eurasian otter is a skilful swimmer from the mustelid family that lives on rivers and lakes. It had almost completely disappeared from Switzerland and is now slowly returning. Anyone who sees a wild otter is very lucky.
wichtigste: The Eurasian otter is a mustelid that lives in and beside water.
Its brown fur is very dense and keeps it warm and dry when diving.
It eats mainly fish, while the beaver, by contrast, eats plants.
When diving, it can close its nose and ears.
The mother usually has two to three young once a year.
In the 20th century, the otter was almost completely wiped out in Switzerland.
Today it is regarded as a symbol of clean, healthy waters.

abschnitte.text: The **Eurasian otter** grows to about 60 to 90 centimetres long without its tail, and a powerful tail of around 30 to 45 centimetres is added to that. It usually weighs between 6 and 12 kilograms. Its body is long and streamlined, and its paws have **webbing**. The brown fur is extremely dense, and air stays trapped between the hairs, which insulates it. When diving, its nose and ears close, and with its long whiskers it senses prey in murky water.

Otters live on rivers, streams, lakes and marshes with natural banks. Clean water, enough fish and hiding places under roots or in bushes are important. Their den is called a **holt**, and the entrance is often under water. An otter's territory stretches along a river and can be several kilometres long. Otters are out and about mainly at dusk and at night.

The otter eats mainly fish, for example perch, trout or white fish. It also catches crayfish, frogs, waterbirds and small mammals. A grown otter needs about a kilogram of food a day. In this it differs clearly from the **beaver**, which eats only plants such as bark, twigs and herbs. Otters hunt alone and are very agile divers.

The otter mother usually has young once a year, often two to three. The young are born blind and have to learn to swim. They stay with their mother for about a year before they look for a territory of their own. Otters are very playful. They like to slide into the water on mud slides or, in winter, on snow.

In the past the otter was regarded as a competitor of fishers and was hunted heavily. In addition there were polluted waters and straightened rivers. It has been protected in Switzerland since 1952, but it still almost completely disappeared, and in 1989 it was considered extinct. Since about 2009, otters have been moving in from Austria along the Inn into the Engadine, and later they also turned up on the Aare and the Rhine. It is regarded as an **indicator species** for intact waters, because it can only live where the water is clean and has enough fish.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of predators with a long, slim body that also includes the badger and the weasel.
The otter's den, often with an entrance under water.
An area that an animal lives in and defends against others of its species.
A species whose presence shows that a habitat is healthy.

gewusst: The otter's fur is among the densest in the animal kingdom, with tens of thousands of hairs growing on one square centimetre.
Otters mark their territory with droppings that, surprisingly, are said to smell a little of jasmine or fish.
Young otters are at first afraid of the water and are sometimes pushed in by their mother.

teile.einleitung: The scarlet darter is a dragonfly whose males are a bright, fiery red. Originally it was at home mainly around the Mediterranean. Because it is getting warmer, it is spreading ever further north and can now also be seen in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The scarlet darter is a bright red dragonfly.
Its scientific name is Crocothemis erythraea.
Only the males are fiery red, the females are yellowish brown.
It belongs to the darters.
It loves warm, sunny ponds and pools.
Its larvae live in the water and hunt small animals there.
It has spread northwards with climate warming.

abschnitte.text: The scarlet darter grows to about 3.5 to 4.5 centimetres long. The males have a broad, flat abdomen that is **bright red**, and even the wing veins shimmer reddish. The females, by contrast, are **yellowish brown** and much less conspicuous. At the base of the wings, both have a small amber-coloured spot.

The scarlet darter occurs in Africa, southern Europe and parts of Asia. It likes warm, shallow, sunny **still waters** such as ponds, pools and gravel pits. In recent decades it has spread strongly northwards because of **climate warming**. In Switzerland it is now found mainly at lower, warm altitudes at many bodies of water.

Scarlet darters are skilful **hunters on the wing**. They catch mosquitoes, flies and other small insects in mid-air. With their huge compound eyes they can see almost all round. The males like to sit on a lookout post on the bank and set off from there on short hunting flights.

The males defend a small **territory** by the water and drive off rivals. After mating, the female dips her abdomen into the water and lays the eggs as she does so. From these hatch **larvae**, which live in the water and eat small water animals. After several moults, the larva climbs up a stalk and the finished dragonfly emerges.

The scarlet darter is regarded as an example of how climate change is altering the animal world. Experts follow its spread closely. It is completely harmless to people, since dragonflies do not sting. Anyone who visits a warm pond in summer can, with a bit of luck, watch it well.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of dragonflies that includes many colourful species with a broad abdomen.
The young form of an insect, which looks different from the adult animal.
Bodies of water without a current, for example ponds and pools.
An area that an animal defends against others of its species.

gewusst: Dragonflies have existed for over 300 million years, much longer than the dinosaurs.
The scientific name erythraea means roughly “the red one”.
Dragonflies can move their four wings independently of one another and can even fly backwards.

teile.einleitung: The true perches are a family of freshwater fish that includes the “Egli” (perch), one of the most popular food fish in Switzerland. Typical of them are two dorsal fins, of which the front one carries spiny rays. Other well known species are the zander and the ruffe.
wichtigste: The true perches form the fish family Percidae.
The “Egli”, also called the river perch, belongs to the true perches.
True perches have two dorsal fins, the front one with hard spines.
There are about 200 species, most of them in North America.
They live almost only in the fresh water of the Northern Hemisphere.
In Switzerland, species found include the perch, the zander, the ruffe and the rare Rhône streber.
Perch fillets (“Eglifilets”) are a typical dish on Swiss lakes.

abschnitte.text: True perches have an elongated body, somewhat flattened at the sides, with hard **scales**. Typical are two dorsal fins: the front one has pointed **spiny rays**, the rear one rather soft rays. Many species have dark cross bands that camouflage them well in dense plants. The spines protect them from predatory fish.

The roughly 200 species live in the fresh water of Europe, Asia and above all **North America**. There are many small, colourful species there that are called darters. Some species such as the zander also tolerate somewhat salty brackish water. In Africa, South America and Australia there are naturally no true perches.

The **Egli** or river perch is at home in almost all Swiss lakes and many rivers. It has a greenish back, five to nine dark cross stripes and reddish pelvic and anal fins. Young perch live in shoals and eat plankton and insect larvae, while large perch hunt small fish. In spring the female lays her eggs in long, net-like **spawn ribbons** on plants or branches.

The **zander** is the largest true perch of Europe and can grow over a metre long. It hunts mainly at dusk and has large eyes and pointed canine teeth. The ruffe is small and has only one continuous dorsal fin. Both also occur in Switzerland, and the zander was introduced into many lakes.

**Perch fillets** are a popular dish in Switzerland, often fried with lemon and chips. Because Swiss fishers do not catch enough perch, a large part of the fillets comes from abroad, for example from Eastern Europe. True perches are also very popular with hobby anglers. In some countries they are raised in fish farms.

Not all true perches are doing well. The **Rhône streber**, a small bottom dwelling fish, lives in Switzerland now only in the Doubs and is threatened with extinction. The reasons are power stations, canalised rivers and poor water quality. People are trying to save it with protection projects.

begriffe.erklaerung: The scientific name of the family of true perches.
A hard, pointed rod that supports a fin.
The eggs of fish and amphibians.
A fish that eats other fish.

gewusst: The word “Egli” is a typically Swiss name, and in Germany people mostly say “Flussbarsch” (river perch).
The spawn ribbons of a female perch can grow over a metre long.
The river perch recognises others of its species by smell and prefers to form shoals with relatives.

teile.einleitung: Carnivores are animals that feed wholly or mainly on other animals. Experts call them carnivores, from the Latin word for meat. From the tiny ladybird to the polar bear, there are carnivores of all sizes.
wichtigste: A carnivore feeds on other animals.
Animals that eat almost nothing but meat are called carnivores.
Pointed canine teeth and sharp carnassial teeth are typical.
Cats are strict carnivores, while dogs and bears also eat plants.
Carnivores are often far up the food chain.
There are even carnivorous plants such as the sundew.
In Switzerland live carnivores such as the lynx, wolf, fox and stoat.

abschnitte.text: A **carnivore** is an animal that feeds on other animals. The opposite is the **herbivore** such as cows and deer. Animals that eat both, such as wild boar, bears or humans, are called **omnivores**. Carnivores hunt their prey themselves, or they eat dead animals, and then they are called scavengers. They include mammals, birds, reptiles, fish, insects and spiders.

Meat-eating mammals usually have long, pointed **canine teeth** for seizing and sharp **carnassial teeth** that cut meat like scissors. Many have claws, a good sense of smell and forward-facing eyes to judge distances well. Their gut is shorter than in herbivores, because meat is easier to digest. Birds of prey such as the golden eagle have sharp talons and a hooked beak. Snakes swallow their prey whole.

**Cats** are strict carnivores, they need certain nutrients that occur only in meat. Wolves and foxes eat mainly meat, but also berries and fruit. The group of **carnivorans** in biology is also called Carnivora, but not all of them eat meat. The giant panda belongs to it and eats almost nothing but bamboo. Conversely, there are many meat-eaters that are not carnivorans, for example dragonflies or sharks.

Carnivores stand higher up in the **food chain** than herbivores. The fox eats the mouse, the mouse eats seeds. At the very top are apex predators such as the wolf, lynx, orca or polar bear, which have hardly any natural enemies. Carnivores regulate the number of their prey animals and so maintain the balance in nature. The lynx in the Swiss Alps and the Jura hunts mainly roe deer and chamois.

A few plants also catch animals. The **sundew** grows in Swiss bogs and catches insects with sticky drops on its leaves. The butterwort also uses sticky leaves. The Venus flytrap from North America snaps its leaves shut in a flash. Such plants mostly grow on soils poor in nutrients and in this way obtain extra nutrients.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technical word for a meat-eater.
A sharp cheek tooth that cuts meat like scissors.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.
A series that shows who eats whom.

gewusst: The giant panda belongs to the carnivorans but eats almost nothing but bamboo.
A ladybird is a carnivore and can eat thousands of aphids in its life.
A wolf can eat several kilograms of meat in a single meal.

teile.einleitung: The yolk sac is a small store bag full of nutrients that hangs on young animals before they can feed themselves. You can see it especially well on freshly hatched fish such as whitefish and lake trout. It is, so to speak, the first packed lunch that the mother gives her offspring.
wichtigste: The yolk sac contains yolk, a mixture of protein, fat and other nutrients.
Freshly hatched whitefish and lake trout live at first from their yolk sac.
Young fish with a yolk sac are called larvae or yolk sac larvae.
When the yolk sac is used up, the young animals have to look for food themselves.
Birds, reptiles and mammals also form a yolk sac as embryos.
In humans the yolk sac helps with blood formation early in pregnancy.
In Swiss fish hatcheries, fish larvae with a yolk sac are raised and then released into lakes.

abschnitte.text: Besides the germ, an egg contains a store of **yolk**. It consists mainly of protein and fat and is full of energy. While the embryo grows, the yolk is wrapped in a skin, the **yolk sac**. Blood vessels carry the nutrients from it to the young animal.

In many fish the young hatch before the yolk is used up. These young fish are called **larvae** or yolk sac larvae. The yolk sac hangs like a small, often orange balloon on the belly. During this time the larvae still eat nothing and move little.

Freshly hatched **whitefish** live in the first days from their yolk sac. Young **lake trout** too live at first on their store while they lie well hidden in the gravel of the river bed. Only when the yolk sac is almost used up do they swim off and eat tiny creatures such as plankton or insect larvae. This changeover is a dangerous time, for many larvae do not find enough food.

A chick in a hen's egg also feeds on the yolk, that is the egg yolk. Shortly before hatching it draws the rest of the yolk sac into its belly. That is why a freshly hatched chick can still manage about two to three days without food. In turtles, snakes and crocodiles it is similar.

Mammals are fed in the womb through the **placenta**. Even so, a human embryo also forms a small yolk sac in the first weeks. There the first **blood cells** arise, before the liver takes over this job. Later the yolk sac shrinks back again.

In Switzerland there are many **fish hatcheries** that hatch eggs of whitefish and trout. In winter the fishers strip eggs and milt from fish that are ready to spawn. In the hatchery the larvae hatch protected in jars with running water. Later the young fish are released into lakes and rivers so that there are enough fish.

begriffe.erklaerung: The nutrient-rich store in the egg, in a hen's egg the egg yolk.
A young animal that still looks different from the adults.
A living thing in its earliest development in the egg or in the womb.
An organ that supplies a baby in the womb with nutrients.

gewusst: Because chicks still live off the yolk sac, hatcheries can transport them shortly after hatching without food.
In some sharks the yolk sac hangs on the young animal while it is still growing inside the mother's body.
Whitefish larvae are only about one centimetre long when they hatch.

teile.einleitung: The true owls are a large family of birds of prey of the night. They include, for example, the tawny owl, the eagle owl and the long-eared owl. With their large eyes, their fine hearing and their silent flight, they are perfect nocturnal hunters.
wichtigste: The true owls form a bird family with the scientific name Strigidae.
The tawny owl belongs to the family of true owls.
Worldwide there are over 200 species.
The second owl family is the barn owls.
Owls mostly hunt at dusk and at night.
Thanks to soft feathers they fly almost silently.
Indigestible remains such as bones and hair they bring up again as pellets.

abschnitte.text: The true owls include wood owls, eagle owls, eared owls and many other species. Together with the **barn owls** they form the order of owls. True owls usually have a round face, whereas barn owls have a heart shaped face. They live on all continents except Antarctica.

Owls have huge eyes that face forwards so that they can judge distances well. They can hardly move their eyes, so they turn the head through about 270 degrees. The **facial disc** of feathers guides sounds to the ears like a funnel. In some species the ear openings are at different heights, so they can locate a mouse even under snow.

The flight feathers of owls have fine fringes at the edge that dampen the rushing of the air. In this way the prey does not hear the owl coming. With their powerful feet and pointed **talons** they seize mice, birds, frogs or insects. Small prey is often swallowed whole, and later they bring up bones and hair as **pellets**.

In Switzerland several species of true owls breed. The **tawny owl** is the most common owl and calls in the forest with the well known “hu-hu-huuu”. The **eagle owl** is the largest owl in Europe and can reach a wingspan of about 1.7 metres. Also living here are the long-eared owl, the little owl, Tengmalm's owl, the scops owl and the small pygmy owl.

Most true owls do not build a nest of their own. They breed in **tree holes**, in rock niches, in old crows' nests or in nest boxes. The female incubates the white eggs, and the male brings food. The young often leave the nest before they can really fly, and are then called branchers.

All species of owl are protected in Switzerland. Some species such as the little owl have become rare because old fruit trees and holes are lacking. With **nest boxes** and the preservation of old trees they can be helped. Owls are also useful to humans, because they eat many mice.

begriffe.erklaerung: A lump of hair and bones that owls bring up.
A young owl that has left the nest and sits on branches, but cannot yet fly well.
In biology, a group of closely related animal species.
An animal that is awake and about mainly at night.

gewusst: The feather ears of the eagle owl and the long-eared owl are not real ears, but just tufts of feathers.
The pygmy owl is the smallest owl in Europe and hardly bigger than a sparrow.
Because owls can hardly move their eyes, they turn the whole head instead.

teile.einleitung: Charles Darwin was an English naturalist who developed the theory of evolution in the 19th century. He explained how living things change over a very long time through natural selection. He also studied closely how important earthworms are for the soil.
wichtigste: Charles Darwin lived in England from 1809 to 1882.
From 1831 to 1836 he travelled round the world on the ship HMS Beagle.
On the Galápagos Islands he observed finches, tortoises and other animals.
In 1859 he published his famous book on the origin of species.
He explained evolution through natural selection.
In his last book he described how earthworms make the soil fertile.
He is buried in Westminster Abbey in London.

abschnitte.text: Charles Robert **Darwin** was born in 1809 in Shrewsbury in England. He was first supposed to become a doctor, then a vicar, but he was much more interested in beetles, plants and rocks. At the age of 22 he got the chance to join a great research voyage as a naturalist. Later he lived with his wife Emma and many children at Down House near London, where he researched and wrote.

From 1831 to 1836 Darwin travelled round the world on the survey ship **HMS Beagle**. He visited South America, the Galápagos Islands, Australia and many other places. On the way he collected thousands of animals, plants, fossils and rocks. The animals of the **Galápagos Islands** in particular set him thinking, because on different islands similar birds and tortoises looked slightly different.

Darwin realised that the offspring of a living thing differ slightly from one another. Those that are better adapted to their environment survive more easily and have more offspring, and he called this **natural selection**. Over very many generations, new species can arise in this way. His book “On the Origin of Species” of 1859 changed biology for ever, and almost at the same time the researcher Alfred Russel Wallace came upon similar ideas.

Over many decades Darwin observed what **earthworms** do in the soil. He found that they eat earth, pull plant remains into the ground and loosen and mix the earth. With experiments in his own garden he showed that stones slowly sink into the earth over the years, because the worms below carry earth away and deposit it on top. His last book of 1881 dealt with exactly this subject and became a great success in his time.

Darwin's ideas are the foundation of modern biology, even though today much more is known about genes and heredity than he knew. His theory explains why living things are so well adapted to their surroundings. In his time there were fierce **discussions**, because his ideas also concerned the origin of humans. After his death in 1882 he was buried in Westminster Abbey in London, where Isaac Newton also lies.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow change of living things over many generations.
Living things that are better adapted survive more easily and pass on their characteristics.
Petrified remains or traces of living things from earlier times.
A group of living things that can reproduce with each other.

gewusst: Darwin was often seasick on the Beagle and spent a lot of time on land.
Darwin even tested whether earthworms react to piano sounds, and found that they pay more attention to vibrations than to notes.
Dozens of animals, plants and places are named after Darwin, for example the city of Darwin in Australia.

teile.einleitung: The European eel is a snake-shaped fish that makes one of the most astonishing journeys in the animal kingdom. It is born in the Sargasso Sea in the middle of the Atlantic, grows up in rivers and lakes of Europe, including in Switzerland. To spawn, it migrates thousands of kilometres back to the sea.
wichtigste: The eel is a fish and breathes mainly with gills.
European eels lay their eggs in the Sargasso Sea in the Atlantic.
Young, transparent eels are called glass eels.
In rivers and lakes they live as yellow eels with a dark brown to olive green back.
In autumn they migrate back to the sea as silver eels.
Females grow larger than males and can become over a metre long.
After spawning the adult eels die.

abschnitte.text: The eel has a long, snake-shaped body and a smooth, slimy skin with very small scales. Dorsal, tail and anal fins form a continuous **fin fringe**. Females usually grow clearly larger than males and can become over a metre long. Males usually stay under half a metre.

European eels lay their eggs in the **Sargasso Sea** in the Atlantic, far from Europe. The tiny, leaf-shaped larvae drift with ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream over several years towards Europe. On the coasts they change into transparent **glass eels** and swim up the rivers. Eels thus make the reverse migration of salmon, because they migrate from river to sea to spawn.

In fresh water the eels grow up for many years as **yellow eels**, with a dark brown to olive green back and a yellowish belly. They eat insect larvae, worms, snails, crayfish and small fish. When they are ready for the return journey, they become **silver eels** with a silvery belly and larger eyes. During the migration to the sea they no longer eat anything, because their gut shrinks.

In the past many eels swam up the Rhine as far as Swiss rivers and lakes. Today **hydroelectric power stations** and weirs block the way for many eels. On the return migration silver eels also often end up in the turbines. That is why fish ladders and protective grilles are being built at some power stations.

The European eel is today regarded as **critically endangered**. Since about 1980 far fewer glass eels arrive on Europe’s coasts than before. Reasons are overfishing, built-up rivers, diseases, parasites and pollutants in the water. Because eels still cannot be bred in captivity, wild glass eels are caught for eel farms.

Eel is eaten smoked or cooked in many countries. The blood of the eel is poisonous raw, because it contains a protein toxin. On heating, this toxin breaks down, which is why cooked or smoked eel is harmless. Because of the threat, nature conservation organisations today advise against eating eel.

begriffe.erklaerung: When fish lay their eggs.
A young, almost transparent eel on the coast.
An adult, silvery eel on its way to the sea.
A sea area in the Atlantic in which eels reproduce.

gewusst: No human has ever observed how European eels mate in the wild.
In wet weather eels can crawl short distances over wet meadows.

teile.einleitung: Chaser was a female Border Collie from the USA who became known as “the cleverest dog in the world”. She learned the names of over a thousand toys and could fetch them on command. Studies with Chaser showed that some dogs can learn to tell apart over a thousand different object names.
wichtigste: Chaser was a Border Collie, a very intelligent herding dog breed.
She lived from 2004 to 2019 in South Carolina in the USA.
Her owner was the psychologist John W. Pilley.
Chaser knew the names of 1,022 toys.
She could also combine simple commands with names.
She matched unknown words to a new toy by ruling out what she already knew.
The research with Chaser changed the picture of how much dogs can learn.

abschnitte.text: Chaser was born in 2004 and lived with the family of **John W. Pilley**, a retired professor of psychology at Wofford College in South Carolina. Pilley wanted to find out how many words a dog can learn. So every day he practised for several hours with his dog in a playful way. Chaser loved these exercises, and for her they were a big game.

Little by little Chaser learned the names of **1,022 toys**, including many cuddly toys, balls and frisbees. Every toy had a name of its own, and Chaser picked out the right one from a big heap on command. The results were published in 2011 in a scientific journal. Before that, the best known was mainly the German Border Collie Rico, who knew about 200 words.

Chaser also understood commands such as “take”, “paw” or “nose” and could combine them with different toys. She also learned general terms such as “ball” for all her balls. Especially exciting was the **principle of exclusion**: if she heard an unknown name, she fetched the only new toy in the heap. This is a learning strategy that is also known in small children.

The **Border Collie** comes from the border region between Scotland and England, hence the name “border”. It was bred as a herding dog for flocks of sheep and is very eager to learn, quick and attentive. Border Collies need a lot of exercise and tasks for the mind, otherwise they get bored. In Switzerland too they are popular in dog sports and on farms.

The studies with Chaser showed that dogs can learn **words** much better than people used to think. Researchers stress, however, that not every dog manages this, since Chaser had a great deal of talent and very intensive training. Today experts at universities all over the world are investigating how dogs process language. Chaser died in 2019, a year after her owner John Pilley.

begriffe.erklaerung: A British herding dog breed that is regarded as especially intelligent.
You find the right thing by ruling out everything you already know.
A word for a whole group, for example “ball” for all balls.
A scientific investigation with exact experiments and measurements.

gewusst: Chaser knew more words than many children can speak at the age of two.
A book was written about Chaser, and she appeared on television programmes.
Chaser lived to about 15 years old and died in 2019.

teile.einleitung: In German, walking “im Gänsemarsch”, literally “in goose march”, means walking one behind the other in a line. The expression comes from geese, which often walk neatly one after another. People, too, walk in single file on narrow paths or in groups.
wichtigste: Walking “im Gänsemarsch” means walking one behind the other in a line.
The expression comes from goose families, which often waddle in a line.
Usually an experienced animal goes at the front and the others follow.
On narrow mountain paths you walk in single file for safety.
Nursery and school classes also often walk in single file.
Many other animals such as ducks, elephants or ants also move in lines.
In the air, wild geese often fly in a V formation.

abschnitte.text: The German **Gänsemarsch** is an idiom and means that several people walk one behind the other in a single line. The expression comes from geese, which often walk neatly one behind the other. Goose families with their chicks in particular move along like this. A similar German expression is “im Entenmarsch”, literally “in duck march”, and in English you say “in single file”.

abschnitte.titel: Why do geese walk in a line?
abschnitte.text: Young geese, the **goslings**, follow their mother from the very first day. After hatching they have imprinted on her and stay close behind her. This way they do not lose each other and are better protected. Often one parent goes at the front and the gander at the back, to watch for dangers.

On narrow **mountain paths** in the Alps you walk in single file so that nobody slips off the side of the path. The person with the most experience often goes at the front and sets the pace. Whoever goes at the back makes sure that nobody is left behind. On glaciers, too, rope teams walk in a line, joined by a **rope**.

Nursery and school classes often walk in single file on outings so that the teacher can see everyone. In Switzerland the rule is that where there is no **pavement**, pedestrians walk at the edge of the road. Outside built-up areas you walk on the left edge, so that you can see the cars coming towards you. A group is then safest walking one behind the other in single file.

It is not only geese that walk one behind the other. Elephants often travel in a long line across the savannah, and ants follow a scent trail along **ant trails**. The caterpillars of the **processionary moth** crawl head to tail in long chains. In the air, wild geese fly in a V formation, with each goose benefiting from the updraught of the one in front.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed group of words with a figurative meaning.
When a young animal binds itself firmly to a particular creature shortly after birth.
Mountaineers who are joined by a rope for safety.
The raised footpath beside the road, called “Bürgersteig” in Germany.

gewusst: By flying in a V formation, wild geese save energy and can cover longer distances.
Processionary moths have their name because their caterpillars travel in long lines as in a procession.

teile.einleitung: Coregonus is the scientific genus name of the whitefish, “Renken” and “Maränen”. With this Latin name researchers all over the world understand each other, no matter what the fish are called in their language.
wichtigste: Coregonus is the scientific genus name of the whitefish.
The genus includes several dozen species.
It belongs to the salmon family, the salmonids.
The name was introduced in 1758 by Carl von Linné.
Every species has a two part name, for example Coregonus albula for the vendace.
Classifying the species is difficult, because many whitefish look very similar.
Several Coregonus species live in only a single Swiss lake.

abschnitte.text: In science, living things get a name in two parts, which is called **binary nomenclature**. The first part is the **genus**, the second the species. In Coregonus albula, Coregonus is the genus and albula the species. Genus names are written with a capital letter and in italics. In this way people all over the world know exactly which animal is meant.

The Swedish naturalist **Carl von Linné** introduced the name Coregonus in the year 1758. Linné developed the system of two part names that is still valid today. The name is formed from ancient Greek words. The fish themselves have many popular names depending on the region, for example “Felchen”, “Renke”, “Maräne” or “Schnäpel”.

Coregonus belongs to the **salmon family**, which also includes trout, salmon and chars. Within this family the whitefish form a group of their own with their closest relatives. Like all members of the salmon family, they have a small adipose fin on the back. Unlike trout, they have larger scales and a small, almost toothless mouth.

The species of the genus Coregonus often look so alike that they are easily confused. Experts therefore compare body shape, spawning time, habitat, the number of **gill rakers** and today also the genetic material. Many species arose only after the last **Ice Age**, about 15,000 years ago, when the lakes formed. That is why experts still argue today about exactly how many species there are.

In Lake Constance lives the Blaufelchen with the name Coregonus wartmanni. Lake Lucerne, Lake Thun and Lake Brienz each have whitefish species of their own. Researchers at Eawag have studied the whitefish of the Swiss lakes closely and in doing so have described new species. This makes Switzerland an especially important region for the diversity of the genus Coregonus.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of closely related species, for example all whitefish.
A group of living things that can reproduce with each other.
The system of two part scientific names.
The Swiss water research institute in Dübendorf.

gewusst: One and the same fish can be called Blaufelchen at Lake Constance, “Renke” in Bavaria and “Maräne” in northern Germany, but its scientific name stays the same.
In only about 15,000 years many new species of whitefish arose in Swiss lakes, which is very fast for evolution.
Carl von Linné gave thousands of plants and animals their scientific names.

teile.einleitung: The durian is a large, spiky fruit from South-East Asia that is famous for its extremely strong smell. Some people find that it smells of cheese, onions or even sewage, while others love its sweet, creamy taste. Many animals in the rainforest, especially orangutans, also eat durians very gladly.
wichtigste: The durian is a fruit from the rainforests of South-East Asia.
Orangutans love durians especially.
It is known for its strong smell, which many find unpleasant.
In South-East Asia it is called the “queen” or “king of fruits”.
The skin is covered with hard, pointed spines.
The flowers are pollinated at night mainly by fruit bats.
In many hotels and on public transport in Asia the durian is banned.

abschnitte.text: The durian grows on tall trees from the **mallow family** (Malvaceae). The fruit grows about 15 to 30 centimetres across and usually weighs one to three kilograms. Its name comes from the Malay word “duri”, which means thorn. Inside lie large seeds, wrapped in yellow, creamy **flesh**.

The ripe durian contains many different **scent compounds**, among them compounds containing sulphur. That is why it smells very strong, and you can often smell it from far away. In Singapore it is forbidden to take durians onto the underground, and many hotels do not allow them. More than once buildings have been evacuated because a gas leak was suspected, but the cause was a durian.

In the rainforest of Borneo and Sumatra, durians are an important food for **orangutans**. They can open the spiky skin with their powerful hands and teeth. Elephants, hornbills, sun bears and other animals also eat the fruits. In doing so they spread the seeds in the forest.

Durian trees flower at night. Their flowers are pollinated mainly by **fruit bats**, that is large fruit-eating bats. Without these animals the trees would bear far fewer fruits. That is why protecting fruit bats is also important for durian farmers.

Today durians are grown in Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines. A large part is exported to **China**, where the fruit is very popular. Good varieties such as “Musang King” are very expensive. In Switzerland you sometimes find durians frozen or fresh in Asian shops.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant family that also includes cocoa, the lime tree and hibiscus.
A large bat that eats fruit and nectar.
The transfer of pollen so that a plant can form fruit.
The soft, edible part of a fruit.

gewusst: A durian that falls from the tree can injure people because of its weight and its spines.
Durian trees can grow over 40 metres tall.
In South-East Asia there is durian ice cream, durian cake and even durian pizza.

teile.einleitung: The Town Musicians of Bremen is a well known fairy tale by the Brothers Grimm about four old animals that join together. A donkey, a dog, a cat and a cockerel want to become musicians in Bremen and on the way drive off a gang of robbers.
wichtigste: The Town Musicians of Bremen is a fairy tale by the Brothers Grimm.
In it a donkey, a dog, a cat and a cockerel appear.
All four animals are old and are supposed to be given away or killed by their owners.
Together they want to become town musicians in the city of Bremen.
With loud noise they drive robbers out of a house in the forest.
They never arrive in Bremen, because they stay happily in the robbers' house.
In Bremen there stands a famous bronze statue of the four animals.

abschnitte.text: An old **donkey** is no longer needed and sets off for Bremen to become a **town musician** there. On the way he meets an old hunting dog, a cat and a cockerel, who also had to flee. The cockerel was even meant to end up in the soup. Together they travel on and in the evening find a house with a light in the forest.

In the house **robbers** are sitting at a richly laid table. The animals stand on top of one another: the donkey at the bottom, on him the dog, then the cat and right at the top the cockerel. Together they make their music: the donkey brays, the dog barks, the cat miaows and the cockerel crows. The robbers take it for a ghost and flee. When a robber comes back at night, he is scratched, bitten and kicked and afterwards tells of terrible monsters.

The fairy tale is in the **Children's and Household Tales** by Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, since the second edition of 1819. The brothers collected stories that people told in Germany and wrote them down. The Town Musicians has the number 27. The story is among the most popular Grimm fairy tales and has often been adapted as a play, a film and a picture book.

The fairy tale shows that you can achieve much more **together** than alone. Each animal is weak on its own, but together they defeat the robbers. It also says that old animals and people are still worth something. And it gives courage to dare a new start when you are no longer needed.

**Bremen** is an old Hanseatic city in the north of Germany. Next to the town hall there has stood since 1953 a bronze statue by the sculptor **Gerhard Marcks**, which shows the four animals on top of one another. Many tourists touch the donkey's front legs because it is supposed to bring luck, and that is why they gleam golden. The town hall and the Roland statue of Bremen are part of the UNESCO World Heritage.

begriffe.erklaerung: A musician who in earlier times played at festivals in the service of a town.
A city that in the Middle Ages belonged to the trading league of the Hanse.
A metal made of copper and tin from which statues are often cast.
An invented story, often with magic and talking animals.

gewusst: The four animals never arrive in Bremen in the fairy tale.
The front legs of the donkey on the bronze statue have been rubbed quite shiny from being touched so much.
The Town Musicians of Bremen are today a landmark of the city of Bremen.

teile.einleitung: A white grub (“Engerling”) is the larva of a scarab beetle, for example of the cockchafer, the rose chafer or the stag beetle. It is whitish, fat and curved in a C shape and lives mostly in the soil or in rotting wood. Only after several years does it turn into a finished beetle.
wichtigste: A white grub is the larva of scarab beetles such as the cockchafer or the stag beetle.
It looks whitish, fat and curved in a C shape.
It has a brownish head and six legs at the front of the body.
White grubs live in the soil, in compost or in rotting wood.
Depending on the species, development into a beetle takes one to several years.
Cockchafer grubs can damage the roots of meadows and plants.
White grubs are an important food for moles, badgers, wild boar and birds.

abschnitte.text: A white grub has a soft, whitish body that is curved like a C. The head is hard and yellow to brown, with powerful **mouthparts** for gnawing. At the front sit six legs, with which it moves only slowly. The rear end is often darker, because there you can see the filled gut through the skin.

White grubs are the **larvae** of scarab beetles. These include the cockchafer, the summer chafer, the rose chafer, the rhinoceros beetle, the dung beetle and the stag beetle. The larva of a dung beetle is also fat, pale and curved in a C shape. Cockchafer grubs grow to about 4 to 5 centimetres long, and the larvae of the stag beetle even over 10 centimetres.

Most white grubs live hidden in the soil. Cockchafer grubs eat the **roots** of grasses and other plants there. Rose chafer grubs, by contrast, live in compost and eat dead plant parts, so they are useful. Stag beetle larvae grow up for several years in the rotting wood of old oaks.

The white grub moults several times, because its skin does not grow with it. When it is big enough, it builds itself a hollow in the ground and becomes a **pupa**. In the pupa its body changes completely into a beetle. This development from egg through larva and pupa to beetle is called complete **metamorphosis**.

In Switzerland cockchafer grubs usually live three years in the soil before they fly out as beetles. That is why in different regions there are particular **flight years**, which are called, for example, the Bernese, Uri or Basel flight year. In some years so many grubs eat at the roots that whole meadows turn brown. Farmers fight them in part with a natural fungus that infects only grubs.

begriffe.erklaerung: The young form of an insect, which looks quite different from the adult animal.
A large group of beetles with fan-like antennae, for example the cockchafer.
A resting stage in which the larva changes into the finished insect.
The transformation of an animal from the young form into the adult form.

gewusst: Rose chafer grubs often crawl forward on their backs.
The larva of the stag beetle can live up to eight years in the wood, and the finished beetle only a few weeks.
In the past there were so many cockchafers that schoolchildren had to collect them.

teile.einleitung: The Galapagos penguin is a very special penguin, because it lives not in the ice but on warm islands on the equator. It is the penguin species that lives furthest north. Sadly, it is also one of the rarest penguins in the world.
wichtigste: The Galapagos penguin lives on the Galapagos Islands in the Pacific, which belong to Ecuador.
It is the penguin species that lives furthest north, even close to the equator.
Unlike many other penguins, it lives not in Antarctica but on warm islands.
It is only about 50 centimetres tall and is one of the smallest penguins.
Cold ocean currents bring it enough fish to eat.
It is considered endangered.
There are only a few thousand animals left, or even fewer.

abschnitte.text: The Galapagos penguin is about 50 centimetres tall and weighs around 2 to 2.5 kilograms. Its back is black, its belly white, and a narrow white band runs across its face. It belongs to the genus of **banded penguins**, which also includes the Humboldt penguin. Like all penguins, it cannot fly, but it is an excellent swimmer.

The **Galapagos Islands** lie in the Pacific about 1,000 kilometres off the coast of Ecuador. Most Galapagos penguins live on the western islands of Isabela and Fernandina. A few animals even live just north of the **equator**, which no other penguin species manages. This is possible because cold ocean currents such as the **Humboldt Current** bring cool, nutrient-rich water.

Galapagos penguins eat small shoaling fish such as sardines and anchovies. They hunt mostly by day near the coast and dive quickly through the shoals of fish. They often hunt in small groups. Because they live close to their feeding grounds, they usually return to land every evening.

On the hot lava rocks the penguins have to protect themselves from overheating. They pant like a dog, look for shade and hold their flippers over their feet to protect them from the sun. They lay their eggs in cool **caves** and rock crevices. When it gets too hot, they go into the water to cool down.

On the Red List, the Galapagos penguin is considered **endangered**. Particularly dangerous is the weather phenomenon **El Niño**, in which the sea warms up and many fish disappear. In such years many penguins starve. The Galapagos Islands are now a national park, and researchers even build artificial nesting caves for the penguins.

begriffe.erklaerung: The imaginary line around the middle of the Earth that divides it into a northern and a southern half.
A stream in the sea that carries water over long distances.
A weather phenomenon in which the Pacific warms up unusually strongly.
A large protected area in which nature is especially protected.

gewusst: The Galapagos Islands became famous because the naturalist Charles Darwin observed animals there in 1835.
Galapagos penguins can breed several times a year if there is enough food.

teile.einleitung: An endemic species is an animal or plant species that occurs naturally only in one particular area. For example, ring-tailed lemurs, a species of lemur, live only on the island of Madagascar. Endemic species are often something quite special, but also especially vulnerable.
wichtigste: An endemic species occurs naturally only in a limited area.
Ring-tailed lemurs are endemic to Madagascar and naturally live only there.
Especially many endemic species exist on remote islands.
Lakes, mountains or caves can also have endemic species of their own.
In Swiss lakes there are species of whitefish that live in only a single lake.
Endemic species are often highly endangered, because they have nowhere else to go.
The opposite is cosmopolitan species, which occur almost everywhere in the world.

abschnitte.text: The word **endemic** comes from Greek and means roughly native. A species is endemic if it lives in nature only in a particular area. This area can be a whole continent, an island, a mountain range or just a single lake. Animals in a zoo do not count here, because it is about the natural **range**.

On islands that have been separated from the mainland for a long time, many species of their own have developed. On **Madagascar**, for example, live ring-tailed lemurs and all the other lemurs, which exist nowhere else. On the Galápagos Islands you find giant tortoises and marine iguanas. In New Zealand the kiwi is endemic, and in Australia koalas and platypuses live only there.

Endemic species often arise through **isolation**. When animals on an island or in a lake are separated from their relatives, they change differently over many generations. In this way, with time, new species develop that are perfectly adapted to their special habitat. This process is called **evolution**.

There are also endemic species in Switzerland. After the last ice age, many different **whitefish species** developed in the Alpine lakes, of which some occur in only a single lake. In the Alps too there are plants and insects that live only in a small mountain area. Switzerland therefore bears a special responsibility for the protection of these species.

Because endemic species live in only one place, a change there can threaten their whole species. Introduced animals such as rats, cats or goats have already wiped out many species on islands. A well known example is the **dodo**, a flightless bird from the island of Mauritius that became extinct in the 17th century. That is why areas with many endemic species are today often protected as nature reserves.

begriffe.erklaerung: Occurring naturally only in a particular area.
The area in which a species lives in nature.
When a group of living things is separated from others.
A species that occurs almost everywhere in the world.

gewusst: Almost all mammals and reptiles on Madagascar are endemic.
Lake Baikal in Russia has a seal species of its own, the Baikal seal, which lives only there.
Some cave animals are known from only a single cave.

teile.einleitung: Falconry is hunting with trained birds of prey such as falcons, goshawks or eagles. It is one of the oldest forms of hunting in the world and is still practised today. A falconer lives closely with his or her bird, and this takes a lot of patience and knowledge.
wichtigste: In falconry, people hunt with trained birds of prey.
The peregrine falcon has been especially prized for falconry for centuries.
Falconry is several thousand years old and probably comes from Asia.
Important equipment includes a leather glove, a hood and jesses.
Since 2010, falconry has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.
Today falconers also use their birds to drive away troublesome birds, for example at airports.

abschnitte.text: A **falconer** raises a bird of prey and trains it to hunt prey and then return. The bird remains a wild animal, and does not become obedient like a dog. It comes back because it is sure to get food from the falconer. The training takes time every day and a lot of trust between person and bird.

Falconry probably arose several thousand years ago on the steppes of Asia. In the Middle Ages it was a popular pastime of kings and nobles in Europe. The Hohenstaufen emperor **Frederick II** wrote a famous book about hunting with birds in the 13th century. In the Arab world and in Central Asia, falconry is still very important today.

The **peregrine falcon** has always been especially sought after because of its speed. In a dive it can reach over 300 kilometres per hour. For hunting in the forest, falconers like to use the goshawk, and in Mongolia riders even hunt with the golden eagle. The Harris's hawk is also very popular today, because it hunts well as part of a team.

The falconer wears a thick **leather glove** so that the sharp talons do not hurt. A small leather cap, the **hood**, covers the bird's eyes and calms it. On its legs the bird wears leather straps by which it can be held. It often also has a little bell or a small transmitter so that it can be found again.

Today falconry is not only hunting but also nature conservation and education. At airports, birds of prey drive away other birds so that there are no dangerous collisions with aircraft. At flying displays, visitors learn a lot about birds of prey. Since 2010, UNESCO has counted falconry as **intangible cultural heritage**. In Switzerland, a permit is needed to keep birds of prey, and animal welfare is strictly regulated.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who keeps and trains birds of prey and hunts with them.
A bird with sharp talons and a hooked beak that hunts other animals.
A leather cap over the bird's eyes that keeps it calm.
Customs and skills that are protected as a valuable heritage of humanity.

gewusst: Many words such as “Beizjagd” (hawking) come from the old language of falconers.
In some Gulf states, falcons even have their own passports for air travel.
In a dive, the peregrine falcon is considered the fastest animal in the world.

teile.einleitung: An exuvia is the empty shell that an animal leaves behind when it moults. The exuviae of dragonflies are especially well known: they stay hanging on reed stems after the dragonfly has emerged. They look like the animal itself, but they are empty and light as a feather.
wichtigste: An exuvia is the empty larval shell that remains after hatching.
It is produced when animals with an outer skeleton moult.
Dragonflies often leave their exuviae on reeds and plant stems.
Spiders, grasshoppers, cicadas and crustaceans also leave exuviae.
In snakes, people speak of the shed skin or the slough.
Researchers use exuviae to work out which species live in a body of water.

abschnitte.text: The word **exuvia** comes from the Latin word for “clothing taken off”. It means the empty shell that an animal leaves behind after **moulting**. It has exactly the shape of the animal, with legs, head and even eyes. Inside, however, it is hollow and very light.

Insects, spiders and crustaceans have a hard outer skeleton that does not grow with them. When the animal gets bigger, a new, soft skin forms underneath. Then the old shell usually splits open along the back, and the animal pulls itself out. The exuvia stays behind, while the new skin hardens within hours.

Dragonfly larvae live in the water for one or several years. To emerge, they climb out of the water on a reed stem or stalk. There the larval skin tears open, and the finished dragonfly squeezes out and pumps up its wings. The empty **larval shell** often stays hanging on the stem for weeks.

Exuviae are very useful for researchers. From them you can tell which **dragonfly species** have developed in a pond without disturbing any animal. In Switzerland, experts collect exuviae to monitor rare species. Because an exuvia shows that the larva has successfully left the water, it proves that the species breeds there.

Cicadas also leave striking exuviae, which stick to tree trunks. Spiders moult several times in their lives, and their shells can be found in webs or corners. Snakes and lizards also moult, and a snake's shed skin is also called a **slough**. Crustaceans such as the freshwater crayfish even cast off their whole hard shell.

begriffe.erklaerung: Shedding the old skin or shell that has become too small.
A young animal that still looks different from the adult.
A hard shell on the outside of the body that gives support.
The shed skin of a snake.

gewusst: A dragonfly exuvia even shows the extendable mask with which the larva seized its prey under water.
Depending on the species, spiders moult several times before they are adult.

teile.einleitung: The lowland tapir is a large mammal from South America with a short, flexible trunk. Although it looks a bit like a pig, it is related to horses and rhinoceroses. It is regarded as the largest native land mammal of South America.
wichtigste: The lowland tapir lives in the forests and wetlands of South America.
It has a short, flexible trunk-like nose with which it grasps leaves.
Tapirs are odd-toed ungulates and related to horses and rhinoceroses.
The lowland tapir eats only plants, mainly leaves and fruit.
It is a good swimmer and likes to flee into the water.
Its enemies include the jaguar and the puma.
The species is considered vulnerable.

abschnitte.text: The **lowland tapir** grows to about two metres long and around one metre high, and can weigh over 200 kilograms. Its fur is short and dark brown to grey. On its neck it has a short, bristly mane. The upper lip and the nose are drawn out into a short **trunk**, which is very flexible. It has four toes on the front feet and three on the hind feet, each with a small hoof.

The lowland tapir lives in large parts of tropical South America, from the north as far as Argentina and Paraguay. It inhabits rainforests, wet savannas and swamps, preferably near water. It is especially widespread in the **Amazon region**. It is out and about mainly at night and at dusk. Real tapir paths form along its routes through the forest.

Tapirs are pure **plant-eaters**. With their trunk they pick leaves, shoots, water plants and fallen fruit. Many seeds pass out again undigested. In this way they spread plants over long distances, which is why they are also called “gardeners of the forest”. As a supplement, they visit salt licks to take in minerals.

Tapirs usually live as **loners**. They swim and dive excellently and flee into the water when in danger. Their greatest natural enemy is the **jaguar**, along with the puma and large crocodiles. After a pregnancy of about 13 months, the female usually gives birth to a single young one. The young animal has brown fur with pale stripes and spots, which camouflages it in the forest like a watermelon.

The lowland tapir is classed as **vulnerable** by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. Its forests are cleared for pastures, fields and roads. It is also hunted for its meat. Because a female has a young one only every two years, populations recover only slowly. Protected areas and breeding programmes in zoos, including in Europe, help the species.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mammals with an odd number of weight-bearing toes, such as the horse, rhinoceros and tapir.
An elongated, flexible nose with which an animal can grasp.
An animal that mostly lives alone.
A spot with salty ground where animals take in minerals.

gewusst: Tapirs have existed for many millions of years and have hardly changed, so they are regarded as living fossils.
A tapir can move along the bottom of a body of water under water and use its trunk like a snorkel.
Young tapirs lose their stripes after about half a year.

teile.einleitung: The European mantis (“Gottesanbeterin”, literally “prayer to God”) is a large, green or brown insect with folded catching arms. Because these arms look like praying hands, it got its name. It is a skilful ambush hunter and in Switzerland is found only in warm areas.
wichtigste: The mantis is called Mantis religiosa scientifically.
It is usually green or brown.
It has its name from the folded catching arms that look like praying hands.
It hunts other insects and eats them.
The female is larger and stronger than the male.
In Switzerland it occurs mainly in warm, dry areas such as Valais and Ticino.
It is harmless to humans.

abschnitte.text: The European mantis has a long, slender body and a triangular head with large **compound eyes**. Females grow about 6 to 7.5 centimetres long, and males are smaller and slimmer. The front legs are converted into **catching arms** with sharp spines. It is green or brown and is thus well camouflaged among grasses and twigs.

The mantis loves warmth and lives on sunny, dry meadows and on embankments with tall grass. Its home is above all southern Europe, Africa and parts of Asia. In Switzerland it is rare and occurs mainly in **Valais** and in **Ticino**, and at warm spots also further north. Because summers are getting warmer, it is slowly spreading in central Europe.

During the day the mantis often sits still in the vegetation lying in wait. It can turn its head and aim at prey precisely. If an insect such as a fly, a grasshopper or a butterfly comes close enough, the catching arms shoot forward in a flash. This way of hunting is called **ambush hunting**.

In late summer the female lays several egg packets, which are called an **ootheca**. They consist of a foamy substance that hardens and protects the eggs. The female sticks the ootheca to plant stems, twigs or stones, where it survives the winter. In early summer the larvae hatch, and the adult animals live only a few months, until autumn.

If a mantis is threatened, it rears up and spreads its catching arms and wings to look bigger. It happens that females eat the male during mating, but this by no means always happens. Because their populations can decline through **loss of habitat**, it is protected in some countries. Anyone who finds one should watch it and leave it in its place.

begriffe.erklaerung: Front legs converted for seizing prey.
A firm egg packet in which many eggs overwinter protected.
Hunting in which an animal waits quietly until the prey comes close.
Colour or shape through which an animal is hardly noticeable in its surroundings.

gewusst: The mantis is one of the few insects that can turn their head over the shoulder.
In 2017 the mantis was chosen as Insect of the Year in Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The brown hare is a fast long-distance runner that lives in open fields and meadows. With its long ears and powerful hind legs it is easy to recognise. Although it looks similar to the rabbit, it is a species in its own right with a different way of life.
wichtigste: The brown hare lives in fields, meadows and at the edge of woods.
It can run at up to about 70 kilometres per hour.
Young hares are born furry and with their eyes open, young rabbits naked and blind.
Brown hares do not dig burrows but rest in a shallow hollow, the form.
Hares are plant-eaters and are not rodents but lagomorphs.
In Switzerland, numbers have fallen sharply since the 1970s.

abschnitte.text: The brown hare is larger than a wild rabbit and usually weighs about 3.5 to 5 kilograms. Its fur is earth-brown to yellowish grey, and the belly is pale. Striking features are the long **ears** with black tips and the long hind legs. Its eyes sit at the sides of its head, so it can see almost all round and notices enemies early.

Brown hares love open landscapes with meadows, fields, hedges and fallow land. It is widespread in Europe, and originally it comes from the steppes. It spends the day crouched in a shallow hollow, the **form**. When in danger, it first lies still and only runs away at the last moment.

The brown hare eats grasses, herbs, clover, buds and, in winter, bark as well. It is mainly active at dusk and at night. When fleeing, it makes lightning-fast **zigzags**, so that a fox or dog has trouble catching it. In spring the hares chase one another and even box on their hind legs, usually a female fending off a male who is too pushy.

A female hare usually has three or four litters a year, each with one to five young. The young are **precocial**: they are born furry and with their eyes open. The mother leaves them alone during the day and suckles them only about once a day, so that no enemies notice them. Anyone who finds a single young hare should therefore definitely leave it where it is.

In Switzerland there are far fewer brown hares today than in the past. The reasons are intensive **agriculture**, fast mowing machines, roads and a lack of hedges and fallow land. Many young hares also die in wet, cold weather. With **flower-rich fallow strips**, hedges and lightly fertilised meadows, people are trying to give them more habitat again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A shallow hollow in the ground in which the hare rests.
Young animals that can see and move soon after birth.
Sudden changes of direction while fleeing.
A strip at the edge of a field with wild flowers that offers animals shelter and food.

gewusst: A brown hare can leap more than two metres from a standing start.
Hares eat some of their droppings a second time, to get more nutrients out of their food.
The Easter bunny is an old custom that has been known in Switzerland and Germany for centuries.
