teile.einleitung: Castoreum, called “Bibergeil” in German, is a strong-smelling liquid that beavers produce in special glandular pouches. With it they mark their territory and communicate with other beavers. In the past castoreum was in great demand and was used as a remedy and as a scent.
wichtigste: Castoreum is called “Bibergeil” in German.
Beavers produce it in two glandular pouches in the rear part of the body.
With castoreum the beaver marks its territory at scent marks.
In the past castoreum was used as a remedy and as a scent.
Because it was so valuable, beavers were hunted heavily.
In Switzerland the beaver had died out and was reintroduced from 1956.

abschnitte.text: **Castoreum** is a yellow-brown, oily mass with a strong, slightly leathery smell. The beaver produces it in two sac-like pouches, the **castor sacs**, which lie close to the anus. The name comes from the Latin word “castor” for beaver. Males and females both have these sacs.

Beavers live in families and defend their **territory** on a river or lake against strange beavers. On the bank they push together small mounds of mud and plants and put castoreum on them. Other beavers smell at these **scent marks** who lives here and whether the area is taken. In this way quarrels and dangerous fights can be avoided.

Even in antiquity and the Middle Ages, “Bibergeil” was regarded as a **remedy**, for example for headaches, fever or cramps. Beavers eat a lot of willow bark, and from it salicylic acid gets into the castoreum, a substance that is related to the active ingredient of aspirin. That is why the remedy really did have a slight effect. The high price, however, led to beavers being hunted all over Europe.

In **perfume making**, castoreum was used to give scents a warm, leathery note. It was also occasionally used in the past as a flavouring in foods. Today almost only artificially made substitutes are used for this. For the animals that is good news.

Because of its fur, its meat and the “Bibergeil”, the beaver was **wiped out** in Switzerland in the 19th century. From 1956 beavers from other countries were released again, for example on the Versoix in the canton of Geneva. Today the beaver is protected and lives again on many rivers and lakes of the Central Plateau, and in the count of 2022 there were around 4,900 animals. Its dams and lodges create valuable habitats for many other animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: The German name for castoreum, the scent mass of the beaver.
A place where an animal leaves its smell to show: I live here.
A substance from willow bark that can work against pain and fever.
To destroy an animal species completely in an area.

gewusst: Because beavers eat willow bark, their castoreum contains a substance similar to the active ingredient of aspirin.
The flat tail of the beaver, the “Kelle” (trowel), serves not only for steering but also as a fat store for the winter.

teile.einleitung: The spotted redshank is a slim wader with long red legs that breeds in the far north of Europe and Asia. In summer its plumage is almost black with white spots, but in winter it is pale grey. On its journey south it also makes a stopover in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The spotted redshank belongs to the wader family (Scolopacidae).
In summer its plumage is almost black with fine white dots.
In winter it is coloured pale grey and white.
It has long, red legs and a long, thin bill.
It breeds in northern Scandinavia and Siberia.
It spends the winter on the Mediterranean, in Africa and in southern Asia.
In Switzerland it is a regular passage migrant in spring and autumn.

abschnitte.text: The spotted redshank is about 30 centimetres long and so somewhat bigger than a blackbird, with long legs. In its summer **breeding plumage** it is almost entirely black with white spots on the back. In its winter **non-breeding plumage** it is grey above and white below. Its **legs** are bright red and in summer almost dark red, and the long bill has a red base below.

It breeds in swamps and bogs of the **taiga** and tundra from northern Scandinavia to eastern Siberia. In autumn it flies south to its winter quarters. These lie on the Mediterranean, in tropical Africa and in South and South-East Asia. On the way it rests on lake shores, river mouths and mudflats.

The spotted redshank looks for food in shallow water. It eats insects and their larvae, small crustaceans, worms and small fish. Often it wades into the water up to its belly and even ducks its head under. Sometimes several birds hunt a **shoal of fish** together.

The nest is a simple hollow on the ground, often in a light wood near the bog. The female usually lays four eggs. Often she leaves the breeding site soon afterwards and travels south, while the **male** incubates and leads the young. The young can walk shortly after hatching and look for food themselves.

In Switzerland the spotted redshank does not breed, and it is a **passage migrant**. You can watch it in April and May and from July to October. Good places are wetlands such as the Fanel on Lake Neuchâtel, the Klingnau reservoir or the Bolle di Magadino in Ticino. Its call is a clear, two syllable “tschu-it”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird with long legs that looks for food in shallow water.
The plumage that a bird wears in the mating and breeding season.
A migratory bird that rests in an area only briefly on its journey.
A huge belt of coniferous forest in the north of Europe, Asia and America.

gewusst: In winter the spotted redshank looks so similar to the common redshank that even experienced birdwatchers have to look closely.
In this species it is usually the father who looks after the young, while the mother is already on her way south.
The spotted redshank can swim in the water, which is rather unusual for a wader.

teile.einleitung: The Gamsbart, or chamois beard, is a traditional hat decoration from the Alpine region. It looks like a bushy brush and is tied from the long back hairs of the chamois. It is part of many traditional costumes, above all in Bavaria and Austria.
wichtigste: The Gamsbart is made from the long back hair of the chamois.
Despite its name, it comes not from the chin but from the back of the animal.
The best hairs come from male chamois in their winter coat.
The hairs are tied into a bushy tuft in a small sleeve.
The Gamsbart is worn at the side or back of a traditional hat.
A large, fine Gamsbart needs hair from several chamois and can be very expensive.
It is found mainly in Bavaria, Austria and South Tyrol.

abschnitte.text: The **Gamsbart** is a tuft of animal hair that is worn as a decoration on a hat. It is usually fixed to traditional hats or hunters' hats. The name is somewhat misleading, because the hairs do not grow on the chamois's chin. They come from a stripe of hair on the back, which is called the **dorsal stripe**.

abschnitte.titel: Where do the hairs come from?
abschnitte.text: In winter the **chamois** grows particularly long hairs on its back, often over 10 centimetres long. They are longest and finest on older bucks. The hairs often have pale tips, which are called **frost**. The more pale tips a Gamsbart has, the more valuable it is.

A Gamsbart is tied by hand, which is an old craft. The hairs are sorted, cleaned and tied together so that the tips fan out nicely. At the lower end they are held in a small metal **sleeve**. For a large Gamsbart you need hair from several animals, and the work can take many hours.

The Gamsbart is a well-known sign of folk culture, above all in **Bavaria**, Austria and South Tyrol. It is part of many traditional costumes there and is worn at festivals, parades and celebrations. Originally it was also a sign of successful hunters. Besides the Gamsbart there are also hat decorations made of deer hair or **badger hair**.

In Switzerland, too, many chamois live, above all in the Alps and in the Jura. They are hunted in the hunting season in autumn under strict rules so that the population stays healthy. In Switzerland the Gamsbart is less common than in Bavaria and Austria, but you can see it on some hunters' hats. The hairs come from animals that were shot during the **hunt**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Traditional clothing of a region that is worn at festivals.
A dark stripe of hair that runs along the back of some animals.
The male of chamois, roe deer or goats.
A small tube in which something is held.

gewusst: Particularly large and fine Gamsbärte can cost several thousand francs.
The hairs for a Gamsbart have to be taken in winter, because the summer coat is much shorter.

teile.einleitung: The egg is one of the most important foods in the world. Usually this means the hen's egg that a hen lays. In a hard shell there is everything that a chick would need to grow, and that is why an egg is also very nourishing for us humans.
wichtigste: Hens lay eggs even without a cockerel being there.
The shell of a hen's egg can be white or brown.
An egg consists mainly of shell, egg white and egg yolk.
A hen's egg usually weighs about 50 to 70 grams.
Eggs contain a lot of valuable protein and important vitamins.
In Switzerland, keeping laying hens in cramped cages has been banned since 1992.
Raw eggs should be stored cool and heated well to avoid illness.

abschnitte.text: On the very outside is the hard **eggshell** made of lime, which has tiny pores through which air can get in. Underneath lie two thin shell membranes, between which a small air cell forms at the blunt end. Inside is the transparent **egg white**, which is also called “Eiweiss” in German, and in the middle the yellow **egg yolk** or “Dotter”. Two twisted cords, the chalazae, hold the yolk in the middle.

Whether an eggshell is white or brown depends on the **breed of hen**. The colour has nothing to do with the health or the taste of the egg. Many hens with white earlobes lay white eggs, and hens with red earlobes often lay brown ones. Some breeds such as the Araucana even lay greenish or bluish eggs.

Eggs can be boiled, fried, poached or made into scrambled egg. When heated, the egg white becomes firm and white, because the **protein** in it changes. In many recipes such as cakes, plaited bread or pasta, eggs hold the dough together. From whisked egg white comes stiff beaten egg white, which is needed, for example, for meringues, a well known Swiss sweet.

An egg contains a lot of high quality protein, which our body needs for muscles. In addition there are vitamins such as vitamin A, D and B12 and minerals such as iron. The egg yolk also contains fat and **cholesterol**. For healthy people one egg a day is fine in a balanced diet.

Switzerland was one of the first countries to ban **battery cages** for laying hens, and the ban has applied since 1992. Many Swiss hens live in free range keeping or barn keeping with a run. On every egg there is a stamp that tells where it comes from and how the hens were kept. At Easter eggs are traditionally dyed, and in the Swiss custom of “Eiertütschen” (egg tapping) the tips are knocked against each other.

Eggs should be kept in the fridge so that they stay fresh longer. On raw eggs there may be bacteria called **salmonella**, which cause stomach ache and diarrhoea. That is why you wash your hands after cracking an egg and heat eggs well. You check freshness with a water test, since a fresh egg sinks to the bottom and an old one floats at the top, because its air cell has become bigger.

begriffe.erklaerung: The transparent part of the egg that turns white when cooked.
Another word for the yellow egg yolk in the middle.
A hen that is kept mainly for laying eggs.
Bacteria that can make you ill and are sometimes on raw eggs.

gewusst: A good laying hen can lay around 300 eggs in a year.
The largest bird's egg is laid by the ostrich, and one weighs about as much as 20 to 25 hen's eggs.
A boiled egg can be spun, and it spins much faster than a raw one, because the liquid inside the raw egg acts as a brake.

teile.einleitung: The African wildcat is a small wildcat that lives in Africa and the Middle East. It is the ancestor of our domestic cats. Anyone who knows a tabby house cat can easily imagine what an African wildcat looks like.
wichtigste: The African wildcat has the scientific name Felis silvestris lybica or, in the newer classification, Felis lybica.
The domestic cat probably descends from the African wildcat.
It lives in Africa, on the Arabian Peninsula and in the Middle East.
Its fur is sandy to greyish brown with fine stripes.
It hunts mainly mice and other small animals.
As long as 10,000 years ago, wildcats began to live near people.

abschnitte.text: The African wildcat is somewhat larger and slimmer than many house cats. It usually weighs about 3 to 6 kilograms. Its **fur** is pale sandy, grey or yellowish brown and has faint dark stripes. Long legs and the reddish backs of the ears are typical.

African wildcats live in savannas, steppes, scrubland and at the edge of deserts. They are found in large parts of Africa, on the **Arabian Peninsula** and in the Middle East. They avoid dense rainforests and completely dry sandy deserts. During the day they hide in caves, rock crevices or dense bushes.

African wildcats are **ambush hunters**, which creep up and pounce in a flash. Their main prey is mice, rats and other small rodents. They also eat birds, lizards and large insects. They mostly hunt at dusk and at night.

abschnitte.titel: From wild animal to house cat
abschnitte.text: When people in the **Fertile Crescent** settled down and stored grain, the stores attracted many mice. The mice in turn attracted wildcats, which in this way came close to people. On Cyprus, researchers found a grave about 9,500 years old in which a person had been buried together with a cat. Later, in ancient Egypt, cats were greatly honoured and even linked with the goddess **Bastet**.

The African wildcat is widespread and is not considered threatened overall. One problem is that it mates with feral house cats, so that **hybrids** appear. No African wildcat lives in Switzerland, but its close relative, the **European wildcat**, does. This has become native again mainly in the Jura and also looks very similar to a house cat.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cat that lives freely in nature and was never tamed by people.
The long process by which wild animals become domestic animals.
An animal that waits quietly or creeps up and then suddenly pounces.
A cross between two different species or forms.

gewusst: All the house cats in the world, from the Siamese to the Persian, have the African wildcat as an ancestor.
Unlike dogs, cats were probably not deliberately tamed but came to people of their own accord.
In ancient Egypt, some cats were even mummified after their death.

teile.einleitung: The waterfowl are a large family of water birds that includes ducks, geese and swans. Almost all have webbed feet and a broad bill. They are found on all continents, including on Swiss lakes and rivers.
wichtigste: The duck belongs to the large bird family of waterfowl.
Waterfowl include ducks, geese and swans.
The scientific name of the family is Anatidae.
Worldwide there are well over 100 species.
Typical are webbed feet, a flat bill and waterproof plumage.
The young are precocial and can swim shortly after hatching.
Swiss lakes are in winter an important resting place for many waterfowl.

abschnitte.text: The family of **waterfowl** includes ducks, geese and swans. It belongs to the order Anseriformes (“Gänsevögel”). The smallest species are small ducks that weigh only a few hundred grams. The largest are the **swans**, and a mute swan can weigh over ten kilograms.

Almost all waterfowl have **webbed feet** between the front toes, with which they swim as if with paddles. Their bill is usually flat and has fine horny ridges at the edge with which they filter food from the water. A preen gland supplies oil that makes the plumage waterproof. Under the contour feathers they wear warm **down**.

Waterfowl live all over the world except in Antarctica, mostly on lakes, rivers, swamps and coasts. Many species are **migratory birds** and fly every year thousands of kilometres between breeding area and wintering area. Geese often eat grass on land, swans and dabbling ducks eat water plants. Diving ducks and mergansers dive for mussels or fish.

Most waterfowl build ground nests that are padded with down. The chicks are **precocial** and follow their parents on the very first day. The researcher Konrad Lorenz showed with young greylag geese that they follow the first moving creature that they see. This process is called **imprinting**.

In Switzerland, for example, the mallard, the red-crested pochard, the tufted duck, the goosander, the greylag goose and the mute swan breed. In winter many guests from the north join them, because the large lakes do not freeze over. Then hundreds of thousands of water birds rest on Lake Constance, Lake Geneva, Lake Neuchâtel and other waters. That is why there are numerous **water bird and migratory bird reserves** in Switzerland.

For thousands of years humans have kept domestic ducks and domestic geese. The domestic duck descends from the mallard, the domestic goose from the greylag goose. Their meat, their eggs and their down for quilts and jackets are used. Geese were even used in the past as loud **guards**.

begriffe.erklaerung: In biology a group of closely related animal species.
Skin between the toes that helps with swimming.
A bird that flies back and forth every year between summer and winter areas.
When a young animal fixes on the first living thing that it follows.

gewusst: Some geese fly over the Himalayas on their migration.
Swans can stay together with the same partner for a lifetime.
In the Roman Empire, cackling geese are said to have betrayed a night attack on Rome.

teile.einleitung: The Dalmatian is a dog breed with a white coat and many black or brown spots. It is a tireless runner and became world famous through books and films about 101 Dalmatians.
wichtigste: The Dalmatian has a white coat with black or brown spots.
It is named after the region of Dalmatia on the coast of Croatia.
Puppies are born completely white, and the spots appear only after a few weeks.
In the past it ran beside horse-drawn carriages as a coach dog.
Dalmatians have great stamina and need a lot of exercise.
In white dog breeds, deaf puppies occur more often, because a white coat colour and malformations of the inner ear are genetically linked.
Through the book and the Disney films about 101 Dalmatians the breed became very well known.

abschnitte.text: The Dalmatian is a medium-sized, slim and muscular dog with a shoulder height of about 54 to 61 centimetres. Its short, smooth coat is **pure white** with round black or liver-brown **spots**. Every Dalmatian has its own pattern of spots, like a fingerprint. The puppies are almost completely white at birth, and the spots show only from about two weeks.

The name refers to **Dalmatia**, a coastal region in what is now Croatia, from where the breed is said to have originally come. The dog became famous above all in England, where it ran beside or under fine carriages as a **coach dog**. It guarded the horses and the carriage when it stopped. In the USA it later accompanied the horse-drawn wagons of the fire brigade and is still a fire brigade mascot there to this day.

In some white dog breeds **deaf puppies** occur more often. The reason is a genetic link between the white coat colour and malformations in the **inner ear**. In Dalmatians a noticeable share of the puppies are deaf in one or both ears. Responsible breeders therefore have the hearing of the puppies checked with a test.

Dalmatians are friendly, playful and affectionate. They have enormous **stamina** and want to run for a long time every day, for example beside a bicycle or when jogging. Without enough exercise and occupation they become restless. In addition, Dalmatians have a special metabolism that can lead to urinary stones, so the right food is important.

The English author Dodie Smith wrote a children's book about 101 Dalmatians in 1956. In 1961 Walt Disney made an animated film of it in which the wicked Cruella de Vil wants to kidnap the puppies. Later came live action films, and afterwards many families wanted a Dalmatian. Experts warned at the time that such an **active dog** does not suit every family.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of domestic animals with the same, deliberately bred characteristics.
The innermost part of the ear, in which sound is converted into nerve signals.
Determined by the genetic material and passed on to the offspring.
A dog that ran beside horse-drawn carriages and guarded them.

gewusst: Dalmatian puppies are almost white without spots at birth.
Some Dalmatians have one blue and one brown eye.
No Dalmatian has exactly the same pattern of spots as another.

teile.einleitung: Echolocation is a method by which some animals “see” their surroundings with sound. They send out sounds and listen to the echo that comes back from objects and prey animals. Bats and dolphins are the best known masters of this technique.
wichtigste: In echolocation, animals send out sounds and evaluate the echo that comes back.
Bats mostly use ultrasound for this, which humans cannot hear.
Dolphins find their prey in dark water with clicking sounds that come back.
The clicking sounds of dolphins are focused by a fat pad in the forehead, the melon.
From the echo the animals recognise the distance, size and even shape of an object.
Some birds, shrews and even blind people also use echolocation.
Technical devices such as sonar and ultrasound work on the same principle.

abschnitte.text: An **echo** arises when sound hits an obstacle and is thrown back. Animals that use echolocation send out short calls and listen closely. The longer it takes for the echo to come back, the further away the object is. In this way a picture of the surroundings arises in the animal's head, even in complete darkness.

Most bats call in **ultrasound**, that is so high that we cannot hear it. With it they recognise insects such as mosquitoes and moths in flight. Shortly before the catch they call very fast one after another, in order to locate the prey exactly. In Switzerland 30 species of bat live, and all are protected.

Dolphins produce quick **clicking sounds** in their head. These are focused, as if by a lens, by the **melon**, a round fat pad in the forehead. They pick up the echo mainly through the lower jaw, which conducts the sound to the ear. In this way they find fish even in murky water or buried in sand. Sperm whales and other toothed whales also locate in this way.

The South American **oilbird**, a bird, and some swiftlets also find their way in dark caves with clicking sounds. Some shrews use quiet ultrasonic notes. Some blind people have learned to recognise their surroundings with tongue clicks. The American Daniel Kish even rides a bike in this way.

As early as around 1790 the Italian researcher **Lazzaro Spallanzani** studied how bats fly in the dark. He noticed that without hearing they bumped into obstacles, but he could not explain it. Only in 1938 did the American **Donald Griffin** prove the ultrasound calls with a special microphone. He also coined the English term “echolocation”.

Ships and submarines use **sonar** to find shoals of fish, obstacles or the sea floor under water. Doctors look into the body with **ultrasound devices**, for example at a baby in the mother's belly. Parking sensors on a car measure the distance to the wall with ultrasound. All these devices have copied something from the animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sound that is thrown back from an obstacle.
Very high notes that humans cannot hear.
A fat pad in the forehead of dolphins that focuses clicking sounds.
A technical device that locates objects under water with sound.

gewusst: Some moths can hear the calls of bats and then drop in a flash.
In water, sound travels about four times faster than in air.
With echolocation, bats can even recognise very thin wires in the dark and avoid them.

teile.einleitung: Many fish do not stay in the same place all their lives but migrate, sometimes thousands of kilometres. They travel to streams, to the sea or to the river where they were born in order to spawn. Such fish are called migratory fish, and the lake trout is an example from Switzerland.
wichtigste: In fish migration, fish move back and forth between different habitats.
Most migrate in order to spawn, that is, to lay their eggs.
The lake trout migrates from the lake into the streams and is therefore a migratory fish.
Salmon migrate from the sea into rivers to spawn there.
Eels do the opposite and swim far out into the sea to spawn.
Migratory fish find their way with their sense of smell and other senses.
Weirs and power stations are a big problem for migratory fish.

abschnitte.text: **Fish migration** is the name for the regular travelling of fish between different waters or parts of waters. Fish that do this are called **migratory fish**. They mostly migrate to spawn, to find food or to reach a sheltered winter spot. Some migrations are only a few kilometres long, others cross oceans. Almost every species of fish migrates some distance at some point in its life.

abschnitte.titel: Salmon: from the sea to the river
abschnitte.text: The **salmon** hatches in a river and migrates to the sea as a young fish. There it grows for a few years and becomes big and strong. Then it swims back into exactly the river in which it was born. It finds it mainly with its fine sense of smell. Fish that move from the sea into fresh water to spawn are called **anadromous**.

abschnitte.titel: Eel: from the river to the sea
abschnitte.text: The European **eel** does exactly the opposite. It grows up in rivers and lakes, including in Switzerland. To spawn, it swims thousands of kilometres to the **Sargasso Sea** in the Atlantic. The tiny larvae drift back to Europe with the Gulf Stream, which takes about one to three years. Fish that go to the sea to spawn are called catadromous.

Even inland, many fish migrate. The **lake trout** lives in the lake and in autumn climbs up into the feeder streams to spawn in the gravel. The grayling and the common nase move in spring to their spawning grounds in rivers. In the past, thousands of salmon swam up the Rhine every year as far as Basel and on into the Aare. Because of power stations and polluted water, the salmon disappeared from Switzerland around the middle of the 20th century.

Weirs, dams and power stations block the way for migratory fish. In the **turbines**, fish migrating downstream can be injured. That is why fish ladders, bypass streams and protective screens are built. Straightened rivers without gravel banks also deprive fish of spawning grounds. When rivers are freely passable again, many migratory fish return.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fish that regularly travels back and forth between different waters.
Laying and fertilising eggs in fish and amphibians.
Migrates from the sea into rivers to spawn, like the salmon.
Migrates from fresh water to the sea to spawn, like the eel.

gewusst: On its migration upstream, a salmon usually no longer eats anything and lives on its fat reserves.
Eels from Swiss waters cover a distance of more than 6,000 kilometres to the Sargasso Sea.
Salmon can smell their home river again even after years in the sea.

teile.einleitung: Chameleons are lizards that can change their skin colour in a flash. With this they adapt to their surroundings and at the same time show their mood, for example anger, fear or readiness to mate. In addition they have eyes that look in two directions at once, and a tongue that snaps faster than the blink of an eye.
wichtigste: Chameleons can change their skin colour very quickly.
The colour change serves for camouflage, but also for communication and for regulating body temperature.
Tiny crystals in the skin steer the light and so produce the colours.
They can move their eyes independently of each other.
With their flicking tongue they catch insects at a distance.
They climb with pincer-like feet and often with a prehensile tail.
Most species live in Africa and on Madagascar.

abschnitte.text: For a long time people believed that chameleons only mixed their colour with pigments, as with a paint box. Researchers at the **University of Geneva** found out in 2015 that in the skin there are tiny crystals in special cells, the **iridophores**. When the chameleon arranges these crystals closer together or further apart, the light is reflected back differently and the colour changes. In this way, for example, green can turn into yellow or orange in a short time.

abschnitte.titel: What the colour change is for
abschnitte.text: Chameleons use colour to adapt to their **surroundings** and to be harder for enemies to see. Even more important, however, is colour for communication with others of their species. An excited male often glows in strong colours to impress rivals or to attract a female. In the morning some chameleons turn darker, because dark skin takes in more heat from the sun.

The eyes of chameleons sit in cone-shaped eyelids that leave only a small hole for the pupil. Each eye can turn **independently** of the other, so a chameleon can look forwards and backwards at the same time. When it spots prey, it points both eyes at it. In this way it can judge the distance exactly.

The **tongue** of a chameleon lies folded up in the mouth and can be shot out in a flash. It is about as long as the body, and in some species even longer. At the tip it is sticky and works almost like a suction cup. In fractions of a second an insect is caught and pulled into the mouth.

Most chameleons live in trees and bushes and move slowly and with a swaying motion, like a leaf in the wind. Their toes are fused into two bundles that grip round branches like a pincer. Many species have a **prehensile tail**, which they wrap round twigs like a fifth hand. Some species carry horns or helmets on the head, like the veiled chameleon or the Jackson's three-horned chameleon.

begriffe.erklaerung: Skin cells with tiny crystals that reflect light and produce colours.
To colour or hide yourself so that enemies or prey do not see you.
A tail with which an animal can hold on to branches.
An animal of the same species.

gewusst: The discovery of how chameleons change their colour was made by researchers in Geneva in Switzerland.
A chameleon can catch an insect without moving away from its branch.
Many chameleons are much paler at night while sleeping than during the day.

teile.einleitung: The tree sparrow is a small songbird and a close relative of the house sparrow, which we call the “Spatz”. You can recognise it by its chocolate-brown cap and the black spot on its white cheek. It prefers to live on the edge of villages and in orchards rather than in the middle of a town.
wichtigste: The tree sparrow is the smaller relative of the house sparrow.
The brown cap and a black cheek spot are typical.
In the tree sparrow, males and females look the same.
It breeds in tree holes, holes in walls and, gladly, in nest boxes.
It eats seeds and feeds its young with insects.
In Switzerland it lives mainly in orchards and on farms.

abschnitte.text: The tree sparrow is about 14 centimetres long and so somewhat smaller than the house sparrow. It has a **brown cap**, a white cheek with a black spot and a narrow white collar. Unlike the house sparrow, males and females look almost **the same**. Its call is a short, somewhat harder “tschet”.

The tree sparrow lives all over Europe and in large parts of Asia. It likes landscapes with **standard orchards**, hedges, fields and farms. In Asia, by contrast, it also lives in the middle of cities, where it takes on the role of our house sparrow. In Switzerland you find it mainly on the Central Plateau and at lower altitudes.

Adult tree sparrows eat mainly seeds of grasses, wild plants and cereals. In winter they like to pick up grain at feeding places. They feed their young, on the other hand, mainly on **insects**, caterpillars and spiders. They therefore need a landscape with plenty of insects.

The tree sparrow is a **hole-nester** and nests in old woodpecker holes, cracks in walls or nest boxes. A pair often raises two or three broods a year. Outside the breeding season, tree sparrows live in flocks, sometimes together with finches and house sparrows. They often bathe in dust together to look after their feathers.

In many European countries the tree sparrow has become rarer. The reasons are the loss of standard trees, hedges and **fallow land**, as well as fewer insects and wild plants. You can help it with **nest boxes** and nature-friendly gardens. Wild flower strips at the edge of fields also offer it seeds and insects.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that builds its nest in a hollow, a hole or a box.
A family of small, sturdy songbirds that includes the house sparrow.
A fruit tree with a tall trunk, typical of old orchards.
Rolling in dust, with which birds look after their feathers.

gewusst: With the tree sparrow, you can hardly tell males and females apart.
In China in the 1950s, tree sparrows were killed in huge numbers as pests, after which insects multiplied strongly.
In winter, tree sparrows often use nest boxes as warm places to sleep.

teile.einleitung: The European perch, usually called Egli in Switzerland, is one of the best-known fish in the country. It has dark vertical stripes, red fins and a spiny dorsal fin. Fried perch fillets are among the most popular fish dishes in Switzerland.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the perch is called Egli, in Ticino Pesce persico and on Lake Constance Kretzer.
It has two dorsal fins, the front one carrying sharp spines.
Dark vertical stripes camouflage it among plants and branches.
It hunts mainly with its eyes.
Very young perch eat tiny zooplankton, large perch also eat smaller fish.
To spawn, it moves into shallow shore zones.
Pike, cormorant and otter are among its predators.

abschnitte.text: The **European perch** usually grows to 15 to 30 centimetres long, and large animals reach close to 50 centimetres. Its back is olive green, and the sides have five to nine dark **vertical stripes**. The pelvic and anal fins are strikingly orange to red. It has two **dorsal fins**, the front one with sharp spiny rays and a dark spot at the end. When in danger, the perch raises this fin with its spines sticking out, so that a predator finds it hard to swallow.

The European perch lives in lakes, slow-flowing rivers and ponds in almost all of Europe and parts of Asia. In Switzerland it occurs in practically all the larger lakes, for example Lake Geneva, Lake Constance, Lake Zurich and Lake Neuchâtel. Here it is mostly called **Egli**, in Ticino Pesce persico and in French-speaking Switzerland perche. Around Lake Constance it is also called **Kretzer**. In winter it stays in deeper water and is less active.

Very young perch eat tiny **zooplankton**, that is, small crustaceans in the water. Later insect larvae, worms and crayfish are added. Large perch hunt small fish and sometimes even eat smaller perch of their own species. The perch tracks down its prey mainly with its eyes, so it hunts by day. Young perch swim in shoals, large ones often in small groups or alone.

In spring the perch move into shallow **shore zones** to spawn. The female lays her eggs in long, transparent **egg ribbons**, which she wraps around water plants, branches or stones. Such a ribbon can be over a metre long and contain tens of thousands of eggs. The perch's enemies are pike, pikeperch, cormorant, great crested grebe and otter. The vertical stripes help it to hide among plants and branches.

**Perch fillets**, fried in butter or breaded, are a classic in Switzerland, especially at the lakes. Professional fishers mostly catch perch with nets, anglers with the rod. Catches vary greatly from year to year. Because Swiss catches come nowhere near meeting demand, a large share of perch fillets is imported. When buying, check the origin if you want perch from a Swiss lake.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss name for the European perch.
A hard, pointed ray in a fin.
Tiny animals that float in the water.
A long, jelly-like ribbon in which the perch lays its eggs.

gewusst: The egg ribbon of a large female perch can be longer than a child is tall.
Experts can read the age of a perch from annual rings on scales or ear stones.
When a perch eats too many others of its own kind, it is called cannibalism, and in large perch this happens regularly.

teile.einleitung: “The Thieving Magpie” is a famous opera by the Italian composer Gioachino Rossini. In it a young maidservant is accused of having stolen a silver spoon, but the real thief is a magpie. The title has shaped the magpie's reputation as a thief of shiny things to this day.
wichtigste: “The Thieving Magpie” is called “La gazza ladra” in Italian.
The opera is by Gioachino Rossini and was first performed in 1817 in Milan.
In the story a magpie steals a silver spoon, and an innocent maid is suspected.
Especially well known is the overture, which begins with drum rolls.
The magpie is a corvid with black and white plumage and a long tail.
That magpies deliberately steal shiny things is, according to what we know today, a myth.
Magpies are among the cleverest birds and also live in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The opera “La gazza ladra” was performed for the first time on 31 May 1817 at the **Teatro alla Scala** in Milan. The music was written by **Gioachino Rossini**, who also composed “The Barber of Seville”. The libretto is by Giovanni Gherardini. A French play with the title “La pie voleuse” served as the model.

The young maid **Ninetta** works for a rich farming family. When a silver spoon disappears, suspicion falls on her. She is arrested and even sentenced to death. Only right at the end is the nest of a magpie found in the church tower, and in it lies the silver. So Ninetta is saved at the last moment.

The **overture** is the piece of music that is played before the opera begins. It begins unusually with **drum rolls** on the snare drum. Today it is often played on its own in concerts. It is also heard in films and in advertising, for example in the film “A Clockwork Orange”.

The **magpie** is a bird from the family of **corvids**. It has black and white plumage that shimmers blue and green in the sun. With its long tail it is about 45 centimetres long. It eats almost anything, for example insects, worms, seeds, eggs and scraps. In Switzerland you often see it in villages, parks and on fields.

Researchers at the University of Exeter in England tested magpies in 2014. They put shiny and dull objects next to food. With shiny things the magpies were rather **cautious** and hardly took them away. The reputation as a thief is therefore mainly a legend from stories and proverbs.

Magpies are very intelligent. They are among the few animals that can recognise themselves in a **mirror**. They build large, roofed nests of twigs high in trees. Magpies often live their whole lives with the same partner.

begriffe.erklaerung: A theatre piece in which the performers sing and an orchestra plays.
Music that is played before the start of an opera.
A bird family with clever species such as ravens, crows, jackdaws and magpies.
The text of an opera, that is what is sung.

gewusst: In Bern and other Swiss cities magpies even breed in the middle of residential districts.
In Italian a chatty person is sometimes called “gazza”, that is magpie.
The magpie is one of the few birds that have recognised their own reflection in the mirror test.

teile.einleitung: A foal is a young horse, a baby horse. Soon after birth it stands on its long, wobbly legs and can soon run alongside its mother.
wichtigste: A baby horse is called a foal.
The mother of a foal is called a mare, the father a stallion.
A mare carries her foal in her belly for about eleven months.
Usually only a single foal is born.
After about an hour, a foal can stand and drink.
A foal recognises its mother by her smell and by staying close to the mare.
After the first year of life, a young horse is called a yearling.

abschnitte.text: A horse in its first year of life is called a **foal**. A male foal is called a colt, a female foal a filly. Young donkeys and ponies are also called foals. After its first birthday, the animal is called a **yearling**.

A mare carries her foal for about eleven months, which is roughly 340 days. Birth often takes place at night and usually lasts only a short time. After about an hour, the foal stands up and looks for its mother's udder. The first milk is called **colostrum** and protects the foal from disease with important defensive substances.

A foal recognises its mother by her smell and because it stays close to her all the time. The mare also sniffs her foal straight after birth and remembers its smell. This close bond is called **imprinting**. In the first weeks, the foal hardly moves away from the mare and follows her everywhere.

Foals have very long legs in relation to their bodies. Their legs are already almost as long at birth as in an adult horse, so that in the wild they can flee with the herd straight away. Instead of a long mane they often have short, fluffy hair and a bushy tail. After a few weeks the foal begins to nibble grass and hay, but still drinks milk for months.

At about six months, a foal is usually separated from its mother, which is called **weaning**. In Switzerland, especially many foals of the Freiberger breed (Franches-Montagnes) are born, above all in the Jura. At the Marché-Concours in Saignelégier, Freiberger horses are presented every year in August. A young horse is ridden only after a few years, when it is fully grown.

begriffe.erklaerung: A female horse, that is, the mother of a foal.
A male horse.
The very first milk after birth, which contains especially many protective substances.
When a foal no longer drinks from its mother and is separated from her.

gewusst: Foals are born with soft pads on the hooves, so that they do not hurt the mother during birth.
Foals play a lot with one another and in doing so practise running, rearing and fighting.

teile.einleitung: Eusociality is the most highly developed form of living together in the animal kingdom. The animals live in one large colony in which the work is divided up and usually only one queen has offspring. Well-known examples are honeybees, ants and termites.
wichtigste: Eusociality is a form of society with a division of labour.
Usually only one queen is able to reproduce.
The other animals look after the young together.
Several generations live together in the colony.
Honeybees, ants, termites and bumblebees, for example, live in a eusocial way.
One mammal, the naked mole-rat, also lives in a eusocial way.
A eusocial colony works rather like one single large organism.

abschnitte.text: The word **eusociality** means roughly “true social life”. Experts use it when three features come together. First, many animals look after the young together. Second, several **generations** live together, and third, reproduction is divided up so that only a few animals have offspring.

In honeybees, only the **queen** lays eggs, sometimes more than a thousand in one day. The **workers** are also females, but as a rule they have no young of their own. They clean the combs, feed the larvae, build, guard the entrance and collect nectar and pollen. The males, the drones, are there only for mating.

All ants and termites, honeybees, bumblebees and some wasps live in a eusocial way. In ants there are often different **castes**, for example workers and large soldiers. In Africa, termites build huge mounds that are several metres high. Among mammals, the **naked mole-rat** lives in a eusocial way in underground tunnels in East Africa.

At first sight it is puzzling why animals give up having young of their own. One explanation is that the workers are closely related to the queen and to one another. When they help their brothers and sisters, they therefore pass on many of their own genes. The American scientist **Edward O. Wilson** studied eusociality thoroughly, especially in ants.

Eusocial insects are enormously successful and are found almost everywhere on Earth. Ants loosen the soil, spread seeds and eat pests. Bees and bumblebees pollinate many plants, including fruit trees and vegetables. In Switzerland, beekeepers keep bee colonies that provide honey and pollinate flowers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Each animal takes on a particular task for the community.
A group of animals in a colony with the same task and often the same body shape.
The female that lays the eggs in an insect colony.
All the animals born at about the same time, such as parents and children.

gewusst: In summer, a bee colony can have around 40,000 to 60,000 bees.
An ant queen can live for many years, while workers usually live only for months.

teile.einleitung: Ganesha is one of the best-known and best-loved gods in Hinduism. You recognise him at once by his elephant head. He is regarded as the god of wisdom and as the remover of obstacles.
wichtigste: Ganesha is a god in Hinduism and has an elephant head.
He is regarded as the son of the god Shiva and the goddess Parvati.
Many Hindus pray to Ganesha before they begin something new.
He stands for wisdom, luck and overcoming obstacles.
His mount is a mouse or rat.
Every year the festival of Ganesh Chaturthi is celebrated in his honour.
In Switzerland, too, there are Hindu temples in which Ganesha is worshipped.

abschnitte.text: **Ganesha**, also called Ganapati, is a god in **Hinduism**, one of the great world religions. He has a human body with a belly, four arms and an elephant head. For Hindus, the elephant is a sign of strength, intelligence and a good memory. Ganesha is among the most revered gods in India and around the world.

abschnitte.titel: How did he get the elephant head?
abschnitte.text: There are various stories about his origin. In one well-known story, the goddess **Parvati** shapes a boy and has him guard her door. When her husband **Shiva** comes home and the boy does not let him in, Shiva cuts off his head in anger. To comfort Parvati, he gives the boy the head of an elephant and makes him an important god.

Ganesha is regarded as the lord of beginnings and as the one who clears **obstacles** out of the way. That is why many Hindus pray to him before they begin a journey, an exam, a wedding or a business. He is also the patron of knowledge, writing and art. He often has a broken tusk, with which, according to tradition, he is said to have written down the great epic **Mahabharata**.

Ganesha's mount is a small **mouse** or rat, which shows that even something small can move something great. In his hands he often holds a sweet, an axe, a noose or a lotus flower. His favourite sweets are **modak**, filled dumplings. Figures of Ganesha can be seen in temples, homes, shops and even in cars.

The biggest festival for Ganesha is called **Ganesh Chaturthi** and takes place in August or September, depending on the lunar calendar. In India, especially in Mumbai, huge, colourful figures are built for it and at the end are carried solemnly into rivers or the sea. Many Hindus live in Switzerland, many of them with roots in Sri Lanka. In several Hindu temples, for example in Adliswil or Trimbach, Ganesha is worshipped.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large religion found mainly in India and Nepal.
One of the most important gods in Hinduism and the father of Ganesha.
A very long, ancient Indian heroic epic.
A building in which believers pray and worship their gods.

gewusst: In India, many celebrations and ceremonies begin with a prayer to Ganesha.
Ganesha is also worshipped or depicted in Thailand, Indonesia and Japan.

teile.einleitung: The spring dor beetle is a native beetle that occurs in Europe and also in Switzerland. It often shines a beautiful blue or green and has an important job: it clears away animal droppings and so improves the soil.
wichtigste: The spring dor beetle is a native dung beetle.
It grows to about 12 to 20 millimetres long.
Its armour usually shines metallic blue, green or almost black.
It is on the move mainly in spring and early summer, hence its name.
It likes to live in dry woods and on sandy soils.
It digs tunnels into the ground and supplies its larvae with the droppings of plant-eaters.
Dung beetles help to break down dung and make the soil fertile.

abschnitte.text: The spring dor beetle has a rounded, domed body and grows to about 12 to 20 millimetres long. Its hard armour often shimmers **metallic** blue, green or violet, and sometimes it looks almost black. The wing cases are fairly smooth. On its front legs it has strong teeth with which it can dig like a shovel.

The beetle lives in Europe, including Switzerland, mainly in light, dry woods, on heaths and at sunny woodland edges. It particularly likes **sandy soils**, which are easy for it to dig into. You often see it crawling about on woodland paths. It has its name because it is active mainly in spring and early summer.

Like all dung beetles, the spring dor beetle feeds on the **dung** of other animals, for example the droppings of roe deer, hares, rabbits or grazing animals. It also eats rotting plant matter and fungi. In this way it helps to break down waste in nature. Such animals are called **decomposers**.

For its offspring, the beetle digs vertical tunnels into the ground, which often begin under a pile of droppings. Into these tunnels it carries dung and shapes it into supplies for the **larvae**. The female lays her eggs there, and later the larvae eat their fill. After pupating in the soil, a new beetle emerges.

Dung beetles are important helpers in the **ecosystem** because they remove droppings quickly. In doing so they bring nutrients into the soil and loosen it with their tunnels. Because woods are getting denser and grazing animals are missing, some species of dung beetle have become rarer. On their armour the beetles sometimes carry small **mites**, which in this way get a lift to fresh dung.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for the droppings or manure of animals.
The young form of an insect, which still looks quite different from the adult animal.
A living thing that breaks down dead plants, animals or droppings.
Shining like metal.

gewusst: The spring dor beetle is not related to the scarab, which rolls its ball across the ground, but buries its supplies in the soil.
If you turn a dung beetle over, you often see that its underside shines even more beautifully than its back.

teile.einleitung: Eawag is the water research institute of Switzerland and belongs to the ETH Domain. Its researchers study, among other things, the fish and the water quality of Swiss lakes and rivers. Its aim is that we have clean drinking water and that our waters stay healthy.
wichtigste: Eawag is a Swiss research institute for water.
It studies, among other things, the fish and the water quality of the lakes.
The headquarters are in Dübendorf in the canton of Zurich, with a second site in Kastanienbaum on Lake Lucerne.
Like ETH Zurich and EPFL, Eawag belongs to the ETH Domain.
Its roots go back to the year 1936.
It researches drinking water, wastewater, lakes, rivers and fish.
Its findings help the authorities to protect the waters better.

abschnitte.text: The name used to stand for “Eidgenössische Anstalt für Wasserversorgung, Abwasserreinigung und Gewässerschutz” (Swiss Federal Institute for Water Supply, Wastewater Purification and Water Protection). Today **Eawag** is simply the name of the **water research institute of the ETH Domain**. Over 500 people work there (as of around 2023), for example biologists, chemists and engineers. They carry out research, advise the authorities and train students.

Eawag came into being in 1936 as an ETH advisory office for wastewater purification and drinking water. Its headquarters are today in **Dübendorf** near Zurich. There stands the Forum Chriesbach building, which uses especially little energy. The **Kastanienbaum** site near Lucerne is devoted mainly to research on lakes and fish.

Eawag researches which species of fish live in Swiss lakes. In the “Projet Lac”, together with other experts, the fish of many large lakes were counted and identified. In doing so, species that had been unknown until then were also discovered. Especially important are the **whitefish**, of which there are many different species in Switzerland.

In the past many Swiss lakes were over-fertilised, because too much **phosphate** from detergents and wastewater got into them. Algae grew strongly, and oxygen was lacking at the lake bottom, so that fish died. Research by Eawag helped to get phosphate banned in detergents in 1986. Today it also studies **micropollutants**, that is tiny remains of medicines and plant protection products in the water.

Eawag researches how treatment plants can clean wastewater even better. Many large treatment plants in Switzerland are getting an additional cleaning stage against micropollutants. Eawag also made the **SODIS** method known, in which water in PET bottles is made germ free with sunlight. This simple method helps people in countries without clean drinking water.

The researchers of Eawag do not work only in Switzerland. They study, for example, the many species of cichlid in Lake Victoria in Africa. Other teams develop toilets and wastewater solutions for cities in poor countries. In this way Eawag helps to protect water worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: The group of two universities and four federal research institutes to which ETH Zurich and EPFL belong.
When too many nutrients get into the water and algae grow too strongly.
Tiny amounts of pollutants such as medicine residues in the water.
A plant that cleans dirty wastewater before it flows into rivers and lakes.

gewusst: With the SODIS method about six hours of sun are enough to make water in a bottle largely germ free.
In the fish count of Projet Lac, the researchers found several previously unknown species of fish in the Swiss lakes.
Almost all households in Switzerland are connected to a wastewater treatment plant.

teile.einleitung: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly. At night they hunt insects and find their way, even in complete darkness, using ultrasound and echoes. Around 30 species of bat live in Switzerland, and all of them are protected.
wichtigste: Bats are mammals that fly with wings made of skin.
They find their way using ultrasound calls and their echoes.
The bats of Switzerland eat mainly insects.
In winter they hibernate in caves, cellars or tree hollows.
Females usually have only one young a year.
Around 30 species live in Switzerland, and all are protected.
Bats are important insect eaters and are therefore beneficial animals.

abschnitte.text: **Bats** are mammals: they have fur and suckle their young. Their wings consist of a thin **wing membrane** stretched between the very long fingers, the body and the legs. With their feet they hang upside down from ceilings and branches. The smallest Swiss species such as the common pipistrelle weigh only about five grams, which is as much as a sugar cube. With a wingspan of about 40 centimetres, the greater mouse-eared bat is among the largest species in Switzerland.

As they fly, bats give out very high calls that people cannot hear, called **ultrasound**. These sounds bounce off obstacles and insects and come back as an **echo**. From the echo, the bat can tell where something is, how big it is and how it is moving. This method is called **echolocation**. In this way it catches small mosquitoes in flight even on a pitch-dark night.

All the bat species of Switzerland feed on insects and arachnids. They catch mosquitoes, moths, beetles and flies. A small common pipistrelle can catch hundreds of mosquitoes in one night. Some species pick their prey from leaves or from the ground, the greater mouse-eared bat for example hunts ground beetles. That is why bats are important helpers in gardens, woods and fields.

In summer, the females gather in **maternity roosts**, for example in attics, in tree hollows or behind shutters. There each female usually has a single young one, which she suckles with milk. After a few weeks the young can fly and hunt for themselves. In autumn the bats eat to build up fat reserves. They spend the winter in **hibernation** in caves, tunnels, cellars or tree hollows, where it is cool but frost-free.

In Switzerland, all species of bat are protected by law. Many are threatened because roosts are lost during renovations, old trees are felled and there are fewer insects. Bright street lamps also disturb some species. The **Bat Conservation Foundation** and cantonal offices advise house owners and help when injured animals are found. Anyone who finds a bat should not touch it with bare hands and should call the bat protection emergency hotline.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thin skin between the fingers, body and legs that forms the wing.
Very high sounds that people cannot hear.
Finding the way using sound waves that are thrown back.
A summer roost in which female bats have and raise their young.

gewusst: Despite their name, bats are not related to mice.
In hibernation, the heart of some bats beats only a few times a minute.
Some bats can live to over 30 years old, even though they are so small.

teile.einleitung: The European wildcat looks like a strong, tabby domestic cat but is a true wild animal. It lives very shyly in forests and avoids humans. In Switzerland it had almost disappeared, but today it roams again through the Jura and parts of the Central Plateau.
wichtigste: The European wildcat is called Felis silvestris scientifically.
It is not the feral form of the domestic cat but a wild species of its own.
Its tail is thick and bushy and has a blunt black tip.
It is much shyer than a domestic cat.
Its main food is mice.
In Switzerland it lives mainly in the Jura.
Hybrids with domestic cats are a danger to the pure wildcat.

abschnitte.text: The wildcat has a grey-brown, faintly tabby coat and, because of its dense fur, looks bigger than a domestic cat. Typical is the thick, bushy **tail** with a few dark rings and a blunt black tip. Along the back runs a dark line that ends at the base of the tail. Males weigh about 4 to 7 kilograms, females somewhat less.

The European wildcat lives in large, quiet **deciduous and mixed forests** with clearings, forest edges and hedges. It occurs in many parts of Europe, but often only in small, separate areas. In Switzerland it lives mainly in the **Jura** and spreads from there into the Central Plateau. As hiding places it uses tree holes, rock crevices or old fox burrows.

The wildcat eats mainly mice, especially voles on meadows at the forest edge. Sometimes birds, lizards or insects are added. It hunts mostly at dusk and at night, waiting for a long time in front of a mouse hole. This **sit-and-wait hunting** requires a lot of patience.

The mating season is in late winter. In April or May the female usually gives birth to two to four young in a sheltered hiding place. The young are blind at first and are looked after by the mother alone. In autumn they are independent and look for a **territory** of their own.

Wildcat and domestic cat look similar but differ clearly. The wildcat has a thicker, bushy tail with a blunt black tip, whereas the tail of the domestic cat is thinner and pointed. In addition the wildcat is much shyer and cannot be tamed. You can often tell the two apart reliably only with a **genetic analysis** of hairs.

In the 19th and 20th centuries the wildcat was hunted heavily and was almost extinct in Switzerland. Today it is protected, and its population has recovered. Dangers are road traffic and mating with feral domestic cats, through which **hybrids** arise. Researchers count wildcats with wooden lure sticks on which the animals rub and leave hairs.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that lives freely in nature and has not been tamed by humans.
An animal whose parents belong to two different species or forms.
A roughened wooden post with scent on which wildcats leave hairs.
Hunting in which the animal waits quietly for a long time until the prey appears.

gewusst: Our domestic cats do not descend from the European wildcat but from the African wildcat of Africa and western Asia.
Young wildcats can hardly be tamed even when humans raise them.

teile.einleitung: The fire salamander is a black tailed amphibian with bright yellow spots that lives in damp deciduous woods. Its vivid colours warn enemies, because its skin contains poison. Especially on warm, rainy nights, you can spot it on woodland paths.
wichtigste: The fire salamander is an amphibian and belongs to the tailed amphibians.
It is black with yellow, sometimes orange, spots or stripes.
Young fire salamanders are born as live larvae that can swim in water.
When seriously threatened, it squirts poison from the glands behind its eyes.
Adult animals breathe through their skin as well as through their lungs.
In winter it rests in frost-free hiding places.
In Switzerland all amphibians are protected, and you must not take them away.

abschnitte.text: The fire salamander usually grows to about 15 to 20 centimetres long. Its glossy black skin has yellow spots or stripes, and the pattern is different on every animal. This **warning colouring** shows enemies that it is poisonous. Behind the eyes are two striking glands, the **parotoid glands**. It usually moves slowly, with a waddling gait, on four short legs.

Fire salamanders live in damp, shady **deciduous and mixed woods** with clear streams. They often avoid open, sunny areas, because their skin would dry out quickly there. During the day they hide under stones, roots or dead wood and come out mainly on damp nights. Many animals stay near the water where they were born all their lives. They spend the winter in **winter rest** in frost-free hiding places, for example in holes in the ground or cracks in rocks.

Adult fire salamanders eat snails, earthworms, spiders, woodlice and insects. They seize their prey with their mouth and swallow it whole. The larvae in the water eat small water insects and the larvae of other animals. A fire salamander can manage for a long time without food.

Unlike frogs, the female does not lay spawn. In spring she deposits live **larvae** in cool, clean streams or springs. You can recognise the larvae by the yellowish spots at the bases of the legs and by the outer **gills**. After a few months they lose the gills and move onto land. Fire salamanders can live to over 20 years old.

In old European legends, the fire salamander was regarded as a creature linked with fire that could survive in it. Probably salamanders crawled out of burning wood in which they had been hiding. In Switzerland it lives mainly in the Jura, on the Central Plateau and in the Pre-Alps, and is on the **Red List**. One danger is an introduced **skin fungus**, which has killed many salamanders in neighbouring countries. Anyone who sees a fire salamander should watch it quietly, without touching it or taking it away.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals that live in water and on land, for example frogs and salamanders.
Striking colours that show enemies that an animal is poisonous.
Glands behind the eyes that give off a poison.
Breathing organs with which animals take in oxygen in water.

gewusst: The yellow spot pattern is as unique to each fire salamander as a fingerprint.
Its poison can cause skin irritation, so you should wash your hands after contact.
The related Alpine salamander is completely black and gives birth to fully developed young.

teile.einleitung: Owls are birds that hunt mainly at dusk and at night. With their large eyes, their fine hearing and their silent flight they are perfect night hunters. Some owls call “hoo-hoo” at night and can turn their head astonishingly far.
wichtigste: Owls form their own order of birds and are mostly nocturnal.
Worldwide there are about 250 species of owl.
Owls can turn their head by about 270 degrees.
Thanks to soft feathers, owls fly almost silently.
Indigestible remains such as bones and hair are brought up again by owls as pellets.
In Switzerland around ten species of owl breed.
The eagle owl is the largest owl in Europe.

abschnitte.text: Owls have a round head and a flat **facial disc** of feathers. Their large eyes look forwards and are firmly fixed in the skull. That is why owls turn the whole head, by about 270 degrees. Some species wear **ear tufts**, which however have nothing to do with hearing.

The real ears lie hidden at the sides of the head and in many species are at different heights. In this way an owl hears exactly where a sound comes from and finds a mouse even under snow. The facial disc guides the sound to the ears like a dish. Fringes on the flight feathers dampen the air turbulence, which is why owls fly **silently**.

Owls eat mainly mice, as well as birds, insects, frogs and, in large species, even hares or hedgehogs. Small prey they usually swallow whole. Bones, fur and feathers they cannot digest and bring up as **pellets**. Researchers examine pellets to find out what owls have eaten.

In Switzerland around ten species of owl breed. Common is the **tawny owl**, which lives in forests and parks and calls “hooo” at night. The eagle owl, with a wingspan of up to about 1.7 metres, is the largest owl in Europe and breeds in rock faces. The pygmy owl, by contrast, is hardly bigger than a sparrow, and the barn owl likes to live in barns and church towers.

Owls do not build proper nests. They breed in tree holes, rock niches, old crows’ nests or in nest boxes. The female usually lays two to six white eggs, and the male brings food. The young hatch one after another, so siblings are often of different sizes.

In ancient Greece the owl was the animal of the goddess Athena and was regarded as a sign of **wisdom**. In the past, by contrast, some people regarded owls as bringers of bad luck. Today all owls in Switzerland are protected. Dangers for them are road traffic, power lines and the loss of old trees and nesting sites.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that is awake at night and sleeps during the day.
A ball of bones and hair that an owl brings up.
The round ring of feathers on an owl’s face that directs sounds to the ears.
Tufts of feathers on the head that look like ears.

gewusst: Owls have 14 neck vertebrae, we humans only seven.
The eagle owl, called “Uhu” in German, has its name from its deep call.
Owl eyes are not balls but rather tubes, which is why they cannot move them.

teile.einleitung: The European tree frog is a small, bright green frog that can climb. With adhesive discs on its toes it holds on to smooth leaves and branches. Although it is only as big as a thumb, it calls astonishingly loudly on spring nights.
wichtigste: The tree frog is called Hyla arborea scientifically.
It belongs to the amphibians.
Fully grown it is only about 3 to 5 centimetres in size.
With adhesive discs on its toes it climbs on leaves and branches.
It breathes with its lungs and additionally through the skin.
Males have a vocal sac at the throat.
In Switzerland it is highly endangered.

abschnitte.text: The tree frog is mostly bright green and has a smooth, shiny skin. A dark stripe runs from the eye along the flank. It can change its colour somewhat, from light green to brownish. On the tips of the toes sit round **adhesive discs**, with which it can hold on even to panes of glass.

The tree frog lives in sunny, bushy landscapes with hedges, reeds and riverside woods. During the day it sits well camouflaged on the leaves of brambles, reeds or trees and basks. For reproduction it absolutely needs a calm, often sunny water without many fish. On the migration to the spawning water it sometimes covers several kilometres.

Tree frogs eat insects such as flies, mosquitoes, beetles and small butterflies as well as spiders. They lie in wait for their prey in bushes and snap it up skilfully. Often they even leap from sitting at flying insects. Tadpoles, by contrast, eat algae and plant remains in the water.

In spring, from about April to June, the males call at night by the water. For this they blow up their **vocal sac** at the throat into a large ball. A chorus of many tree frogs is very loud and can be heard far away. With the call the males attract females.

A female tree frog lays several hundred eggs in small clumps on water plants. From them hatch **tadpoles**, which need about two to three months until they become the finished frog. Waters without fish are important so that fish do not eat the eggs and tadpoles. In summer the small frogs leave the water and climb into the bushes.

The tree frog is highly endangered in Switzerland and is on the **Red List**. It is threatened especially by the disappearance of near-natural ponds and pools. Nature conservation groups therefore create new ponds, for example in the Reuss valley and in other river landscapes. Where there are suitable waters again, the tree frog often returns quickly.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals such as frogs and newts that live in water and on land.
Round pads on the toes with which the tree frog holds on.
A stretchable skin at the throat that makes the call louder.
The larva of a frog, which lives in water.
A register of the animals and plants that are endangered.

gewusst: In the past tree frogs were kept in jars with a small ladder as “weather frogs”, which is forbidden today and does not work.
North of the Alps the tree frog is the only native frog with adhesive discs on its toes.

teile.einleitung: The quill is the hard, hollow part of a bird's feather, to which the vane is attached. For many centuries people wrote with cut quills, mainly from goose feathers. That is why we still say “fountain pen” and “pen” (the German word “Feder” means “feather”), although pens have long been made of metal or plastic.
wichtigste: The quill is the stem of a bird's feather.
Its lower, hollow part sits in the bird's skin.
Goose feathers were especially often used in the past as writing quills.
In Europe people wrote with quills from about the early Middle Ages until the 19th century.
The tip had to be cut again and again with a small penknife.
In the 19th century, steel nibs replaced the goose quill.

abschnitte.text: A feather consists of the quill and the soft **vane** on both sides. The lower, hollow part of the quill is called the **calamus** and sits in the bird's skin. The upper part, the **shaft**, carries the fine branches of the vane. The quill is made of keratin, the same substance as our hair and fingernails. It is light, flexible and yet very sturdy.

As early as the early Middle Ages, monks in monasteries wrote on parchment with quills. The most popular were large flight feathers of **geese**; for fine lines, raven or swan feathers were sometimes used. The tip was cut at a slant and split in the middle so that the **ink** flowed evenly. To write, you dipped the quill into the inkwell again and again.

Because the tip quickly became blunt, it had to be recut often. For this a small, sharp **penknife** was used. From this the English name for the pocket knife, “penknife”, developed. Good writers could sharpen their quill to a new point in a few seconds.

In the 19th century, **steel nibs** were made in large quantities in England. They were cheap, lasted a long time and no longer had to be cut. Soon afterwards, fountain pens with their own supply of ink appeared. After that, the goose quill was needed almost only by calligraphers and enthusiasts.

Quills are still used today. A professional badminton shuttlecock is made of 16 goose feathers set in a cork head. In old keyboard instruments such as the **harpsichord**, small pieces of quill used to pluck the strings. And in calligraphy courses, people learn how to create beautiful writing with pen and ink.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hollow lowest part of the quill that sits in the skin.
The flat, soft surface of the feather to the left and right of the quill.
The art of writing especially beautifully by hand.
A hard protein from which feathers, hair and nails are made.

gewusst: For right-handers, feathers from the left wing were often used, because they curve to suit the hand.
The expression “from the pen of” still reminds us of writing with quills.
A badminton shuttlecock for competitions contains exactly 16 feathers.

teile.einleitung: Endothermy means that an animal produces its body heat itself. Mammals and birds are endothermic, and they are also called warm-blooded. That is why they can stay active even in the cold, but they need a lot of food for it.
wichtigste: Endothermic animals produce their body heat themselves, ectothermic animals do not.
Endothermic animals include above all mammals and birds.
Fish, amphibians, reptiles and insects are mostly ectothermic.
The heat arises through metabolism, that is in the burning of food.
Warm-blooded animals stay active regardless of the surrounding temperature.
The disadvantage is that they need much more food.
A human has a body temperature of about 37 degrees Celsius.

abschnitte.text: The word **endothermy** comes from Greek and means heat from within. Endothermic animals keep their body temperature almost always the same, whether it is hot or cold outside. In **ectothermic** animals, by contrast, body heat depends on the surroundings. A lizard therefore has to warm up in the sun first before it can run fast.

The heat arises in **metabolism**, when the body converts food into energy. Part of this energy becomes heat, similar to an engine. The brain constantly measures the temperature and controls it like a thermostat. When it is cold, the muscles shiver and so produce additional heat.

So that heat is not lost, mammals have a **fur** and birds a coat of feathers. Many animals in cold regions also have a thick layer of fat, for example seals and polar bears. In heat they have to get rid of warmth. Humans sweat for this, dogs pant, and elephants fan themselves with their large ears.

Warm-blooded animals stay active regardless of the surrounding temperature. That is why they even live in the Arctic, in the Antarctic and high in the Alps. The great disadvantage is the high **energy requirement**, because the heating in the body needs a lot of food. Small animals such as shrews have to eat almost constantly, because they cool down quickly.

Some endothermic animals save energy in winter by greatly lowering their body temperature. The **marmot** in the Swiss Alps goes into a long hibernation in which its body temperature drops to a few degrees above zero. Hedgehogs and dormice also hibernate. Other animals such as migratory birds simply fly to warmer regions in autumn.

Not everything is quite so simply divided. Some fish such as the **tuna** can keep certain parts of the body warmer than the water. Bumblebees also warm up before flying by shivering with their flight muscles. Researchers also suppose that some dinosaurs were at least partly warm-blooded.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that produces its body heat itself, also called warm-blooded.
An animal whose body heat depends on the surroundings, also called cold-blooded.
All the processes in the body in which food is converted and used.
A long resting state in winter in which the body saves energy.

gewusst: Birds often have a body temperature of around 40 degrees, that is higher than we humans.
A human needs a large part of the energy from food just to stay warm.
A shrew has to eat each day about as much as it weighs itself.

teile.einleitung: The Chinook salmon is also called the king salmon in German (“Königslachs”) and is the largest of all Pacific salmon. It grows up in the sea and then swims hundreds or even thousands of kilometres upriver to spawn where it hatched itself.
wichtigste: The Chinook salmon is the largest Pacific salmon and is therefore also called the king salmon.
Its scientific name is Oncorhynchus tshawytscha.
It lives in the northern Pacific and in the rivers of North America and north-eastern Asia.
It hatches in fresh water, grows up in the sea and returns to its home river to spawn.
After spawning the adult salmon die.
Bears, eagles and orcas depend on this salmon as food.
Many stocks are threatened by dams, overfishing and warm water.

abschnitte.text: The king salmon has a powerful, streamlined body with silver sides and a blue-green back. On the back and the tail fin it has small black spots. Typical is its **black gum line** in the lower jaw. It often grows to just under a metre long, and large animals reach about 1.5 metres and over 40 kilograms. At spawning time many fish turn reddish to dark olive.

Originally the Chinook salmon lives in the northern **Pacific**. It spawns in rivers from California to Alaska, for example in the Columbia River and in the Yukon, and also in rivers in Russia. In the sea it travels far out and for several years feeds up fat reserves. Humans have also released it in New Zealand and in South America, where it now occurs as well.

Salmon that migrate from the sea into rivers to spawn are called **anadromous**. The Chinook salmon probably finds its home river again mainly with its fine **sense of smell**. In the Yukon some fish swim almost 3,000 kilometres upstream and leap over rapids on the way. On the journey they eat nothing more and live only off their reserves. After spawning they are completely exhausted and die.

Young salmon eat insect larvae and small crustaceans in the river. In the sea the larger fish hunt mainly other fish such as herring and anchovies, as well as squid. The salmon itself is an important prey for **orcas**, seals, grizzly bears and bald eagles. The dead salmon after spawning even fertilise the forests on the bank, because their nutrients get into the soil.

For many indigenous peoples of North America, salmon has been an important food and part of their culture for thousands of years. Today it is a sought-after food fish and is also kept in fish farms. **Dams** block the way to their spawning grounds for many salmon, which is why fish ladders are built. Water in rivers that is too warm and overfishing also cause problems for the stocks. In Switzerland the king salmon does not live, and here in the past only the Atlantic salmon was at home in the Rhine.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fish that live in the sea and migrate up into rivers to spawn.
When fish lay their eggs and fertilise them.
A group of salmon species that live in the Pacific, for example king salmon and sockeye salmon.
A kind of staircase of pools by which fish can get past an obstacle such as a dam.

gewusst: The orcas off the coast of Washington feed mainly on king salmon.
After years in the sea, a Chinook salmon finds exactly the stream again in which it hatched.
The name Chinook comes from an indigenous people on the Columbia River.

teile.einleitung: The Freiberger is the only horse breed still bred today that originally comes from Switzerland. It comes from the Freiberge (Franches-Montagnes) in the Jura and is known for its calm nature and its versatility.
wichtigste: The Freiberger originally comes from Switzerland.
It has its name from the Freiberge, in French Franches-Montagnes, in the canton of Jura.
It is strong, hardy and has a friendly, calm nature.
Most Freiberger are brown or chestnut.
Freiberger are used for riding, driving and work.
The Swiss National Stud Farm is in Avenches in the canton of Vaud.
