Every year in August the Marché-Concours takes place in Saignelégier.

abschnitte.text: The Freiberger is a medium-sized, compact horse with a strong body and powerful legs. It usually measures about 150 to 160 centimetres at the withers. Most common are **bays** with a black mane and **chestnuts** with reddish-brown coats. A friendly look and a good-natured character are typical.

The breed comes from the **Freiberge**, a high plateau in the canton of Jura. The farmers there needed a robust horse for field work, transport and the harsh climate. In the 19th century, the native horses were crossed with other breeds, for example with English and Arabian horses. This is how the Freiberger as we know it today came about.

In the past, the Freiberger was an important **working horse** in agriculture and in the army. In the Swiss army, the horses carried loads through rough terrain. Today it is used mainly for leisure riding, carriage driving and in equestrian sport. Because of its calm character, it is also well suited to children and to **riding therapy**.

At the **National Stud Farm** in Avenches in the canton of Vaud, Freiberger stallions are kept and breeding is supported. Every year in August the **Marché-Concours** takes place in Saignelégier, a large horse festival. There, Freiberger are shown off, and there are races and displays. The festival attracts many thousands of visitors every year.

The Freiberger is regarded as part of Switzerland's cultural heritage and as part of the landscape of the Jura. On the pastures of the Freiberge you often see horses grazing freely among fir trees. These pastures with scattered trees are called **wooded pastures**. To keep the breed healthy, breeders make sure that animals that are too closely related are not mated.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals of one species with shared features that has been deliberately bred.
An operation in which horses are bred.
The highest point on a horse's back, where its height is measured.
A horse with a reddish-brown coat and a mane of the same colour or lighter.

gewusst: The Freiberger is the last still living horse breed that is originally Swiss.
At the Marché-Concours in Saignelégier there are also races with farm horses and carriages.

teile.einleitung: The banded demoiselle is a shimmering damselfly that lives on streams and rivers. It has its name because the males carry a dark band on their wings. When it flutters in the sunlight, it looks like a flying jewel.
wichtigste: The banded demoiselle is called Calopteryx splendens in science.
It stands out for its dark banded wings.
The males shine metallic blue, the females greenish.
It belongs to the damselflies.
It lives on slow-flowing streams and rivers.
Its larvae grow up in the water and hunt small animals there.
In Switzerland it is found mainly on the Central Plateau.

abschnitte.text: The banded demoiselle is about 4.5 to 5 centimetres long. The male has a metallic blue-green shining body and in the middle of each wing a broad, dark blue **band**. The female is coloured green-bronze and has transparent, slightly greenish wings. Like all **damselflies**, it folds its wings together over its back at rest. Its flight looks fluttering, almost like that of a butterfly.

The species lives in large parts of Europe and in parts of Asia. It needs **flowing waters** with clean water that does not flow too fast. Sunny banks with reeds, grasses and water plants are important. The males like to sit on leaves that stick out over the water. From there they guard their small territory.

The adult damselflies are hunters. They catch small insects such as mosquitoes and flies in flight. Their large eyes help them to spot prey quickly. The larvae in the water also live as predators and eat mosquito larvae, small crustaceans and other water animals.

The males defend their territory against other males and perform a fluttering **courtship flight** for the females. After mating, the female pricks her eggs into water plants below the surface of the water. Larvae hatch from the eggs and mostly live in the water for about one to two years. Then they climb up a plant stem, the skin splits open and the finished damselfly emerges. The adult animals fly from about May to September.

In Switzerland the banded demoiselle occurs mainly at lower altitudes on the Central Plateau, for example on streams and smaller rivers. It is regarded as a sign of fairly clean water. Where streams are straightened or polluted, it disappears. The **restoration** of streams, that is, turning them back into natural waters, helps it. A close relative is the beautiful demoiselle, whose males have almost entirely dark wings.

begriffe.erklaerung: A delicate dragonfly that folds its wings together at rest.
The young form of an insect, which still looks different from the adult animal.
An area that an animal defends against others of its species.
Making a straightened body of water more natural again.

gewusst: The shimmering blue of the males is not caused by pigment but by light that is scattered by fine structures.
Dragonflies existed over 300 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs.
The larva breathes under water with small gill plates at its rear end.

teile.einleitung: The gelada is a monkey that lives only in the highlands of Ethiopia and eats mainly grass. It is related to the baboons and stands out because of a bright red, bare patch on its chest. Geladas live in huge herds on green high plateaus and sleep at night on steep cliff faces.
wichtigste: Geladas are relatives of the baboons that live at high altitudes in Ethiopia and eat grass.
They live at heights of about 1,800 to over 4,000 metres.
Grass makes up the largest part of their food, which is unique among monkeys.
On the chest they have a red, hairless patch.
The males wear a long, dense mane.
Geladas sleep on steep cliff faces, where they are safe from enemies.
They live in herds that can include several hundred animals.

abschnitte.text: Geladas have a dense, brown coat and a dark face. Typical is the **red chest patch** in the shape of an hourglass, which is why they are also called “bleeding-heart baboons”. In males the patch glows especially strongly when they are doing well. Males are much bigger than females and wear a magnificent **mane** around head and shoulders.

Geladas exist only in the **highlands of Ethiopia**. They live on grassy high plateaus at the edge of deep gorges. A well known area is the **Simien National Park**, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site. There it gets cold at night, and the thick coat keeps them warm.

Geladas are the only monkeys that feed mainly on **grass**. They pluck blades of grass with their nimble fingers and also eat seeds and roots. When feeding they often sit and shuffle on along on their bottoms without standing up. Their teeth are especially well suited to grinding grass.

A small family unit usually consists of one male, several females and their young. Many such families join together into large **herds** that can include several hundred animals. Geladas have a great variety of sounds and facial expressions. At night they climb up steep **cliff faces** to sleep, where leopards and hyenas can hardly reach them.

There are still quite a lot of geladas, but they are regarded as in need of protection. Their habitat is getting smaller, because people create fields and let cattle graze. Climate change too could change the high plateaus. In protected areas such as the Simien National Park they can be observed well, and **tourists** bring money for their protection.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large area that lies high above the sea.
A large group of animals that live together.
Long, dense hair on the head, neck and shoulders.
A natural area that UNESCO protects as especially valuable for all humanity.

gewusst: Geladas spend a large part of the day sitting eating grass.
In females the red chest patch shows whether they are ready to mate.
The sounds of geladas sometimes resemble human speech in their rhythm.

teile.einleitung: The egg tooth is a small, hard bump or tooth with which a young animal in the egg breaks open the shell from the inside. Chicks, young turtles, crocodiles, lizards and snakes have it. Shortly after hatching it has done its job and disappears again.
wichtigste: The egg tooth helps the chick to break open the hard eggshell from the inside.
In birds it sits at the front on the tip of the bill.
Reptiles such as snakes, lizards, turtles and crocodiles also have an egg tooth.
In snakes and lizards it is a real tooth, in birds a hard horny bump.
After hatching the egg tooth falls off or shrinks away.
The platypus also has an egg tooth when it hatches.

abschnitte.text: The **egg tooth** is a pointed, hard bump on the head of an animal that is growing in the egg. It serves only one purpose, namely hatching. In chicks it sits as a small white dot on the upper side of the **tip of the bill**. You can see it well in freshly hatched chicks.

A hen's chick hatches after about 21 days of incubation. First it pierces the inner membrane and reaches the **air cell**, where it breathes air for the first time. Then it presses the egg tooth against the shell and taps against it again and again until a small hole appears. This first hole is called pipping (“Anpicken”). Then the chick turns in the egg and cracks the shell open all the way round, until it can push it open with head and legs.

So that the chick has enough strength, it has in its neck an especially strong **hatching muscle**. It helps to thrust the head with the egg tooth powerfully against the shell. Hatching is hard work and can take many hours. In between, the chick takes breaks again and again.

Many **reptiles** also need an egg tooth. Young snakes and lizards have a real little tooth at the front of the upper jaw with which they slit the leathery egg membrane. Turtles and crocodiles, by contrast, have, like birds, a horny bump on the snout. Crocodile mothers sometimes additionally help their young by gently cracking the eggs in their mouths.

After hatching, the young animal no longer needs the egg tooth. In chicks it usually falls off within a few days. In snakes and lizards the tooth also falls out soon. The egg tooth is a lovely example of an **adaptation** that is important only for a short moment in life.

begriffe.erklaerung: When a young animal comes out of the egg.
A small space with air at the blunt end of the egg.
Creeping animals such as snakes, lizards, turtles and crocodiles.
A characteristic that helps a living thing to cope well in its environment.

gewusst: Despite its name, the egg tooth in birds is not a real tooth at all.
Chicks in a clutch can communicate with quiet sounds in the egg so that all hatch at about the same time.
Mammals other than the platypus and the echidna need no egg tooth, because they do not hatch from eggs.

teile.einleitung: The chamois is a skilful climber of the Alps. It leaps safely over steep rocks and is seen as a symbol of the Alpine world. In Switzerland you can watch it in many mountain areas and also in the Jura.
wichtigste: The chamois feels most at home in steep mountain regions with rocks.
A female is called a doe, a male a buck, and the young a kid.
A doe usually gives birth to a single kid in May or June.
Its horns grow throughout its life and are not shed.
Chamois eat grasses, herbs and lichens, and in winter also buds, moss and bark.
Chamois can jump up to about 2 metres high.
According to the international Red List, the chamois is not endangered.

abschnitte.text: The chamois is about as big as a goat and usually weighs between 25 and 50 kilograms. In summer its coat is reddish brown, in winter almost black and much denser. Typical is the pale face with a dark stripe from the eyes to the muzzle. Both sexes carry hook-shaped **horns**, which are also called **crooks**.

The horns of a chamois differ greatly from the antlers of a deer. They grow throughout its life and are never shed. Every winter a growth ring forms, from which the age can be read. Behind the horns of the buck lies a **scent gland**, which grows larger during the rut and is used for marking.

Chamois live in steep mountain regions with rocks, often at the tree line up to over 2,500 metres high. Their hooves have soft, elastic **pads** with a hard rim, which grip like climbing shoes. The two toes can spread so that the chamois does not slip. This is how it can jump up to about 2 metres high and much further.

Chamois are plant-eaters and **ruminants**. They eat mainly grasses, herbs and lichens. In winter, when little green grows, they also eat buds, moss and bark. Then they often move to lower levels or to windy slopes where the snow is blown away.

The mating season, the **rut**, takes place in November and December. The bucks chase each other across the slopes to win the does for themselves. In May or June a doe usually gives birth to a single **kid**. After just a few hours the young animal can follow its mother over rocks.

In Swiss stories and songs, chamois are often seen as a symbol of the Alpine world. Tens of thousands of chamois live in Switzerland, and on the international Red List the species is not considered endangered. Good places to watch them are the **Swiss National Park** in the Engadine or the Freiberge in the Jura. With binoculars you can often see them standing on rock ledges early in the morning.

begriffe.erklaerung: The female of chamois, ibex and goats.
The young of a chamois, roe deer or goat.
The mating season in deer, chamois and similar animals.
An animal that brings its food back up and chews it again, like cows or chamois.

gewusst: When in danger, chamois give a loud whistle that warns the other animals.
From the long back hairs of the chamois the Gamsbart is tied, a traditional hat decoration.

teile.einleitung: The European pond turtle is the only turtle that occurs naturally in central Europe and Switzerland. It lives in calm fresh waters and likes to bask on tree trunks. Today it has become very rare and needs our protection.
wichtigste: The scientific name is Emys orbicularis.
It lives in fresh water, not in salt water.
It mostly feeds and mates in the water.
To warm up its body, it likes to lie in the sun.
The female lays the eggs in a pit that she digs herself on land.
Pond turtles can live to be several decades old.
They become sexually mature only after several years.

abschnitte.text: The European pond turtle has a flat, dark shell with many small yellow dots or lines. The **carapace** is usually 12 to 20 centimetres long. Its feet have webbing and strong claws. Males often have reddish eyes, females more yellowish ones.

It lives in calm, plant-rich **fresh waters** such as ponds, oxbows, marshes and slow-flowing streams. Sunny places such as tree trunks or banks, where it can warm up, are important. As a **cold-blooded** animal it has no body warmth of its own and needs the sun. It spends the winter in cold torpor in the mud at the bottom of the water.

The pond turtle mostly feeds in the water. On its menu are insect larvae, snails, worms, tadpoles and small fish. It also eats dead animals and sometimes water plants. In this way it helps to keep waters clean.

Mating takes place in spring, mostly in the water. In early summer the female leaves the water and digs a pit in a sunny place, in which she usually lays about 5 to 15 eggs. The warmth of the ground decides whether males or females hatch from the eggs. The newly hatched **young** are only about 2 to 3 centimetres in size.

Foxes, badgers and martens often dig up the eggs and eat them. Young pond turtles are caught above all by herons and crows. Even more dangerous is humans, who have drained many wetlands and built up waters. In addition, released foreign turtles such as the **red-eared slider** compete with it for food and basking places.

In Switzerland the European pond turtle is threatened with extinction and strictly protected. Natural populations hardly exist any more. In some areas, for example in the canton of Geneva, **reintroduction** projects are under way. For this, new ponds are created and egg-laying sites protected.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water in streams, rivers, lakes and ponds that is not salty.
The body temperature adapts to the surroundings.
A state in winter in which a cold-blooded animal rests almost motionless.
Old enough to have young.

gewusst: Whether a male or a female hatches from an egg depends in its case on the ground temperature.
Pond turtles can pull their head completely back under the shell.

teile.einleitung: Down feathers are the especially soft, fluffy feathers that birds wear under their outer contour feathers. They keep warm so well that people have long used them for quilts, pillows and winter jackets.
wichtigste: Down feathers are soft, fluffy feathers directly on the skin of birds.
They have no firm quill, but many fine little branches.
Air is held between the little branches, which insulates very well against cold.
Water birds such as geese, ducks and eider ducks have especially much down.
Down from geese is often used today to fill warm jackets and quilts.
Newly hatched chicks wear a coat of down.
When buying, you should make sure that the down was not plucked from living animals.

abschnitte.text: A **down feather** is a feather without a firm shaft. From a tiny core, many fine, soft branches grow out on all sides, similar to a dandelion clock. Down feathers sit directly on the skin, under the larger **contour feathers** that shield the bird from the outside. From outside you can therefore hardly see them.

The fine branches hook loosely into one another and form an airy cushion. A lot of **air** is trapped in it, and still air conducts heat very badly. In this way the body warmth of the bird stays close to its skin. The more down fluffs up, the better it insulates, and this is called **fill power**. If down gets wet, however, it collapses and hardly warms at all.

Water birds such as geese, ducks and swans have especially much down because they swim in cold water. Many chicks, for example of ducks and hens, hatch with a fluffy **coat of down**. The eider duck even plucks down from its breast and pads its nest with it. In Iceland people carefully collect this **eiderdown** from abandoned nests, and it is among the most expensive down in the world.

Down is used for **duvets**, pillows, sleeping bags and winter jackets. It is very light and can be compressed a great deal, which is why mountaineers like to take down sleeping bags with them. The down usually comes from geese and ducks that are kept for their meat. Because down warms badly when wet, there are also fillings made of synthetic fibres.

One problem is **live plucking**, in which the feathers are torn out of geese while they are still alive. This is painful for the animals, and in Switzerland it is forbidden. Quality labels on jackets and quilts show whether the down comes from a controlled source. Anyone who wears a down jacket for a long time and looks after it well also spares the animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A soft feather without a firm shaft that sits directly on the skin.
An outer, firm feather that protects the plumage from the outside.
To protect something so that heat or cold hardly gets through.
Plucking out feathers from living animals, which is cruelty to animals.

gewusst: The German word “Daune” comes from the Norse languages and is related to the English word down.
For a down quilt you need the down of many geese.
Without down, many water birds could not survive in ice cold winter water.

teile.einleitung: Fire jellyfish are jellyfish whose touch burns strongly on the skin, almost like fire. The term mainly means the hair jellyfish, which are common in the North Sea and the Baltic Sea. Their long tentacles are covered with thousands of tiny stinging cells.
wichtigste: When you touch a fire jellyfish you usually feel a strong burning on your skin.
“Fire jellyfish” is an everyday name, usually for hair jellyfish of the genus Cyanea.
They belong to the cnidarians, like corals and sea anemones.
With stinging cells on their tentacles, they paralyse their prey.
The yellow hair jellyfish can have very long tentacles.
Jellyfish are almost 99 per cent water.
After contact, it helps to rinse the spot with sea water, not with fresh water.

abschnitte.text: “Fire jellyfish” is not a scientific name but an **everyday name** for strongly stinging jellyfish. It usually means the **hair jellyfish**, especially the yellow hair jellyfish and the blue jellyfish. Like all jellyfish, they have a bell-shaped umbrella and long tentacles. They have neither brain nor heart and consist almost entirely of water.

On the **tentacles** sit countless **stinging cells**. In each one is a coiled tube with poison that shoots out in a flash on contact. In this way fire jellyfish paralyse small fish, crustaceans and other jellyfish. In humans the poison causes burning pain, redness and sometimes weals.

Hair jellyfish live in cool seas of the Northern Hemisphere, for example in the **North Sea** and the Baltic Sea. In summer they often drift onto the beaches in large numbers. Most are about 10 to 40 centimetres wide. The Arctic form of the yellow hair jellyfish, the **lion's mane jellyfish**, however, is regarded as one of the largest jellyfish in the world and can have tentacles over 30 metres long.

Jellyfish have a special **alternation of generations**. From the eggs come small larvae, which settle on the sea floor and become polyps. In spring these polyps bud off tiny jellyfish, which swim away and grow up. Most hair jellyfish live as free-swimming jellyfish for only about a year.

You should not touch fire jellyfish, not even when they lie dead on the beach, because their stinging cells keep working for a while. If you have touched one, rinse the spot with **sea water** and do not rub. Fresh water can set off even more stinging cells. Remains of tentacles are removed carefully, for example with a card, and if the symptoms are severe, you go to a doctor. There are no fire jellyfish in Swiss lakes, where only the tiny, harmless freshwater jellyfish lives.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals with stinging cells that includes jellyfish, corals and sea anemones.
Long, flexible grasping arms with which animals catch prey.
A tiny cell with a poison tube that shoots out on contact.
A stationary life form of cnidarians from which new jellyfish arise.

gewusst: Even torn-off tentacles can still sting.
The lion's mane jellyfish can be longer than a blue whale.
Jellyfish have existed in the seas for over 500 million years.

teile.einleitung: Fish stocking means that people release young fish into a body of water. The aim is to support fish populations or to build up new ones. In Switzerland, stocking has been usual for over a hundred years, but today it is looked at more closely.
wichtigste: In fishing, stocking means that young fish are released into a body of water.
The young fish mostly come from fish farms.
In Switzerland, mainly trout, whitefish and grayling are stocked.
Stocking is meant to make up for a lack of natural reproduction.
Wrong stocking can spread diseases or push out native species.
Today there is more emphasis on natural habitats than on a lot of stocking.

abschnitte.text: In **fish stocking**, fish eggs, larvae or young fish are put into lakes, rivers or streams. The fish are usually raised in **fish farms**. For this, fish ready to spawn are caught in winter, their eggs are collected and left to hatch in hatcheries. Later the young fish are released at selected places.

Many waters have been greatly changed by power stations, straightening and building work. There, **spawning grounds** and hiding places for young fish are often missing. With stocking, people try to keep the number of fish high for fishing. Sometimes they also want to save rare species or rebuild extinct populations.

In Switzerland, the **cantons** and fishing clubs look after stocking. Brown trout, lake trout, whitefish and grayling are especially often stocked. In the large lakes, fish farms have long helped to support whitefish numbers for professional fishing. Which fish may be released is regulated by the laws of the Confederation and the cantons.

Stocking is not always successful, because many farmed fish survive poorly in the wild. If fish from other waters are released, they can change the **genetic diversity** of native populations. Diseases can also be brought in. Non-native species such as the rainbow trout can push out native fish and may therefore no longer be released in many places.

Today the success of stocking in Switzerland is studied more closely, for example with markings and DNA analysis. Many experts say that good habitats are more important than lots of released fish. That is why rivers and streams are **restored**, that is, made more natural again. Where fish can breed well by themselves, stocking is increasingly given up.

begriffe.erklaerung: A facility in which fish are raised from eggs.
A place where fish lay their eggs.
A body of water is made more natural again, with gravel, bends and hiding places.
The differences in the genes within a species, which make it resilient.

gewusst: From a single female trout, over a thousand eggs can be obtained in a farm.
Farmed fish are often worse at recognising enemies than fish that grew up in the wild.
The rainbow trout originally comes from North America.

teile.einleitung: Millipedes are animals with a long body divided into many rings and very many legs. They belong to the myriapods and have two pairs of legs on most body rings. In the forest they are important helpers, because they eat dead leaves and turn them into fertile soil.
wichtigste: Millipedes have two pairs of legs on most body segments.
They usually move slowly with wave-like leg movements.
Most eat dead plant material such as leaves.
When in danger many curl up in a spiral and give off a defensive secretion.
Young millipedes get new segments and legs at every moult.
About 12,000 species have been described worldwide.
Millipedes are not insects and are not to be confused with the predatory centipedes.

abschnitte.text: Millipedes have a head with antennae and a long trunk of many rings. Two rings at a time are fused into a **double segment**, which is why almost every ring carries two pairs of legs. The body is protected with a hard armour of chitin and lime. The name “Tausendfüsser” (thousand footer) usually exaggerates, for many species have only a few dozen up to a good hundred pairs of legs.

Millipedes live almost everywhere in the world in damp, dark places. They are found under leaves, stones, bark and in the soil. Most feed on **dead plant material** such as leaves and rotting wood. In doing so they break down leaves and make the **nutrients** usable again for plants. In winter they retreat to deeper, frost-free layers of the soil.

A millipede moves slowly forwards. Its many legs move in **waves** from back to front along the body. In this way it can push with great force and press through earth and leaves. Millipedes cannot run fast, however.

Predators include hedgehogs, toads, shrews and some birds. When in danger many millipedes curl up in a **spiral**, and the pill millipedes even into a ball. Many have **defensive glands** from which a foul smelling secretion comes. In some large tropical species the secretion can irritate and stain the skin. Some birds rub millipedes into their plumage, because the secretions work against parasites.

In many species the males have modified legs, the **gonopods**, with which they transfer packets of sperm to the female. The female often lays the eggs in small earth hollows or in the soil. The young hatch with only a few pairs of legs. At every **moult** they gain new segments and legs, until they are adult.

Many species also live in Swiss forests and gardens. Common are the black, shiny **snake millipedes** (“Schnurfüsser”), which curl up in a spiral. The pill millipedes look like large woodlice and roll up into a ball. All of them are harmless to humans and very useful for the soil.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two body rings fused together with two pairs of legs in all.
Shedding the old body covering that has become too small as the animal grows.
A gland that gives off an unpleasant substance for defence.
Modified legs of the males that help with mating.
Living things that break down dead plants and animals and turn them into soil.

gewusst: The record holder is a millipede from Australia that was described in 2021 and has over 1,300 legs.
Millipedes are among the first animals that lived on land over 400 million years ago.
A prehistoric relative called Arthropleura grew over two metres long.

teile.einleitung: Flamingos are large, pink waterbirds with long legs, a long neck and a curved beak. They often live in huge colonies on salty lakes and lagoons. They do not have their pink colour from birth, but from their food.
wichtigste: Flamingos form the family Phoenicopteridae and the order Phoenicopteriformes.
Usually six living species of flamingo are distinguished.
The greater flamingo is the largest species, the lesser flamingo the smallest.
The Andean flamingo is regarded as the rarest species.
The pink colour comes from carotenoids in their food.
Flamingos filter their food from the water upside down with their beak.
Their closest relatives are, surprisingly, the grebes.

abschnitte.text: **Flamingos** have very long legs, a long, flexible neck and a beak that is bent downwards. The **greater flamingo** is the largest species and can stand about 1.4 metres tall. The **lesser flamingo** is the smallest species. The plumage is pale pink to bright red, depending on the species, and the wings have black flight feathers. The name comes from the Portuguese or Spanish word “flamengo”, which means flame-coloured, and the genus name Phoenicopterus means crimson-winged.

Usually six species are distinguished: greater flamingo, American flamingo, Chilean flamingo, Andean flamingo, James's flamingo and lesser flamingo. They live in Africa, southern Europe, Asia and Central and South America. The greater flamingo also breeds in Europe, for example in the **Camargue** in southern France and in Spain. The lesser flamingo is the most common species, and as many as around two million animals can gather on the lakes of East Africa. The Andean flamingo lives on salt lakes high in the Andes and is regarded as the rarest species.

Flamingos eat small crustaceans, algae, insect larvae and other tiny living things. To do so, they hold their head upside down in the water and **filter** the food out with fine plates in the beak, rather like a baleen whale. Many of these crustaceans and algae contain **carotenoids**, red and orange pigments. These are stored in the feathers and colour them pink. If flamingos in a zoo are not given food containing pigments, they gradually become pale.

Flamingos live and breed in large **colonies**. They build a cone-shaped mound of mud as a nest and usually lay a single egg on it. Both parents incubate and feed the young one with a red nutritious liquid from the crop, called **crop milk**. The chicks are grey at first and have a straight beak. Later the young birds gather in large groups that are guarded by some adults.

For a long time it was unclear who flamingos are related to. Today the **grebes**, which include the great crested grebe on Swiss lakes, are regarded as their closest relatives. Together they form the group **Mirandornithes**. Several species of flamingo are threatened by water extraction, mining at salt lakes and disturbance at the breeding sites. In Switzerland you see flamingos mainly in zoos, and only very rarely does a single wild bird turn up.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of animals that breed together in one place.
Red and orange pigments that are also found in carrots, for example.
An animal that sieves tiny food out of the water.
A nutritious liquid with which flamingo parents feed their chicks.

gewusst: Flamingos often stand on one leg, probably because they lose less heat that way and need hardly any muscle power.
Flamingos eat with their head down, and their beak is then upside down in the water.
Male flamingos also produce crop milk and feed the chicks with it.

teile.einleitung: The common toad is the most common toad in Switzerland and in Europe. It has a warty, brownish skin and golden eyes. Every spring it migrates in large numbers to the ponds in which it was born itself.
wichtigste: The common toad is an amphibian and is called Bufo bufo scientifically.
Its skin is mostly brownish to grey-brown and warty.
Females grow up to 13 centimetres, while males stay smaller.
It likes best to eat insects, snails and worms.
It spends the winter in winter torpor.
The toad migration takes place in early spring, often at night in rain.
Through metamorphosis, tadpoles turn into small toads.

abschnitte.text: The common toad has a broad, stocky body and a dry, **warty** skin. Its colour is mostly brownish to grey-brown, so that it is well camouflaged on the ground. The eyes shine golden yellow to copper red and have a horizontal pupil. Behind the eyes lie two large glands that produce a poisonous secretion against enemies.

Toads have shorter hind legs than frogs and crawl rather than leap far. The common toad therefore usually moves in small steps. Its skin is drier and warty compared with the smooth, moist skin of frogs. Toads and frogs both belong to the **anurans**.

The common toad hunts mainly at dusk and at night. It likes best to eat insects, snails, worms and spiders. Its sticky **tongue** shoots forward in a flash and seizes the prey. On land it can see quite well and reacts especially to movement.

In early spring, often at night in rain, thousands of common toads migrate to their spawning ponds. They usually return to the pond in which they were born themselves. Because they have to cross roads in doing so, many are run over. In Switzerland volunteers therefore put up **amphibian fences** and carry the animals across the road in buckets, and in some places there are also tunnels under the road.

At the pond the smaller male clasps on to the back of the female. If a male clasps another male by mistake, the latter gives out a squeaking **release call**. The female lays long strings of spawn with several thousand eggs, which she winds round water plants. From them hatch black **tadpoles**, which in a few weeks turn into small toads through metamorphosis.

The natural enemies of the common toad include the grass snake, the hedgehog and various birds. Its skin poison protects it from many predators, and fish too dislike its tadpoles. In autumn the common toad buries itself in the ground or under leaves and falls into **winter torpor**. Because many ponds have disappeared, it has become rarer in many places in Switzerland and is protected by law.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that lives in water and on land, for example a frog, toad or newt.
The eggs of frogs, toads or fish.
The larva of frogs and toads, which lives in water and has a tail.
A state in which cold-blooded animals get through the winter almost motionless.
The transformation from tadpole to toad.

gewusst: A string of common toad spawn can be several metres long.
Common toads can live to over ten years old.
Many common toads migrate over a kilometre every year to their pond.

teile.einleitung: The crown-of-thorns starfish is a large starfish covered in poisonous spines from the Indian and Pacific Oceans. It eats living corals and, in large numbers, can destroy whole coral reefs. That is why it counts as one of the greatest natural threats to reefs such as the Great Barrier Reef.
wichtigste: The crown-of-thorns starfish is a starfish that sometimes destroys coral reefs.
Its scientific name is Acanthaster planci.
It has many arms and is covered in long, poisonous spines.
It eats coral polyps by pushing its stomach out over them.
In population explosions it can eat large parts of a reef bare.
A female can lay many millions of eggs in a season.
Divers fight it by injecting the animals with a lethal solution.

abschnitte.text: The crown-of-thorns starfish is usually 25 to 35 centimetres across, and individual animals grow clearly larger still. It has not just five arms, but often **more than a dozen arms**. Its upper side is covered with **spines** up to five centimetres long. Depending on the region it is red, violet, grey or greenish in colour.

It lives in **tropical coral reefs** from the Red Sea across the Indian Ocean to the Pacific. It is especially well known from the Great Barrier Reef off Australia. During the day it often hides in crevices. In Switzerland you can see it at most in a large aquarium.

The starfish crawls onto a coral and pushes its **stomach** out over it. With digestive juices it dissolves the soft **coral polyps** and sucks them in. All that is left is the white limestone skeleton. A single animal can in this way eat several square metres of coral in a year.

Normally there are only a few crowns-of-thorns in a reef. Since the 1960s, however, there have been repeated **population explosions** with thousands of animals. Possible causes are thought to be fertiliser washed from the land into the sea, which provides food for the larvae, and the catching of their enemies. These enemies include the large **triton's trumpet**, a sea snail, and some fish.

The spines contain a **poison**. Anyone who is pricked by them has severe pain, swelling and sometimes nausea. Divers and snorkellers should therefore never touch the starfish. For healthy people, however, a sting is usually not life threatening.

In Australia and other countries divers search specifically for the starfish. They inject them with a solution of **bile salts** or vinegar, which kills them without harming the reef. Researchers have even developed underwater robots that can recognise the animals. Healthy reefs with many fish are, however, the best protection.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny animal that forms a coral together with many others.
A huge structure of limestone built up by corals in warm sea.
When an animal species multiplies extremely strongly in a short time.
A large sea snail that eats crown-of-thorns starfish.

gewusst: A crown-of-thorns starfish can grow back a lost arm.
In one breeding season a female can release up to about 60 million eggs.
The starfish can survive for several months even without food.

teile.einleitung: Trout are fast, spotted fish that live in cold, clear streams, rivers and lakes. In Switzerland they are among the best-known fish and a popular food fish.
wichtigste: Trout belong to the salmon family.
They need cold, clean, oxygen-rich water.
In Switzerland, brown trout, lake trout and rainbow trout are best known.
The flesh of some trout is pink to orange, depending on their food.
Many people in Switzerland go angling for trout because they are tasty food fish.
A popular way of cooking is trout meunière, dusted in flour and fried.
Trout lay their eggs in the gravel of streams.

abschnitte.text: Trout have a slim, streamlined body and small scales. The native **brown trout** can be recognised by red and black spots with a pale edge. The **rainbow trout** originally comes from North America and has a pink shimmering stripe on its side. The lake trout lives in large lakes and can grow much larger than the brown trout.

Trout live in cool, clear waters with plenty of **oxygen**, for example in mountain streams and rivers. If the water gets too warm in summer, they do badly. In Switzerland they occur from the streams of the Central Plateau up to high in the Alps. In a stream, brown trout often defend a fixed spot behind stones.

Trout are predators and hunt insect larvae, freshwater shrimps, worms and small fish. They also snap up insects that fall onto the surface of the water. The flesh of some trout is pink to orange because they eat crustaceans. These contain red pigments called **carotenoids**.

Brown trout mostly spawn in late autumn and winter. The female beats a pit into the gravel with her tail fin, into which she lays the eggs, the so-called **spawn**. The male fertilises the eggs, and then they are covered with gravel. The young fish hatch after a few weeks and at first still live off the yolk sac.

Many people in Switzerland like to angle for trout, because they are a popular and tasty food fish. Anyone who wants to angle needs a permit for it, the so-called **fishing licence**. A popular way of cooking is trout **meunière**, which is dusted in flour and fried in butter. Many trout in the shops come from fish farms, while wild brown trout have become rarer in some waters.

begriffe.erklaerung: The eggs of fish or frogs.
A family of fish that includes salmon, trout, char and whitefish.
A permit that you need for angling in many waters.
Red and orange pigments that are also found in carrots.

gewusst: Lake trout migrate from the lakes up into the rivers to spawn, like salmon.
In “trout au bleu”, the skin turns bluish when cooked, because the layer of slime on the skin is left intact.

teile.einleitung: Fish fins are the body parts with which fish swim, steer and brake. They are made of thin skin supported by fine rays. Each fin has its own job, rather like the parts of a boat.
wichtigste: Fish move through the water with their fins.
The tail fin gives the fish most of its forward thrust.
The dorsal fin and anal fin stop the fish from tipping over.
Pectoral fins and pelvic fins help with steering, braking and holding still.
A distinction is made between paired fins and unpaired fins.
Fin rays support the thin fin membrane.
Trout and salmon have a small adipose fin without rays.

abschnitte.text: **Fins** are flat, movable body parts of fish. They are made of thin skin supported by **fin rays** of bone or cartilage. In perches such as the perch, some rays are sharp and hard, and are called spiny rays. Other rays are soft and flexible. With muscles the fish can raise, fold and turn its fins.

Fish have two groups of fins. The **paired fins** occur on the left and right: the pectoral fins behind the head and the pelvic fins on the belly. In the history of evolution, they correspond to our arms and legs. The **unpaired fins** lie in the middle of the body: the dorsal fin, anal fin and tail fin. Some fish have two dorsal fins, the perch for example.

In most fish the **tail fin** is the engine. The fish moves its rear body and the tail fin strongly back and forth and so pushes the water backwards. This pushes it forwards. In the carp and the trout, most of the thrust comes about this way. Fast open-sea fish such as the tuna have a narrow, sickle-shaped tail fin for high speed.

The dorsal fin and the anal fin work like the keel of a sailing boat and stop the fish from tipping sideways. With the pectoral fins a fish can brake, turn corners or paddle backwards. A goldfish in an aquarium stays in one place with small movements of its pectoral fins. The pelvic fins help with going up and down and with hovering calmly. In this way all the fins work together.

Trout, salmon and grayling have a small **adipose fin** without rays between the dorsal fin and the tail. Flying fish have huge pectoral fins with which they glide over the surface of the water. Seahorses swim mainly with their fluttering dorsal fin. In the ray, the pectoral fins are so broad that they look like wings. In some bred goldfish, the fins are so long that they look almost like veils.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin rod that supports the fin membrane like the spokes of an umbrella.
Fins that occur on the left and right of the body, that is, pectoral and pelvic fins.
Fins in the middle of the body, that is, dorsal, anal and tail fins.
A small fin without rays in trout and salmon.

gewusst: From the paired fins of ancient fish, the legs of the first land animals developed about 370 million years ago.
Flying fish can glide several dozen metres through the air with their large pectoral fins.
Seahorses beat their small dorsal fin very fast, but they are still among the slowest fish.

teile.einleitung: The German wasp is one of the best known species of wasp and is also very common in Switzerland. In late summer it likes to visit cake, ice cream and sweet drinks, but it is also a hard working insect hunter.
wichtigste: The German wasp is a common species of wasp in Switzerland.
Its scientific name is Vespula germanica.
It has a black and yellow pattern and belongs to the short-faced wasps.
It builds its nest from a kind of paper, often in holes in the ground or dark cavities.
A wasp colony lives only one summer, and only the young queens survive the winter.
It feeds its larvae with insects, so it is also useful in the garden.
Unlike the honey bee, it can sting several times.

abschnitte.text: The German wasp has the typical **black and yellow** warning colours. Workers grow about 12 to 16 millimetres long, queens up to about 2 centimetres. On its yellow face it usually has three small black dots, by which it can be told apart from the very similar **common wasp**. Between the thorax and the abdomen it has the narrow wasp waist.

The German wasp lives in gardens, parks, at the edge of woods and in the middle of towns. It often builds its nest in **abandoned mouse holes** in the ground or in dark cavities such as roller shutter boxes and attics. To do so it chews wood fibres with saliva into a mass that, when dry, looks like grey **paper**. Originally it lives in Europe, North Africa and Asia, but with humans it also reached North America, Australia and New Zealand.

In spring a **queen**, who has survived the winter alone, founds a new nest. She lays the first eggs and raises the first workers. By late summer the colony grows to several thousand animals. Then young queens and males hatch, and they mate. In autumn the old queen and all the workers die, and the nest is not used again.

Adult wasps feed on **sugar**, for example from nectar, ripe fruit and plant sap. Their larvae, by contrast, are fed with chewed up **insects** such as flies, caterpillars and mosquitoes. In this way a wasp colony eats large amounts of other insects in summer. In late summer there are fewer larvae to look after, so the workers then search especially greedily for sweet things and end up at our dining table.

Wasps usually sting only when they feel threatened, for example when you hit out at them. Staying calm and walking slowly away is therefore best. Drinks should be covered outdoors and drunk through a straw, so that you do not swallow a wasp. For people with an **allergy** a sting can be dangerous, and they need medical help at once. A nest in an awkward place should be removed only by an expert.

begriffe.erklaerung: Conspicuous colours such as black and yellow that warn enemies of poison or stings.
The only female in the colony that lays eggs.
A female wasp that builds, looks for food and cares for the larvae.
The young form of an insect, which still looks quite different from the adult animal.

gewusst: Wasps were the first paper makers, long before humans invented paper.
The sting of the wasp has no barbs, so it does not stay stuck in the skin.
Only female wasps have a sting, and the males cannot sting.

teile.einleitung: The Gallic rooster is a well-known symbol of France. You see it on the shirts of sportswomen and sportsmen, on monuments and on old coins. Behind the symbol lies a funny pun from the Latin language.
wichtigste: The Gallic rooster is a well-known national symbol of France.
In Latin, the word “gallus” means both rooster and Gaul.
The Gauls were the Celtic inhabitants of ancient France in Roman times.
The rooster stands for courage, pride and watchfulness.
You can see it, for example, on the shirts of French sports teams.
The official emblem of the French Republic, however, is Marianne.
The rooster is the male of the domestic chicken.

abschnitte.text: The **Gallic rooster** is an emblem of France, much as the edelweiss or the Matterhorn stand for Switzerland. It is not an official state symbol, but it is known throughout the country and around the world. The official emblem of the French Republic is **Marianne**, a female figure. The rooster is used mainly in sport and at celebrations.

About 2,000 years ago, the Romans called the area of present-day France **Gaul** and its inhabitants Gauls. In Latin, “gallus” means both “rooster” and “Gaul”. Even the Romans made fun of this pun. Later the French proudly adopted the rooster as their own sign.

During the **French Revolution** from 1789, the rooster became popular as a sign of the people. It appeared on flags, coins and seals. After the First World War, many French communities put up monuments with a rooster. It stands for courage, pride and **watchfulness**, because the rooster is the first to crow in the morning.

Today you see the Gallic rooster mainly on the **shirts** of French national teams. The French national football team wears it in its badge on the chest. Rugby players and many other sports teams also use it as an emblem. Fans sometimes even bring rooster costumes or rooster figures to the stadium.

The rooster is the male of the **domestic chicken**, and the female is called a hen. It has a red comb, wattles and often magnificent, glossy tail feathers. With its loud crowing it marks its territory. In Switzerland, too, you see roosters not only on farms but as a **weathercock** on many church towers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sign that stands for something bigger, for example for a country.
The Celtic peoples who lived in the area of present-day France in Roman times.
A female figure that is the official emblem of the French Republic.
A rooster figure on roofs or church towers that shows where the wind is blowing from.

gewusst: The Belgian region of Wallonia also has a rooster as its heraldic animal.
Gauls such as Asterix and Obelix are invented comic characters, but the Gauls themselves really existed.

teile.einleitung: Dolphins are clever, playful marine mammals that look like fish but breathe air. They live in groups, communicate with whistles and find their prey with echolocation, a kind of ultrasound.
wichtigste: Dolphins are mammals and belong to the whales.
They breathe air through a blowhole on top of the head.
Their body is streamlined so that they can swim fast.
With clicking sounds and echolocation they find prey even in murky water.
Every dolphin has its own signature whistle, which works like a name.
A group of dolphins is called a school.
Baby dolphins are born tail first.
Dolphins need clean water, which is why protecting the seas is important.

abschnitte.text: Dolphins have a **streamlined** body, a dorsal fin and a horizontal tail fin, the fluke. Many species have a long snout with many **pointed teeth**, with which they hold slippery prey but do not chew it. There are over 30 species, from small species about 1.5 metres long to the orca, the largest dolphin. The best known is the bottlenose dolphin, which can grow to about 4 metres long.

Dolphins live in almost all the seas of the world, especially in warm and temperate waters. Some dolphins even live in rivers, for example in the Amazon. Because they are mammals, they have to come regularly to the surface to take in air through their **blowhole**. When sleeping, only one half of their brain rests at a time, while the other stays awake and makes sure that they keep breathing.

Dolphins give out quick **clicking sounds** and listen to the echo that comes back from fish or rocks. In this way they recognise the size, shape and distance of their prey, even in murky water. This ability is called **echolocation**. For communication they use whistles, and every dolphin has its own **signature whistle**, with which it introduces itself as if with a name.

Dolphins eat mainly fish and squid. They often hunt as a team: they circle a **shoal of fish** and drive it tightly together so that they can snap at it more easily. Dolphin mothers show their calves how to catch fish. Large sharks and orcas can be dangerous to dolphins.

Dolphins live in groups that are called a **school**. A dolphin calf is born tail first, so that it does not want to take a breath too early under water. Then the mother swims it to the surface for its first breath. The young animal drinks its mother's milk and usually stays with its mother for several years. Dolphins like to play: they leap, surf in waves and even blow **air rings** that they play with.

Many dolphins die as bycatch in fishing nets. Polluted water, plastic and underwater noise from ships also cause them problems. Dolphins need **clean water** to live, which is why protecting the seas is so important. Switzerland has banned the import of dolphins, and since 2013 no dolphins have been kept here.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal whose young drink their mother's milk, for example dolphin, dog and human.
Finding your way by sounds and their echo, as bats do.
A whistle of its own by which other dolphins recognise a dolphin.
The horizontal tail fin of whales and dolphins.
Animals that end up in fishing nets unintentionally.

gewusst: The orca, also called the killer whale, is actually the largest dolphin.
Dolphins sleep with only one half of the brain while the other stays awake.
Dolphins have ancestors that lived on land about 50 million years ago.

teile.einleitung: A fin is a flat body part with which animals move and steer in the water. Fish have fins, but whales, dolphins, seals and penguins also have fin-like limbs. Even people put on fins when they dive or snorkel.
wichtigste: In the water, fins are used for propulsion, steering and braking.
In fish such as the lake trout and salmon, the tail fin mainly provides propulsion.
Fish have paired and unpaired fins.
Whales, dolphins, seals and penguins also have fins, although they are not fish.
The fins of these animals developed independently of one another.
Fish tail fins stand upright, the tail flukes of whales horizontally.
Divers use artificial swim fins to swim faster.

abschnitte.text: Fish have several **fins** supported by fine fin rays. The pectoral and pelvic fins occur in pairs, the dorsal, anal and tail fins only singly. The lake trout and the salmon use mainly their **tail fin** for propulsion. With powerful strokes to the left and right, they push themselves forward against the current. The other fins help with steering and keep the fish balanced.

Whales and dolphins are mammals that have returned to the water. Their front legs have turned into **flippers** in which you can still find bones like those in a hand. The tail fin is called a **fluke** and is made not of bone but of firm connective tissue. It stands horizontally and is moved up and down, quite unlike in fish. Many whales and dolphins also have a dorsal fin.

In seals, arms and legs have become flippers with which they swim elegantly. Harbour seals propel themselves with the rear flippers, sea lions more with the front ones. Penguins are birds, and their wings have developed into hard, narrow **flipper-wings**. With them they literally fly under water. Sea turtles also paddle with fin-like legs.

Fish, whales, penguins and seals are not closely related and yet have similar fins. Experts call this **convergent evolution**. Life in the water makes the same demands everywhere, so similar shapes arise. The body, too, often becomes streamlined like a torpedo. This helps to lose as little energy as possible against the resistance of the water.

People have no fins, so they invented artificial **swim fins**. With them the area of the feet is increased, and you get forward faster with less effort. Divers, snorkellers and lifeguards use them. In finswimming there are even competitions with a single broad **monofin**, which is reminiscent of a dolphin's tail. The idea of strapping fins to the feet was already had by the young Benjamin Franklin in the 18th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: A flat body part for swimming and steering in water.
The horizontal tail fin of whales and dolphins.
When unrelated animals independently develop similar features.
A body shape that lets water or air flow easily round it.

gewusst: From the pattern of the fluke, individual humpback whales can be recognised like people by their fingerprints.
In a whale's flipper are five finger bones, like in our hand.
The young Benjamin Franklin made himself swim fins out of wood for his hands.

teile.einleitung: Grooming means that animals keep their fur clean, smooth and healthy. Some clean themselves, while others groom one another and so strengthen their friendship. Pets such as dogs, cats and horses also sometimes need help from people with this.
wichtigste: Grooming keeps the fur clean and free of parasites.
A cat spends several hours a day cleaning itself.
Cats clean themselves with their rough tongue, which has fine little hooks.
In monkeys, mutual grooming is important for the community.
Dogs, horses and long-haired cats have to be brushed regularly.
During the moult in spring and autumn, many animals lose especially many hairs.

abschnitte.text: Well-kept fur protects against cold, wet and sun. During cleaning, dirt, loose hairs and **parasites** such as fleas are removed. In addition, the animal spreads skin oil that makes the fur water-repellent. Matted or dirty fur, on the other hand, can itch and lead to skin diseases.

A cat spends several hours a day cleaning itself. Its **tongue** is covered with many small, backward-pointing hooks that work like a comb. When cleaning, the cat swallows loose hairs, which it sometimes brings up again as a **hairball**. Cleaning also calms cats and helps them cool down on hot days.

Many sociable animals groom one another, which is called **social grooming**. Monkeys such as chimpanzees or baboons pick through one another's fur for hours and so show who is friends with whom. Horses nibble each other on the neck and back, where they cannot reach themselves. This grooming reduces stress and strengthens the bonds within the group.

Dogs with long fur should be **brushed** regularly so that no tangles form. Horses are curried before riding and their hooves are picked out. Long-haired cats such as Persians often cannot manage grooming on their own and need help every day. Bathing too often, on the other hand, is usually bad, because it removes the skin's natural layer of oil.

In spring many animals lose their thick **winter coat**, and in autumn it grows back. At this time daily brushing helps especially much. For children, brushing is a lovely way of building trust with an animal. You should be gentle and stop if the animal becomes restless.

begriffe.erklaerung: Small animals such as fleas or ticks that live on other animals and harm them.
When animals clean one another and so strengthen their relationship.
A lump of swallowed hair in the stomach that cats often bring up again.
The change between a thick winter coat and a thinner summer coat.

gewusst: In some monkeys, mutual grooming lasts several hours every day.
Cats often clean themselves straight after being stroked, to restore their own smell.
Many birds take a dust or water bath to look after their plumage.

tpy52bq.t: The Wolf and the Seven Young Kids

teile.einleitung: The Wolf and the Seven Young Kids is a well known fairy tale by the Brothers Grimm. In it a cunning wolf tries to eat seven young goats while their mother fetches food in the forest.
wichtigste: The Wolf and the Seven Young Kids is a fairy tale by the Brothers Grimm.
It appeared in 1812 in the first volume of their Children's and Household Tales.
In it a wolf wants to eat seven young goats.
With chalk he makes his voice fine and with flour he makes his paw white.
Only the youngest kid hides in the clock case and escapes.
The mother rescues her children from the wolf's belly.
The fairy tale warns children not to open the door to strangers.

abschnitte.text: An old nanny goat has to go into the forest and warns her **seven kids** about the wolf. The wolf knocks, but the children recognise him by his rough voice. He eats **chalk** so that his voice sounds finer, and has dough and flour spread on his black paw. Now the kids open up, and the wolf swallows six of them. Only the youngest has hidden in the **clock case**.

The mother comes home and finds the wolf asleep under a tree. She cuts open his belly, and all six kids jump out alive, because the wolf had swallowed them whole. Then they fill his belly with **stones** and sew it up again. When the thirsty wolf wants to drink at the well, the heavy stones pull him in and he drowns. The kids dance with joy round the well.

**Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm** were two brothers and language scholars from Hesse in Germany. They collected fairy tales that people told one another and from 1812 published them as the **Children's and Household Tales**. In them are also Little Red Riding Hood, Hansel and Gretel and Snow White. The collection of fairy tales is today part of the UNESCO Memory of the World register.

The fairy tale shows children that they should **not simply open the door to strangers**, even if they sound friendly. It also shows that a villain can disguise himself and use tricks. At the same time it gives courage: the smallest kid is clever and helps to save everyone. As in many fairy tales, evil is punished in the end.

In the fairy tale the wolf is the villain, but real wolves are shy wild animals that mostly avoid humans. In Switzerland the wolf was wiped out for a long time and has been returning from Italy since 1995. Today several hundred **wolves** live again in many packs, for example in the cantons of Graubünden and Valais. Because they sometimes kill sheep and goats, farmers protect their flocks with fences and **livestock guardian dogs**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss and southern German word for a female goat.
A young kid.
The tall wooden case of a grandfather clock in which the pendulum swings.
A large dog that lives with a flock of sheep and protects it from wolves.

gewusst: In the Children's and Household Tales the fairy tale has the number 5.
In the fairy tale the wolf eats chalk to disguise his voice, which of course does not work in reality.
The fairy tales of the Brothers Grimm are among the most translated books in the German language.

teile.einleitung: The gallop is the fastest gait of a horse. The horse moves forward in powerful bounds and for a brief moment has all four hooves in the air. In horse racing, horses reach breathtaking speeds at the gallop.
wichtigste: The fastest gait of a horse is called the gallop.
Horses have three basic gaits: walk, trot and gallop.
The gallop is a three-beat gait with a short moment of suspension.
In the moment of suspension, no hoof touches the ground.
A distinction is made between the right-lead gallop and the left-lead gallop.
Racehorses can reach over 60 kilometres per hour at the gallop.
Only photographs from the year 1878 proved exactly how a gallop works.

abschnitte.text: A **gait** is the way a horse moves its legs. Horses have three basic gaits: the leisurely **walk**, the springy trot and the fast gallop. The gallop is the fastest of them and in nature is used mainly for escape. A relaxed canter is often more comfortable for riders than a bumpy trot.

The gallop is a gait in **three beats**, so you hear three hoofbeats one after another. First one hind leg lands, then at the same time the other hind leg and the diagonally opposite front leg, and last the second front leg. After that comes the **moment of suspension**, in which all four hooves are in the air. Depending on which front leg reaches further forward, people speak of a right-lead gallop or a left-lead gallop.

A normal gallop on a hack is about 20 to 30 kilometres per hour. At full speed it becomes the **racing gallop**, in which the rhythm turns into four beats. English thoroughbreds then reach over 60 kilometres per hour. Over short distances, quarter horses are even faster.

For a long time people argued about whether a galloping horse ever has all four hooves in the air at the same time. With the naked eye, nobody could tell. In 1878, **Eadweard Muybridge** photographed a horse one after another with several cameras. His series of pictures proved the moment of suspension and is regarded as a forerunner of **film**.

In **flat races**, horses with jockeys compete against each other on a racecourse. In Switzerland there are races in Frauenfeld, Aarau, Dielsdorf and Avenches, for example. World famous is the **White Turf** race in St. Moritz, which takes place in winter on the frozen lake. There the horses gallop over snow and ice.

begriffe.erklaerung: The way a horse places its legs when moving.
A rhythm with three beats that repeat.
The moment when no hoof touches the ground.
A rider in horse races.

gewusst: Besides walk, trot and gallop, Icelandic horses have further gaits such as the tölt.
Muybridge's series of pictures of horses in motion are regarded as important forerunners of the cinema film.

teile.einleitung: The hawksbill turtle is a sea turtle that lives in tropical coral reefs all over the world. Its shell is beautifully patterned, and that was exactly what proved its undoing: in the past it was often hunted for this pattern. Today it is critically endangered and strictly protected.
wichtigste: The hawksbill turtle is a sea turtle of the tropics.
In the past it was often hunted for the beautiful pattern of its shell.
From its shell plates, tortoiseshell was made for combs, glasses and jewellery.
Its mouth is pointed and curved like a bird's beak.
It eats mainly sponges that grow in coral reefs.
According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), it is regarded as critically endangered.
International trade in tortoiseshell has been banned for decades.

abschnitte.text: The hawksbill turtle usually grows 60 to 90 centimetres long and weighs about 40 to 80 kilograms. The horny plates on its shell overlap like **roof tiles**. They are mottled brown, yellow and orange and gleam beautifully. Its head is narrow with a curved, pointed **beak**, with which it looks for food in crevices.

It lives in warm seas in the Atlantic, the Indian Ocean and the Pacific. It likes best to stay in **coral reefs**, lagoons and on rocky coasts. Young animals drift for the first years in the open sea among seaweed. Later hawksbill turtles often travel long distances between feeding grounds and nesting beaches.

The hawksbill turtle eats mainly **sponges**, which it pulls out of reef crevices with its beak. Some sponges contain glass needles and toxins, but it hardly minds. In addition it eats jellyfish, sea anemones and algae. Because it keeps sponges in check, corals have more room to grow, and that helps the reef.

The females come at night to **sandy beaches**, often to the beach where they hatched themselves. They dig a hole and usually lay over a hundred eggs in it. After about two months the little turtles hatch and run straight into the sea. The temperature in the sand determines whether an egg becomes a male or a female.

From the horny plates of the shell, **tortoiseshell** was made in the past. Combs, hair slides, glasses frames and jewellery boxes were made from it. For this, millions of animals were killed over many centuries. Since 1977 the species has been strictly protected under the **Washington Convention on endangered species (CITES)**, and international trade is banned.

Despite the ban, the hawksbill turtle is still poached in some regions. Further dangers are built up beaches, plastic waste, fishing nets and the dying of coral reefs. Conservationists guard nesting beaches and count the nests. Tourists should not buy souvenirs made of tortoiseshell, because importing them into Switzerland is forbidden.

begriffe.erklaerung: The horn from the shell plates of hawksbill turtles, formerly used for jewellery.
A simple animal without organs that lives attached to the sea floor.
An international treaty that regulates trade in endangered animals and plants, also called CITES.
The place where an animal lays its eggs.

gewusst: In 2015 researchers discovered that a hawksbill turtle glowed red and green under water in the light of a special lamp.
The name “hawksbill” means hawk's beak, because of its pointed mouth.
Many glasses and combs that look like tortoiseshell today are in fact made of plastic.

teile.einleitung: An exoskeleton is a hard skeleton on the outside of the body, like a suit of armour. Insects, spiders, crustaceans and millipedes all have this kind of outer skeleton. We humans, by contrast, have our skeleton on the inside, beneath muscles and skin.
wichtigste: An exoskeleton is an outer skeleton.
All arthropods such as insects, spiders, crustaceans and millipedes have an exoskeleton.
It consists mainly of chitin.
It protects the body and gives it support.
Because it does not grow with the animal, the animals have to moult.
We humans have an inner skeleton made of bones.
Machines that help people to carry things or to walk are also called exoskeletons.

abschnitte.text: An **exoskeleton** is a hard shell that surrounds an animal's whole body. The garden spider wears its hard outer skeleton on the outside of its body, quite unlike us. Woodlice, millipedes, beetles and crustaceans also have this kind of outer skeleton. All these animals belong to the **arthropods**, the group of animals with the most species on Earth.

The exoskeleton consists mainly of **chitin**, a tough, light substance, and of proteins. In crustaceans and woodlice, lime is also stored in it, which makes the shell especially hard. On the outside there is often a thin layer of wax that stops the animal from drying out. At the joints the shell is thin and flexible, so that the legs can move.

The outer skeleton protects the soft organs from injuries and enemies, like armour. The **muscles** attach to it on the inside, so that the animal can move. It keeps water inside the body and protects against drying out. In many beetles it also forms the hard wing cases.

An exoskeleton cannot grow with the animal. An arthropod therefore has to **moult** again and again. A new, soft skin forms under the old shell, then the old one splits open and the animal slips out. The empty shell is called an **exuvia**, and until the new shell is hard, the animal is vulnerable.

Humans and all other vertebrates have an **endoskeleton**, that is, an inner skeleton made of bones. It grows with the body and allows large bodies. An exoskeleton would become very heavy in large land animals. That is why insects and spiders on land are mostly small, while in the water some crustaceans grow quite large.

Engineers also build exoskeletons, as devices that people wear on the body. Such robot suits help workers, for example, to lift heavy loads. People with a spinal cord injury can use them in therapy to practise taking steps again. Research on such devices is carried out at ETH Zurich and other universities.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals with an outer skeleton and jointed legs, such as insects and spiders.
A hard, light substance that the outer skeleton is made of.
Shedding the old shell that has become too small.
A skeleton inside the body, as in us humans.

gewusst: The Japanese spider crab has an exoskeleton and, with its legs stretched out, can be over three metres wide.
Some insects eat their old shell after moulting, to reuse the valuable substances.

teile.einleitung: The European beaver is a large rodent that can grow almost a metre long and fells whole trees. With branches, mud and stones it builds dams and lodges in rivers and streams. Hardly any other animal changes its surroundings as much as it does.
wichtigste: The beaver is the largest rodent in Europe and without its tail can grow almost a metre long.
With its sharp gnawing teeth it fells trees.
With branches it builds dams and lodges in rivers.
The entrance to the beaver lodge lies under water.
With dams the beaver dams up streams into ponds.
Beavers are pure herbivores.
Through its constructions habitats arise for many other animals.

abschnitte.text: The beaver has four large, orange **gnawing teeth**. The colour comes from iron in the enamel, which makes the teeth especially hard. Because the teeth keep growing, they do not wear down when gnawing. A beaver can fell a thin tree in a single night, and thick trees it gnaws at over several nights.

Beavers live in an **earth burrow** in the bank or in a **beaver lodge**. A lodge is a large heap of branches, twigs and mud. Inside lies a dry living chamber above the water level. The entrance lies under water so that enemies such as foxes cannot get in.

If a stream is too shallow, the beaver builds a **dam** of branches, stones, mud and plant parts. In this way it dams the water up into a pond so that the entrance to its lodge always lies under water. Dams can be many metres long and are constantly repaired. In the water the beaver can also transport wood safely to its lodge.

In summer beavers eat herbs, grasses and water plants. In winter they feed on bark and twigs, which they store under water as a supply. A beaver family consists of the parents and the young of the last two years. The young are born in spring and can swim after only a few days.

Through the beaver ponds new **wetlands** arise with pools, dead wood and clearings. There dragonflies, frogs, fish, birds and many plants find room. That is why the beaver is called an ecosystem engineer. The dams also hold back water and can thus help in times of drought.

In Switzerland the beaver was exterminated at the beginning of the 19th century and resettled from 1956. Today it lives on many rivers and lakes in the Central Plateau, for example on the Aare, Reuss, Thur and Rhine. Sometimes there is trouble when beavers flood fields or undermine bank paths. Then specialists help to find solutions for people and beavers together.

begriffe.erklaerung: A structure of branches and mud in which the beaver family lives.
A bank that dams up water.
An area with a lot of water, such as a marsh or pond.
An animal that changes its surroundings so that new habitats arise.

gewusst: The longest known beaver dam is in Canada and is around 850 metres long.
Beavers can close their nose and ears when diving and draw their lips together behind the gnawing teeth so that no water gets into the mouth.

teile.einleitung: The elk is the largest species of deer in the world. With its long legs, its hanging upper lip and the huge palmate antlers of the males, it is unmistakable. It lives in the cool forests of the north, for example in Scandinavia, Russia and Canada.
wichtigste: The elk belongs to the deer family and is called Alces alces scientifically.
It is the largest species of deer in the world.
Males carry large, flat, palmate antlers.
A female elk is called a cow.
Its habitat is often the taiga, a northern coniferous forest.
In autumn is the rutting season, and then the bulls bellow.
Elks can swim very well, even over longer distances.

abschnitte.text: A bull elk can reach a shoulder height of over two metres and usually weighs between 400 and 600 kilograms. The coat is dark brown to blackish brown, and the legs are paler. Typical are the broad, overhanging upper lip and a flap of skin on the neck that is called the **“Bart”** (beard or bell). The **palmate antlers** of the bulls can have a spread of more than 1.5 metres and are shed every winter.

Elks live in the northern forests of Europe, Asia and North America. This belt of coniferous forests is called the **taiga**. They like to stay near swamps, lakes and rivers. The animals in Europe and Asia are called the **Eurasian elk**, and in North America the elk is called moose. In the past elks also lived in Central Europe, and today they are found, for example, in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Poland and Russia.

Elks are plant eaters and eat many kilograms of food a day. In summer they eat leaves, herbs and water plants, for which they even dive under. In winter they especially like to nibble **twigs** and bark of trees such as willows, birches and pines. As ruminants they chew their food several times.

In autumn is the elk's **rutting season**. Then the bulls bellow loudly and fight with their antlers for the females. In spring the cow gives birth to one or two calves, which are coloured reddish brown. The calves stay with their mother for about a year, until the next young is born.

Natural enemies of the elk are **wolves** and bears, which attack mainly young, old or sick animals. A healthy elk defends itself with powerful kicks of its front legs, which can badly injure a wolf. Often it also flees into the water, where as a good swimmer it has the advantage. For drivers, elks on roads are a danger, which is why in Scandinavia many signs warn of them.

In Scandinavia the elk is a popular symbolic animal and is also hunted there. Well known is the so called **elk test**, in which cars have to carry out a sudden evasive manoeuvre. In Switzerland no elks live in the wild. But you can watch them in some animal parks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge coniferous forest in the cool north of the Earth.
The mating season in deer, in which the males court the females.
Broad, flat antlers that look like a shovel.
A plant eater that brings its food back up and chews it again.

gewusst: An elk can dive under for up to a minute for water plants.
The huge antlers of a bull elk grow back completely new every year.
The name elk test comes from an evasion test with cars in Sweden.

teile.einleitung: The Eurasian beaver is the largest rodent in Europe and lives on streams, rivers and lakes. It is the beaver that is native to Europe and thus also to Switzerland. After it had been exterminated in Switzerland, it is back today and spreading again.
wichtigste: The Eurasian beaver is called Castor fiber scientifically.
It is native to Europe and thus also to Switzerland.
It is the largest rodent in Europe.
Besides it there is only one other species of beaver, the North American beaver in North America.
In Switzerland the beaver was exterminated at the beginning of the 19th century.
From 1956 beavers were released again in Switzerland.
In a count in 2022 around 4,900 beavers lived in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Including the tail, the Eurasian beaver grows over a metre long and can weigh up to about 30 kilograms. It has a dense, brown coat that keeps it warm and dry in the water. Its flat, scaly tail is called the **paddle** and serves as a rudder and fat store. Between the toes of the hind feet it has **webbing**.

In the past the Eurasian beaver lived almost everywhere in Europe and in the north of Asia. Because of its fur, its meat and **castoreum** it was hunted heavily. Around 1900 only a few remnant populations were left, for example on the Elbe, on the Rhône in France and in Norway. Thanks to protection and reintroductions it lives again today in many countries.

There are two species of beaver worldwide: the Eurasian and the **North American beaver**. Both look very similar but have a different number of chromosomes and cannot reproduce with each other. In Finland North American beavers were once released, and they have spread there. In Switzerland only the Eurasian beaver lives.

In Switzerland the beaver disappeared at the beginning of the 19th century. From 1956 to 1977 beavers were released at various places, above all animals from France and Norway. Since 1962 it has been **protected** in Switzerland.
